items.title: What smart people are saying about an AI-assisted theory of quantum gravity
items.summary: A physicist published a paper that may have united Einstein's theory of general relativity with quantum mechanics. Lambert/Keystone/Getty Images First AI came for mathematics, and now it's coming for physics. A physicist at Stanford said he made progress on unifying two theories of the universe with AI. Physics professionals have questioned the results, and the paper is not yet peer-reviewed. A scientist using ChatGPT's Astra model may have made progress on the biggest unsolved problems in physics. And people have thoughts. Venkatesa Chandrasekaran, a physicist at Stanford who is also employed at OpenAI, published a paper on Wednesday that claims to make strides on unifying two dueling theories that govern how the universe works . Chandrasekaran said he arrived at several calculations "through detailed, back and forth collaboration with GPT-6 Astra" and spent about 400 million tokens — the units of data AI models process and how AI companies charge for compute. On one side is general relativity: a blueprint for gravity masterminded by Albert Einstein in 1916. Broadly, it explains how planetary-sized objects bend the fabric of space and time, thereby creating the attractive force of gravity. On the other side is quantum mechanics, a dense web of equations describing the behavior of particles smaller than the atom. Though the two theories work in their respective domains, combining them into a unified framework has proven difficult. Physicists have spent about a century knocking their heads together to do that. Chandrasekaran's paper, which has yet to be peer-reviewed, puts forth a mathematical theory that he says combines the theories in limited conditions. The paper's claims — and the fact that OpenAI helped produce it — have roiled physicists and tech bros alike. Many called it bunk, while others said its propositions are illuminating. Here's what smart people are saying. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Sam Altman congratulated tktk for his work. Spencer Platt/Getty Images In an X post, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman congratulated Chandrasekaran for his work and said he was one of the "earliest believers that we could use our then-current model to solve millennium prize problems ." "Being brilliant and also having correctly-placed confidence and courage to keep pushing on something that others don't think is possible is a very valuable thing and fairly rare," he wrote on X. In the acknowledgments section of the paper, Chandrasekaran thanked Altman and others at the company for providing for his compute usage and "encouragement throughout the project." Jonathan Oppenheim, physics professor Jonathan Oppenheim, a professor of physics at University College London, poured cold water on the significance of Chandrasekaran's research. In a Substack post, Oppenheim wrote the paper "doesn't even come close to establishing a quantum theory of gravity." Oppenheim said the proposed unification was a false alarm and added that he dispatched a swarm of Claude agents to check it. He said the agents identified more than a dozen issues with the paper. "We will keep getting false alarms like this one unless we find other ways to separate signal from slop," Oppenheim wrote. Peter Woit, mathematician at Columbia University Peter Woit, a mathematician at Columbia University, said the paper's findings did not check out or advance the field in any way. He called it a "publicity stunt" by OpenAI. "It's more OpenAI worthless slop ," Woit wrote on his website. "For physics theory claims like this one, there's no reason to believe there's anything worthwhile there," he added. Woit said he's reviewed thousands of papers making "similar claims" about quantum gravity and none have checked out. "The only different thing about this one is that it's written by a machine and funded by a company that now has a track record of putting out misleading claims about physics," he wrote. Hontas Farmer, theoretical astrophysicist Hontas Farmer, a theoretical astrophysicist and professor at Chicago State University, said that while the paper checks out, it doesn't add anything to the conversation. "It does not propose anything testable," she wrote on X. "It overlaps with many already published and or pre-printed ideas." She said " AI boosters " are stoking hype for the paper, calling it "THE SOLUTION." Nirmalya Kajuri, theoretical physicist Nirmalya Kajuri, a theoretical physicist and science writer, said the paper doesn't solve quantum gravity, though it does make advancements toward the theory. In a Substack post, he said in pre-AI days , a paper like this one wouldn't have gotten a lot of attention. "It's an interesting project," he said. "Let us wait for another 400 milli tokens to see where it goes!" Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
A physicist published a paper that may have united Einstein's theory of general relativity with quantum mechanics.

Lambert/Keystone/Getty Images

  • First AI came for mathematics, and now it's coming for physics.
  • A physicist at Stanford said he made progress on unifying two theories of the universe with AI.
  • Physics professionals have questioned the results, and the paper is not yet peer-reviewed.

A scientist using ChatGPT's Astra model may have made progress on the biggest unsolved problems in physics.

And people have thoughts.

Venkatesa Chandrasekaran, a physicist at Stanford who is also employed at OpenAI, published a paper on Wednesday that claims to make strides on unifying two dueling theories that govern how the universe works.

Chandrasekaran said he arrived at several calculations "through detailed, back and forth collaboration with GPT-6 Astra" and spent about 400 million tokens — the units of data AI models process and how AI companies charge for compute.

On one side is general relativity: a blueprint for gravity masterminded by Albert Einstein in 1916. Broadly, it explains how planetary-sized objects bend the fabric of space and time, thereby creating the attractive force of gravity.

On the other side is quantum mechanics, a dense web of equations describing the behavior of particles smaller than the atom.

Though the two theories work in their respective domains, combining them into a unified framework has proven difficult. Physicists have spent about a century knocking their heads together to do that.

Chandrasekaran's paper, which has yet to be peer-reviewed, puts forth a mathematical theory that he says combines the theories in limited conditions.

The paper's claims — and the fact that OpenAI helped produce it — have roiled physicists and tech bros alike. Many called it bunk, while others said its propositions are illuminating.

Here's what smart people are saying.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman
Sam Altman congratulated tktk for his work.

Spencer Platt/Getty Images

In an X post, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman congratulated Chandrasekaran for his work and said he was one of the "earliest believers that we could use our then-current model to solve millennium prize problems."

"Being brilliant and also having correctly-placed confidence and courage to keep pushing on something that others don't think is possible is a very valuable thing and fairly rare," he wrote on X.

In the acknowledgments section of the paper, Chandrasekaran thanked Altman and others at the company for providing for his compute usage and "encouragement throughout the project."

Jonathan Oppenheim, physics professor

Jonathan Oppenheim, a professor of physics at University College London, poured cold water on the significance of Chandrasekaran's research.

In a Substack post, Oppenheim wrote the paper "doesn't even come close to establishing a quantum theory of gravity."

Oppenheim said the proposed unification was a false alarm and added that he dispatched a swarm of Claude agents to check it. He said the agents identified more than a dozen issues with the paper.

"We will keep getting false alarms like this one unless we find other ways to separate signal from slop," Oppenheim wrote.

Peter Woit, mathematician at Columbia University

Peter Woit, a mathematician at Columbia University, said the paper's findings did not check out or advance the field in any way. He called it a "publicity stunt" by OpenAI.

"It's more OpenAI worthless slop," Woit wrote on his website.

"For physics theory claims like this one, there's no reason to believe there's anything worthwhile there," he added.

Woit said he's reviewed thousands of papers making "similar claims" about quantum gravity and none have checked out.

"The only different thing about this one is that it's written by a machine and funded by a company that now has a track record of putting out misleading claims about physics," he wrote.

Hontas Farmer, theoretical astrophysicist

Hontas Farmer, a theoretical astrophysicist and professor at Chicago State University, said that while the paper checks out, it doesn't add anything to the conversation.

"It does not propose anything testable," she wrote on X. "It overlaps with many already published and or pre-printed ideas."

She said "AI boosters" are stoking hype for the paper, calling it "THE SOLUTION."

Nirmalya Kajuri, theoretical physicist

Nirmalya Kajuri, a theoretical physicist and science writer, said the paper doesn't solve quantum gravity, though it does make advancements toward the theory.

In a Substack post, he said in pre-AI days, a paper like this one wouldn't have gotten a lot of attention.

"It's an interesting project," he said. "Let us wait for another 400 milli tokens to see where it goes!"

items.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
items.summary: Open video on YouTube ↗ Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue , the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation . By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion → Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion → $1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion → Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion → No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion → Built for every agent, not just Clay's Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected. The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion → Keep building when the plan blows up Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did. When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion → Agents still can't debug agents What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand. Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand. Jump to the agent debugging discussion → Show notes Clay — the go-to-market platform where Jeff is Head of AI. Clay raises $115M to be the AI growth engine for every company — the September Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation, led by Wellington. Clay acquires Avenue to help growth teams act on intent signals — the January 2025 deal that brought Jeff's team to Clay. How Clay Scales GTM Agents — Jeff's LangChain Interrupt talk on running Clay's agents in production. Clay Agent Plugin (CLI & API) — the CLI and API that let Claude Code and Codex work directly with Clay. Inside Clay Workflows — how Workflows was built, including the table view customers asked to get back. Sellers have a new AI edge: Clay in ChatGPT — the ChatGPT app launch from Jeff's story. Sculpt recap: Building the self-learning revenue engine — Clay's October launches, including its new agent and Workflows. TypeSafe launched Jev because sequential LLMs are "totally useless for computers" — The New Stack on the classifier model behind Jeff's $1,500 math. Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use.

Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation.

By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph.

Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute.

Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent.

When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings.

The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows.

Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together.

Jump to the Sculptor discussion →

Most companies post-train too early

For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks.

Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million.

Jump to the post-training discussion →

$1,500 to score every company in the world

Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market.

Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one.

Jump to the Jev discussion →

Customers hate the model selector

Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company.

The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto.

Jump to the model routing discussion →

No Temporal, no LangGraph

Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work.

Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows.

Jump to the infrastructure discussion →

Built for every agent, not just Clay's

Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected.

The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there.

Jump to the agent platform discussion →

Keep building when the plan blows up

Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did.

When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today.

Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion →

Agents still can't debug agents

What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand.

Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand.

Jump to the agent debugging discussion →

Show notes

  • Clay — the go-to-market platform where Jeff is Head of AI.

  • Clay raises $115M to be the AI growth engine for every company — the September Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation, led by Wellington.

  • Clay acquires Avenue to help growth teams act on intent signals — the January 2025 deal that brought Jeff's team to Clay.

  • How Clay Scales GTM Agents — Jeff's LangChain Interrupt talk on running Clay's agents in production.

  • Clay Agent Plugin (CLI & API) — the CLI and API that let Claude Code and Codex work directly with Clay.

  • Inside Clay Workflows — how Workflows was built, including the table view customers asked to get back.

  • Sellers have a new AI edge: Clay in ChatGPT — the ChatGPT app launch from Jeff's story.

  • Sculpt recap: Building the self-learning revenue engine — Clay's October launches, including its new agent and Workflows.

  • TypeSafe launched Jev because sequential LLMs are "totally useless for computers" — The New Stack on the classifier model behind Jeff's $1,500 math.

items.title: Your Smartest AI Shouldn’t Be Doing Your Cheapest Work
items.summary: The interesting race in AI isn’t just intelligence anymore. It’s intelligence allocation. I’ve been spending a fair amount of time lately exploring agentic AI architecture, particularly in the context of building an autonomous growth department across our portfolio of dating platforms. In doing so, I’ve found myself increasingly less interested in which AI model is the smartest and considerably more interested in the economics of deploying that intelligence. This chart from Artificial Analysis illustrates why. The economics of AI intelligence: a roughly 44-fold difference in inference cost across models illustrates why intelligent model routing and resource allocation matter. Source: Artificial Analysis ( artificialanalysis.ai ) The disparity in inference costs between models is considerably more pronounced than the disparity in benchmark performance. Which brings me to a relatively obvious observation that I suspect will have increasingly significant commercial implications: Using the smartest AI model for every task is the computational equivalent of having your CEO answer customer support tickets. I’m sure they’re capable of doing it. I just wouldn’t want to explain it to the shareholders. Giving AI an organizational chart The architecture my business partner and I are exploring is essentially a hierarchical multi-agent system. Rather than building one enormously capable agent with access to every tool and responsibility imaginable, the idea is to distribute those responsibilities across a number of specialized agents, coordinated by a central orchestration layer. At the top sits what we’re referring to as an AI Growth Director. The director would run on a frontier reasoning model with access to our business objectives, acquisition costs, revenue data, conversion funnels, historical performance and the output of its subordinate agents. Its primary function is strategic reasoning, task decomposition, prioritization and resource allocation. Below it sits a collection of specialized agents: An SEO agent monitoring search performance, identifying ranking opportunities and evaluating content gaps. An outreach agent responsible for prospect discovery, backlink qualification and partnership opportunities. An analytics agent monitoring acquisition costs, revenue, retention and anomalies in business performance. A content agent responsible for research, drafting and optimization. A paid media agent evaluating campaign performance and identifying opportunities to improve acquisition efficiency. Each agent would have its own instructions, tools, permissions and relatively narrow domain of responsibility. They wouldn’t necessarily run on the same underlying model, either. For much of the execution layer, something like a lower-cost DeepSeek model may be perfectly adequate. I don’t particularly care whether the agent compiling a list of potential backlink opportunities can solve graduate-level mathematics. I care whether it can compile a good list of potential backlink opportunities. Separating reasoning from execution Consider a relatively straightforward SEO workflow. The Growth Director identifies a commercially valuable keyword cluster where we’re ranking just outside the first page of Google. It decomposes the objective into smaller tasks and delegates them to the relevant agents. The SEO agent retrieves ranking data through the Google Search Console API and identifies competing pages. The outreach agent discovers and qualifies relevant backlink prospects. The content agent evaluates our existing content against competing results and identifies potential improvements. Their findings are returned as structured outputs, stored in a shared data layer and made available to the director for evaluation. Rather than repeatedly feeding an increasingly enormous conversation history into an expensive reasoning model, the director can retrieve the relevant state, evaluate the findings and determine the next course of action. The more computationally expensive reasoning is concentrated around decision points rather than every intermediate operation. And where an operation is entirely deterministic, such as calculating conversion rates, deduplicating URLs or retrieving data from an API, there’s often no reason to involve a language model at all. Paying a frontier AI model to do something a few lines of Python could accomplish is an excellent way to contribute to the economic prosperity of the inference provider. Congratulations, your AI department made a dollar Imagine that six months after deploying this system, we’re able to attribute an 8% increase in monthly revenue to its activities. Let’s say that’s $50,000. Fantastic. Now imagine it consumed $49,999 worth of tokens in the process. We’ve successfully built an autonomous, hierarchical, multi-agent system capable of generating a dollar in incremental revenue after inference costs. And that’s before accounting for infrastructure, third-party APIs, development costs or the time spent supervising it. I’m not sure I’d be putting that particular achievement on my resume. Coming from a performance marketing background, I find it somewhat peculiar that so much of the discussion surrounding AI agents revolves around their ability to complete tasks, with relatively little attention paid to the unit economics of completing them. In paid acquisition, we don’t evaluate a campaign solely on its ability to generate customers. We evaluate the cost of acquiring those customers relative to the economic value they generate . Why should an autonomous growth department be any different? Every agent invocation, every reasoning loop, every retry and every unnecessarily large context window has an associated cost. Individually, those costs may appear negligible. Across dozens of workflows running continuously, they can become a meaningful operating expense. Consider a hypothetical workflow involving 10,000 monthly execution tasks and 200 strategic reasoning tasks. If each task costs $0.60 to execute on a cheaper model and $26 on a frontier model, running everything through the frontier model would cost $265,200 per month. Routing the execution tasks to the cheaper model and reserving the frontier model for the 200 strategic tasks would bring that figure down to $11,200. Obviously, these are illustrative numbers rather than projections of our actual inference costs, and the cheaper model would need to demonstrate sufficient competence at the assigned tasks. But the two architectures could, in principle, produce comparable commercial outcomes while having radically different economics. At that point, model routing is no longer merely an engineering consideration. It’s a margin consideration. Intelligence without an economic constraint The recent developments surrounding AI and mathematics provide a rather extreme illustration of this distinction. Earlier this year, OpenAI reportedly spent $15 million deploying thousands of AI systems to solve part of a Millennium Prize mathematical problem. More recently, an Anthropic researcher announced a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis with the assistance of Claude, a problem carrying a $1 million prize if the solution is formally accepted. Obviously, neither company is particularly concerned with the profitability of mathematical prize money. The scientific, reputational and commercial implications of demonstrating those capabilities dwarf the value of the prize itself. But it does illustrate an important distinction between demonstrating that artificial intelligence can accomplish something and demonstrating that it can accomplish it economically. For a research laboratory, solving a historically difficult mathematical problem at an enormous computational cost may constitute a spectacular success. For a business operating on considerably less glamorous objectives, such as improving its customer acquisition costs, that same disregard for computational expenditure would be somewhat less impressive. I suspect a lot of technically impressive agentic systems will turn out to be commercially mediocre for precisely this reason. Giving agents a budget One of the more interesting considerations in designing these systems is how to impose economic constraints on autonomous decision-making. A human marketing director doesn’t simply receive an objective and an unlimited budget with which to pursue it. There’s a point at which the marginal return on additional expenditure no longer justifies the investment. An AI agent should arguably operate under similar constraints. Consider an outreach agent tasked with acquiring backlinks. It could theoretically spend hours researching a single prospect, evaluating their content, analyzing their backlink profile, identifying the appropriate contact and generating a meticulously personalized email. At some point, however, the expected value of acquiring that backlink no longer justifies the cost of pursuing it. The system should be capable of recognizing that point. This introduces a number of considerations beyond simply selecting an underlying model: Inference budgets: Establishing maximum computational expenditure per task, workflow or objective. Dynamic model routing: Selecting models according to measured performance, cost and task requirements. Stopping conditions: Terminating workflows when further execution is unlikely to generate sufficient incremental value. Context optimization: Retrieving relevant information rather than repeatedly processing the entire execution history. Caching and deterministic execution: Avoiding unnecessary inference calls where previously generated results or conventional software would suffice. Cost attribution: Tracking expenditure across agents, workflows and business objectives. Ideally, the Growth Director would have visibility into the cost of executing its own recommendations. If an initiative is consuming considerably more resources than anticipated, the system should be capable of reassessing its priority, modifying its approach or abandoning it altogether. Persistence is an admirable quality in an employee. Less so in an autonomous agent burning through an API budget in pursuit of a backlink from a website nobody reads. The economics of being wrong Of course, minimizing inference costs isn’t necessarily the same thing as maximizing profitability. Model routing should also account for the economic consequences of failure. An agent incorrectly categorizing a keyword is a minor inconvenience. An agent misinterpreting acquisition data and recommending that we reallocate $50,000 in advertising spend is a somewhat less charming mistake. In the latter scenario, spending considerably more on inference suddenly seems quite reasonable. Ideally, the system would incorporate validation and escalation logic. A task that fails certain quality checks, produces conflicting results or exceeds a predetermined risk threshold could be routed to a more capable model or escalated for human review. For high-impact decisions, the director itself would still be subject to human approval. I’m quite enthusiastic about autonomous AI systems, but I’m not yet enthusiastic enough to give one unrestricted access to our advertising budgets. A cheap model that requires three retries, extensive validation and subsequent correction by an expensive model may not actually be particularly cheap. Similarly, an expensive model that reliably identifies a commercially significant opportunity overlooked by its cheaper counterparts may turn out to be extraordinarily inexpensive relative to the value it generates. The objective isn’t to minimize the cost per token, or even the cost per completed task. It’s to maximize the incremental economic value generated relative to the total cost of operating the system. And measuring that value introduces many of the same attribution problems we’ve been dealing with in digital marketing for years. Did revenue increase because of the agent’s recommendations, or would it have increased anyway? What was the incremental contribution margin? How much human intervention was required? Would a simpler, non-agentic workflow have produced a comparable result? These are considerably less exciting questions than whether an AI agent can autonomously execute a 47-step workflow. They’re also the questions that determine whether building one was worth the trouble. The competitive advantage may be architectural As AI models become increasingly capable and accessible, I find it difficult to imagine access to any particular model remaining a durable competitive advantage for most businesses. My competitors will have access to largely the same models I do. What they won’t necessarily have is the same proprietary data, orchestration logic, evaluation frameworks, accumulated execution history or understanding of which business problems warrant which level of intelligence. Over time, a system that records the cost, reliability and commercial outcome of its workflows could develop a fairly sophisticated understanding of where expensive intelligence actually pays for itself. It could discover that a particular inexpensive model performs remarkably well at prospect qualification, that another is better at content classification, and that certain strategic decisions consistently benefit from frontier-level reasoning. These systems also needn’t be particularly dependent on any single model provider. With a sufficiently modular architecture, the underlying models could be replaced as the economics and capabilities of competing models evolve. The intelligence itself becomes an interchangeable component. The system you’ve built around it becomes considerably less so. We’ve spent the better part of a century developing theories around organizational structure, delegation, specialization and resource allocation. It would be rather amusing if, after spending billions of dollars developing artificial intelligence, we discovered that a good portion of the knowledge required to deploy it effectively was already sitting in a dusty management textbook from 1965. The best AI systems won’t necessarily use the smartest models. They’ll know when not to. Your Smartest AI Shouldn’t Be Doing Your Cheapest Work was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Sakana AI Releases Namazu Small, a 30B Model Built on Nemotron 3 Nano
items.summary: Sakana AI has announced Sakana Namazu Small , a 30-billion-parameter reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano. The Japan-based lab ran continued pretraining and post-training in-house, starting from Nemotron 3 Nano’s pretrained base. Sakana AI team states that the result beats NVIDIA’s 120B Nemotron 3 Super on its 25-benchmark average. TL;DR Size: 30B total parameters, 3B active (labeled 30B-A3B in Sakana’s chart). Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: Hardware not disclosed. Sakana says it is small enough for your own environment. The Nemotron 3 Nano base was designed for DGX Spark, H100 and B200 GPUs. Performance: 60.1 average on 25 benchmarks, ahead of Nemotron 3 Super (56.2) and Nano (50.2). Self-reported. Best: BrowseComp 73.5, about 2x Nemotron 3 Super’s 36.1. Worst: SimpleQA Verified 6.8, below Nemotron 3 Nano (9.1) and Super (18.1). What is Sakana Namazu Small? Sakana Namazu Small is a 30B-A3B reasoning model from Sakana AI, tuned for web research and long-document QA. “Sakana Namazu” names models Sakana builds on open models and finishes with its own post-training. The larger Sakana Namazu is based on Kimi K2.6. Namazu Small is the compact member of that family. Sakana AI targets 3 kinds of work: everyday conversation, research with web search, and reading long documents. It was developed as a reasoning model. It organizes the information it needs and reasons step by step toward an answer. How was Namazu Small trained? Sakana started from the pretrained base of Nemotron 3 Nano, not NVIDIA’s post-trained release. It then applied continued pretraining and post-training techniques built for this release. These sit on top of methods Sakana developed for the original Sakana Namazu. The base architecture matters for deployment. Nemotron 3 Nano is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model. NVIDIA lists it at 30B total and 3B active parameters , with context up to 1M tokens. How does Namazu Small perform on benchmarks? Sakana compared it against 2 NVIDIA models, both post-trained by NVIDIA. These are Nemotron 3 Nano (30B-A3B) and Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B). The suite spans 25 benchmarks in 3 groups. All scores are self-reported by Sakana . items.summary_html:
Sakana AI has announced Sakana Namazu Small, a 30-billion-parameter reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano. The Japan-based lab ran continued pretraining and post-training in-house, starting from Nemotron 3 Nano’s pretrained base. Sakana AI team states that the result beats NVIDIA’s 120B Nemotron 3 Super on its 25-benchmark average.

TL;DR
  • Size: 30B total parameters, 3B active (labeled 30B-A3B in Sakana’s chart). Context length: Not disclosed.
  • Runs on: Hardware not disclosed. Sakana says it is small enough for your own environment. The Nemotron 3 Nano base was designed for DGX Spark, H100 and B200 GPUs.
  • Performance: 60.1 average on 25 benchmarks, ahead of Nemotron 3 Super (56.2) and Nano (50.2). Self-reported.
  • Best: BrowseComp 73.5, about 2x Nemotron 3 Super’s 36.1.
  • Worst: SimpleQA Verified 6.8, below Nemotron 3 Nano (9.1) and Super (18.1).
What is Sakana Namazu Small?

Sakana Namazu Small is a 30B-A3B reasoning model from Sakana AI, tuned for web research and long-document QA. “Sakana Namazu” names models Sakana builds on open models and finishes with its own post-training. The larger Sakana Namazu is based on Kimi K2.6. Namazu Small is the compact member of that family.

Sakana AI targets 3 kinds of work: everyday conversation, research with web search, and reading long documents. It was developed as a reasoning model. It organizes the information it needs and reasons step by step toward an answer.

How was Namazu Small trained?

Sakana started from the pretrained base of Nemotron 3 Nano, not NVIDIA’s post-trained release. It then applied continued pretraining and post-training techniques built for this release. These sit on top of methods Sakana developed for the original Sakana Namazu.

The base architecture matters for deployment. Nemotron 3 Nano is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model. NVIDIA lists it at 30B total and 3B active parameters, with context up to 1M tokens.

How does Namazu Small perform on benchmarks?

Sakana compared it against 2 NVIDIA models, both post-trained by NVIDIA. These are Nemotron 3 Nano (30B-A3B) and Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B). The suite spans 25 benchmarks in 3 groups. All scores are self-reported by Sakana.

Benchmark groupNamazu Small (30B-A3B)Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B)Nemotron 3 Nano (30B-A3B)Overall (25 benchmarks)60.156.250.2Web search (9)59.954.649.3Context grounding and instruction following (8)67.156.453.9Knowledge (8)53.257.847.6 Where does it win?

Web research is the standout. On BrowseComp, Namazu Small scores 73.5 versus 36.1 for Super and 29.3 for Nano. On DeepSearchQA it reaches 84.3, against 65.4 for Super.

Grounded long-document answering also jumps. LLM-jp LongBench rises to 86.0, versus 67.0 for the Nano baseline. FaithEval reaches 78.3 versus 59.1 for Super. LongBench-Cite hits 80.2 and ALCE reaches 60.2, both citation-focused tasks.

Where does it fall short?

Closed-book knowledge is the weak spot. On SimpleQA Verified it scores 6.8, below Super (18.1) and Nano (9.1). Japanese SimpleQA lands at 8.0, versus 24.9 for Super. HealthBench drops to 40.6, under Nano’s 47.5. Sakana itself says tasks using only internal knowledge did not improve much.

Per benchmark, Namazu Small beats Super on 13 of 25 tests. It beats Nano on 22 of 25.

items.title: 'A golden age for builders': Here's what business leaders are thankful for this year
items.summary: Sam Altman, Fei-Fei Li, and Bill Ackman posted about what they were thankful for this Thanksgiving. Getty Images CEOs, VCs, and other business leaders are feeling reflective. Sam Altman said being a dad never gets old. Bill Ackman thanked the healthcare workers who have helped his daughter. Fei-Fei Li and Brian Armstrong took different approaches to expressing their gratitude. It's not just your neighbor or family friend firing off a Thanksgiving post. Business leaders can't seem to resist either. Sam Altman took the opportunity to reflect on fatherhood. "I am thankful for a lot of things in life, but my family is the best thing that has ever happened to me," the OpenAI CEO wrote on X. "Most good things get a little less satisfying the 100th time you do them," Altman added. "A quiet evening hanging out with your kids, even doing very mundane stuff, is in the rare category of something repetitive just getting better and better." Altman is among a number of tech leaders, investors, and AI researchers who took to the internet to share what they're thankful for this year. Healthcare workers got a shoutout from billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who expressed appreciation for all the doctors, nurses, and others who helped his daughter with her recovery after she suffered a massive brain hemorrhage in February. She spent weeks in a coma and six months in the hospital. "Healthcare is a field, perhaps more so than any other, where people make a massive personal sacrifice of their lives, their time, their sleep, and their energy to help others," Ackman wrote on X. Investor and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, who has warned of a looming US debt crisis , emphasized the importance of connection amid turmoil in a post on LinkedIn. "I hope that we can keep in mind that despite all the challenges and conflicts in the world today, the most important thing is how we choose to be with each other," wrote Dalio. In a post on X, "Godmother of AI" Fei-Fei Li thanked the people in her life, including her students, colleagues, mentors, friends, and family, after noting that people often talk more about machines than each other. Li recently sold a startup she cofounded to AMD in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $8.2 billion. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong leaned into the machine talk. "Today I'm thankful for technology, and living in a golden age for builders," he wrote, also on X. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger had technology, people, and religion on his mind. He said he was thankful for the teams he works with, the opportunity to build AI that serves humanity, his family, and his faith. Similarly, Apple executive chairman Tim Cook said he was grateful for family, friends, and the tech giant's employees and customers. He wasn't the only representative of the iPhone maker. Dinner with the Markkula's. Of course the pie was Apple. pic.twitter.com/uaI6Jy4CHv — Steve Wozniak (@stevewoz) November 26, 2026 Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak also showed his holiday spirit. He shared a photo on X of himself dining with Mike Markkula, an early Apple investor who later served as the company's CEO and chairman. "Of course the pie was Apple," Wozniak wrote. items.title: AI could be used to write your child’s report. Is this a problem?
items.summary: Tony Anderson/Getty For many families, it’s that time of year when school reports land in parents’ inboxes. This is not simply something schools want to do. The federal government requires schools to report to parents twice a year. It must also be “ readily understandable ” to a parent or caregiver. But as artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by teachers across schools – what does this mean for reports?
items.summary_html:
Tony Anderson/Getty

For many families, it’s that time of year when school reports land in parents’ inboxes.

This is not simply something schools want to do. The federal government requires schools to report to parents twice a year. It must also be “readily understandable” to a parent or caregiver.

But as artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by teachers across schools – what does this mean for reports?

Read more: Why do I find my child’s school report so hard to understand?

What are the rules?

Currently, there is no consistent national guidance for AI use in school reports.

For example, in New South Wales, public school teachers can use the state’s own AI platform to assist with report comments. In Queensland, state school teachers can use AI for “developing written content”.

But in Victoria, teachers are not allowed to use AI write student reports.

All policies are clear that teachers remain responsible for judgements about students’ learning.

What do reports need to have?

For students from Years 1 to 10, the report must give “accurate and objective assessment” of the student’s progress and achievement.

Reports must also:

  • assess against any available national standards

  • assess relative to the performance of the student’s peer group

  • present results as A, B, C, D or E (or on an equivalent five-point scale) for each subject studied.

What makes a good report?

Australian research on school reporting suggests parents want information about their own child’s progress, while students value specific comments that help them understand how to improve.

This can be easier said than done. A report comment can be polished, positive and completely forgettable. “A pleasure to teach” might sound warm, but it tells a family nothing about what their child has learned.

A student should be able to recognise themselves in what their teacher says about their progress, strengths and next steps. That recognition is part of the relationship between a teacher and student.

I see what you do. I understand where you are going. I can help you get there.

Pre-written comments are not new

Some readers may remember reports featuring handwritten comments and marks or grades from teachers. But reports have long been generated on computers.

Many schools have actually used pre-written report comments for decades.

This is where teachers include comments that describe content covered in class, curriculum outcomes achieved, or other comments from “banks” to reduce workload.

For example,

Taylor is a dedicated and enthusiastic member of class, always willing to share what they know.

There are good reasons for using comment banks. Teachers write reports for many students in a concentrated, busy period. Shared or common comments can support consistency across classes, reinforce school priorities, and reduce spelling and grammar errors.

In some systems, teachers selected preset codes from a database for behaviour, progress or subject achievement, which the software assembled into a comment. A student’s name or pronoun might be inserted automatically. The sentence could look individualised on the page, while saying very little that was individual about the student.

While schools don’t tend to proactively disclose they use these programs, it becomes obvious when multiple children in one family can have almost identical comments for very different personalities.

So, what about AI?

In theory, AI writing tools such as ChatGPT could offer a way to keep the consistency of a comment bank while making the wording more individual.

For example, a teacher might provide their own notes about a student’s progress and ask AI to turn them into a clear, concise draft. The teacher then checks that it matches the evidence and sounds like their judgement. The tool helps with the wording but the knowledge of the student stays with the teacher.

This potential comes with a catch

AI can only work with the information someone gives it. It will still depend on a teacher genuinely knowing a student and understanding their progress to produce a useful comment.

And if a teacher enters names, learning records or sensitive details into an unapproved tool to achieve personalisation, they may put student privacy at risk.

The bigger picture

The question is not simply whether AI appears in the process. It is whether its use strengthens or weakens the teacher’s attention to and knowledge of the child.

A generic comment is not proof AI was used. But when a report could apply to almost anyone, it is fair to ask what it communicates about the relationship behind it.

Does the comment show the teacher knows the student, or just that the report has been completed?

Families should also remember, a written report can only tell us so much, no matter how it was created. The best way to know how our students are going is to chat with the teacher.

items.title: We built an AI you can dance with. It taught us about developing the technology responsibly
items.summary: arc/sec Lab, AI-generated image , CC BY-NC-ND In recent months, top researchers have quit leading artificial intelligence companies, warning the AI race is moving too quickly, with too little oversight and accountability. When those building this technology sound the alarm , we should pay attention. But more than warnings, what’s needed are working examples of how AI could be developed differently. In an Auckland dance studio, we’ve found one. Over ten months, our team built an AI dance partner in “extended reality” (which blends the physical world with digital elements) as part of our laboratory’s research into the relationships between people and digital-physical environments . We wanted to know whether an architectural avatar – a digital structure that moved in response to a dancer – could become an improvisational dance partner, and what would make it a good one. Dancing with an AI A choreographer, an architectural designer and two professional dancers developed and tested our AI dance partner. The dancers wore motion-capture suits tracked by ten cameras. Where large language models such as ChatGPT learn from text , our generative AI learned from their movements. The dancers met their partner through a headset blending digital images with the real room, while the rest of us watched on screens. A test run as seen on screen: a dancer’s captured movement, shown as the pink figure, beside the AI partner, an architectural form that moves with the dancer. arc/sec Lab , CC BY-NC-ND Improvisational dance is a tough test for AI. Partners read each other in fractions of a second, through movement, breath, rhythm and weight. This let us test whether a machine could respond like part of a duet. We worked out what mattered, and to whom, by moving with the AI as we developed it. One dancer wasn’t enough. The AI had to be trained on a duet because what we wanted it to learn lived in the space between the dancers. We were composing a relationship. A small set of choreographed duets taught the system better than a large library of generic movement. Tango gave it a structure it could read, but limited the dancers. Improvisation confused it, and it struggled with floor work, central to much contemporary dance in Aotearoa. Sticks extending from the dancers’ elbows made the patterns of distance and direction between them more readable. For most of the ten months, the partner only followed. Training it to offer anything back took patient work. Mixing dance styles produced bland, in-between moves. When the system stopped responding to a dancer’s small gestures, the dancer stopped making them. This concerned us. If AI routinely ignores what we bring to it – our movements, writing, judgements or minority views – we may gradually stop contributing them. Over time, what we think and create could become limited to what the machine recognises and rewards. The studio work left us with questions the technology cannot answer. Whose movement should the system learn from, which kinds, and how much? What makes a good partner, and a relationship worth having? And who gets to be the choreographer? Being ‘response-able’ Models such as ChatGPT are built to talk and write like a person. We built our dance partner as a responsive space, something people move with. The dancers whose movement trained the system also tested and judged it, shaping what it became. Recordings stayed on local encrypted drives, the dancers retained ownership of their data, and any choreography was credited as a joint creation. When the people who know the work stay close to a system, they become what feminist philosopher and science studies scholar Donna Haraway calls “ response-able ”: responsive to the system and one another, and accountable for what happens. Bring a skilled person into the loop and the system rises to meet them. Build it to serve everyone at once, and the responses drift toward a bland, generic in-between. The companies racing toward “ superintelligence ” work from the opposite logic. Add more data, computing power and scale, and intelligence will appear. Their models learn from vast quantities of scraped material, relevant and irrelevant. The writers, news agencies and artists whose work trains AI often have little say in what the models become. Built from that scraped mix and tuned to be agreeable, the models can favour widely represented views over less common perspectives, even when those perspectives are correct. When people with the knowledge to notice and judge are absent from how these models are built and used, accountability can spread so thinly that no one holds it. What could NZ do differently? The size of the model may not be what matters most. A small country can build and reward AI specific to its users. Māori data sovereignty , advanced by groups such as Te Mana Raraunga , a network advocating Māori rights and interests in data, wants data to stay connected and accountable to the communities it comes from. arc/sec Lab, AI-generated image, CC BY-NC-ND

In recent months, top researchers have quit leading artificial intelligence companies, warning the AI race is moving too quickly, with too little oversight and accountability.

When those building this technology sound the alarm, we should pay attention.

But more than warnings, what’s needed are working examples of how AI could be developed differently. In an Auckland dance studio, we’ve found one.

Over ten months, our team built an AI dance partner in “extended reality” (which blends the physical world with digital elements) as part of our laboratory’s research into the relationships between people and digital-physical environments.

We wanted to know whether an architectural avatar – a digital structure that moved in response to a dancer – could become an improvisational dance partner, and what would make it a good one.

Dancing with an AI

A choreographer, an architectural designer and two professional dancers developed and tested our AI dance partner.

The dancers wore motion-capture suits tracked by ten cameras. Where large language models such as ChatGPT learn from text, our generative AI learned from their movements. The dancers met their partner through a headset blending digital images with the real room, while the rest of us watched on screens.

A test run as seen on screen: a dancer’s captured movement, shown as the pink figure, beside the AI partner, an architectural form that moves with the dancer. arc/sec Lab, CC BY-NC-ND

Improvisational dance is a tough test for AI. Partners read each other in fractions of a second, through movement, breath, rhythm and weight. This let us test whether a machine could respond like part of a duet. We worked out what mattered, and to whom, by moving with the AI as we developed it.

One dancer wasn’t enough. The AI had to be trained on a duet because what we wanted it to learn lived in the space between the dancers. We were composing a relationship.

A small set of choreographed duets taught the system better than a large library of generic movement. Tango gave it a structure it could read, but limited the dancers.

Improvisation confused it, and it struggled with floor work, central to much contemporary dance in Aotearoa. Sticks extending from the dancers’ elbows made the patterns of distance and direction between them more readable.

For most of the ten months, the partner only followed. Training it to offer anything back took patient work. Mixing dance styles produced bland, in-between moves.

When the system stopped responding to a dancer’s small gestures, the dancer stopped making them.

This concerned us. If AI routinely ignores what we bring to it – our movements, writing, judgements or minority views – we may gradually stop contributing them. Over time, what we think and create could become limited to what the machine recognises and rewards.

The studio work left us with questions the technology cannot answer. Whose movement should the system learn from, which kinds, and how much? What makes a good partner, and a relationship worth having? And who gets to be the choreographer?

Being ‘response-able’

Models such as ChatGPT are built to talk and write like a person. We built our dance partner as a responsive space, something people move with. The dancers whose movement trained the system also tested and judged it, shaping what it became.

Recordings stayed on local encrypted drives, the dancers retained ownership of their data, and any choreography was credited as a joint creation.

When the people who know the work stay close to a system, they become what feminist philosopher and science studies scholar Donna Haraway calls “response-able”: responsive to the system and one another, and accountable for what happens.

Bring a skilled person into the loop and the system rises to meet them. Build it to serve everyone at once, and the responses drift toward a bland, generic in-between.

The companies racing toward “superintelligence” work from the opposite logic. Add more data, computing power and scale, and intelligence will appear. Their models learn from vast quantities of scraped material, relevant and irrelevant.

The writers, news agencies and artists whose work trains AI often have little say in what the models become. Built from that scraped mix and tuned to be agreeable, the models can favour widely represented views over less common perspectives, even when those perspectives are correct.

When people with the knowledge to notice and judge are absent from how these models are built and used, accountability can spread so thinly that no one holds it.

What could NZ do differently?

The size of the model may not be what matters most. A small country can build and reward AI specific to its users.

Māori data sovereignty, advanced by groups such as Te Mana Raraunga, a network advocating Māori rights and interests in data, wants data to stay connected and accountable to the communities it comes from. Our dance study points the same way.

It could hold AI companies responsible for their systems after release, and require them to account for costs they may otherwise pass on to the public, including the use of data and the energy and water their systems consume. It could also fund shared tools so communities can build AI systems that answer to them.

Our study offers one small example of an alternative approach to AI development. The challenge now is to ensure our institutions recognise and reward such alternatives.

items.title: China car ban at the 'one yard line' in Congress
items.summary: A BYD Shark Truck is displayed at a BYD showroom on May 21, 2026, in the Santa Fe business district of Mexico City. Alejandra Rajal / For The Washington Post via Getty Images A proposed ban on Chinese car imports is gaining support among lawmakers, POLITICO reports . Discussions are at the "one yard line," said one person familiar with the talks, with the substance of the changes resolved. Passing the legislation would be another sign of Capitol Hill's hardening position on China. Congress is looking increasingly likely to pass bipartisan legislation this year banning the import of Chinese autos, after the bill's Senate backers won over key parts of the auto industry. The Connected Vehicle Security Act , sponsored by Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), would ban US sales of cars that are made with components from adversaries like China and Russia. Moreno and Slotkin are aiming to pass the legislation by a voice vote in December, and are working with House colleagues to fast track the measure in that chamber, as well. Senate leadership from both parties have already signaled support for the bill, according to a person familiar with the conversations, and Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) helped advance the measure out of the Senate Commerce Committee earlier this year. Getting European and US car companies, who had concerns about parts of the legislation, to line up behind it greatly improves the odds of that happening. According to the same person and another familiar with the talks, the lawmakers agreed to tweak language in the bill to address concerns from several European automakers and their defenders, including GOP Sen. Rand Paul, whose state of Kentucky is an auto manufacturing hub and has courted more than $10 billion in investment from international automakers, according to Autos Drive America. Discussions are at the "one yard line," said one of the people, with the substance of the changes resolved and only wording and text left to iron out. Like others in this story, they were granted anonymity to share details of the closed-door discussions. A spokesperson for the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which advocates for many of the largest automakers, including Mercedes, Volvo, GM, Ford and Stellantis told POLITICO the organization is "very supportive" of the bill. Winning over the Kentucky senator, as well as others like Alabama Sen. Katie Britt, whose state is home to a Mercedes plant , is crucial to getting the unanimous consent in the Senate to pass the legislation by voice vote — a necessity given the end-of-year floor time crunch, as lawmakers race to complete votes on must-pass bills before this Congress expires. Passing the legislation would be another sign of Capitol Hill's hardening position on China, in defiance of President Donald Trump, who has defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid a Chinese espionage scandal as he pushes to do more business with Beijing — and even mused about allowing Chinese car companies to build plants and sell their vehicles in the US. And it could further heighten US-China tensions as the administration continues to negotiate another extension to the two country's trade truce, which is due to expire on Jan. 10. Chinese vehicles are already effectively blocked from the US market by steep 100% tariffs, first imposed by] Trump and raised by former President Joe Biden, as well as Commerce Department restrictions on vehicle components. But some in the domestic auto industry have been pushing Congress to codify the blockade to provide greater certainty and help firms make long-term sourcing decisions. Moreno, Slotkin and the bill's other House and Senate backers have been negotiating with German manufacturer Mercedes, as well as advocacy groups that represent them, on provisions in the bill defining what qualifies as a Chinese vehicle, said the two people familiar and three others briefed on the talks. The original language banned sales of cars made by companies with more than 15% Chinese ownership. Chinese investors own nearly 80% of Volvo and 20% of Mercedes. Paul told Reuters in September that he thought the bill unfairly singled out Mercedes, with its criteria for determining Chinese ownership. Paul and Britt's offices did not respond to a question on whether they would support the legislation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its position on the bill. A GOP staff member who worked on the legislation and a second person familiar with the deal said that under the agreement reached with lawmakers, neither company would be blocked from selling cars in the US. The bill will now include more flexibility for companies with silent shareholders, like Mercedes, according to the people. Volvo has already been able to secure federal authorization to sell cars in the U.S. despite its China ties. A Mercedes-Benz spokesperson declined to comment on whether a deal has been reached, but said the company "applauds the constructive discussions with key US lawmakers including Senator Moreno, Senator Slotkin and [Senate Commerce Committee] Chairman [Ted] Cruz (R-Texas)." A Volvo Cars spokesperson reiterated to POLITICO that the company has "specific authorization to continue to sell connected vehicles in the US." "We continue to monitor developments closely and we are actively engaged with policymakers on the potential business and consumer impacts of this US legislation," they added. Lawmakers also kept batteries out of the list of components covered by the legislation and opted not to tighten restrictions on battery technologies, despite calls from parts of the domestic industry to do so. Ford Motor Co. resisted efforts for tighter curbs on batteries, which could have affected the US automaker's partnership with Chinese battery manufacturer CATL to license its technology. Lawmakers will not include language on batteries in the final version of the bill, four of the people said. The language in the bill instead focuses only on battery management systems, which should leave Ford's partnership unaffected. Ford declined to comment. Negotiators also agreed to include a sunset provision for the vehicle ban, after some environmentally-minded lawmakers expressed concern that indefinitely banning Chinese cars, including the country's affordable electric vehicles, could slow decarbonization efforts, according to three of the people This is "a freight train that's moving," said one of the people familiar with the discussions. "Slotkin and Moreno are putting people in rooms to make this stuff happen." This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from The Telegraph, POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.
