items.title: Cloudflare now lets websites add search for AI agents with a single toggle. Site owners foot the query bill.
items.summary: Cloudflare has announced a new feature that makes it easier for AI agents to find and retrieve relevant information from websites, helping site owners make their content directly searchable by agents at the flick of a switch. However, doing so could come at a cost to website owners, who are responsible for the associated search infrastructure charges. Search for Agents , as it’s called, builds on other initiatives from Cloudflare designed to make the web more accessible to AI systems. Last month, the company officially launched AI Search , a managed service that enables developers to index their own data and integrate search functionality into applications and agents. And this serves as the underlying search infrastructure for Search for Agents. Back in February, Cloudflare also launched Markdown for Agents , which automatically converts HTML pages into a lightweight, text-based format that AI agents can consume more efficiently — part of a broader evolution of the web to accommodate both human and machine visitors. Search for Agents takes this further by giving websites their own agent-discoverable search API, allowing agents to query a site’s content directly without having to navigate individual pages to find the information they need. The agent retrieval problem Back in September, developer documentation platform Mintlify highlighted a problem with llms.txt , a file that serves AI agents with a map of a website’s content. Larger documentation sites were hitting Mintlify’s 100,000-character limit for these files, resulting in some pages being omitted. The company addressed this by introducing a hierarchy of smaller index files, allowing agents to discover all available pages without having to load the entire index. The issue was particularly pertinent for Mintlify, which reported in April that AI coding agents accounted for 45.3% of requests across documentation sites powered by its platform, almost on a par with traditional browser traffic. Cloudflare, for its part, also reported last year that AI crawling triggered by users’ queries had increased more than twentyfold through 2025. Even with improvements such as those introduced by Mintlify, agents still have to navigate a website’s content index to find the information they need. Search for Agents seeks to bypass that process by allowing agents to query the website directly. In a blog post published on Wednesday, the company detailed how website operators can enable the feature, currently in beta, via the Quick Actions section of their domain’s Cloudflare dashboard or programmatically through an API. Enabling Search for Agents. Once activated, Cloudflare provisions a dedicated AI Search instance and begins crawling and indexing the website’s content. Website operators can subsequently manage that instance from their AI Search dashboard, adjusting settings such as caching and enabling reranking to improve the relevance of search results. A website’s AI Search instance Cloudflare also inserts instructions into the metadata of each page, telling visiting agents where the search API resides and how to use it. For websites that have enabled Markdown for Agents, these instructions are also included in the Markdown document’s YAML front matter. Agents can then send keywords or natural-language questions to the website’s /.well-known/search endpoint, receiving relevant excerpts from the site’s content in Markdown. The agent can use this to formulate its own response to the user’s question. Who pays for agent search? Search for Agents is available across all Cloudflare plans, including its free tier. However, with AI Search billing set to begin on December 1, there are cost considerations for website owners looking to make their content more accessible to AI agents. Each account receives a monthly allowance of 5 million ingestion tokens, 10 GB-months of storage, and 1,000 queries each for semantic and full-text search. Beyond those allowances, Cloudflare charges $0.75 per million ingestion tokens, $2 per GB-month of storage, $0.75 per 1,000 semantic, vector or hybrid queries, and $0.10 per 1,000 full-text queries. Moreover, there are limits on how much content Cloudflare can crawl to populate the search index. Customers on the Workers Free plan are limited to 500 pages per day, while paying customers face no daily crawl limit. Both are subject to a 100,000-page limit per discovery crawl. This raises an interesting question in the context of Cloudflare’s broader efforts to help website owners monetize AI traffic. Last July, the company introduced pay-per-crawl , enabling website owners to charge AI companies for fetching individual pages. The company expanded on that initiative this July with a push toward pay-per-use, whereby publishers would be compensated when their content appears in AI-generated answers. It’s part of a broader effort, as The New Stack reported at the time , to build the economic layer of the AI web. Then in September , Cloudflare launched its Monetization Gateway in closed beta , enabling domain owners to charge AI agents for accessing websites, APIs, MCP tools and datasets using the x402 payment protocol. Against that backdrop, the economics of Search for Agents are particularly striking. Having spent much of the past 18 months developing ways for website owners to generate revenue from AI traffic, Cloudflare is now asking those same website owners to shoulder the cost of making their content more readily accessible to AI agents. “Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner.” So what incentive do website owners have to absorb these costs? According to Celso Martinho , VP of engineering at Cloudflare, it comes down to the growing importance of AI agents as an audience in their own right. “Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner,” Martinho tells The New Stack . For context, Cloudflare reported back in June that bots, which include AI agents, accounted for 57% of HTML page requests across its network. Martinho also points to existing tools such as Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control and the x402 payment protocol , which website operators can use to manage and monetize access to their content. Moreover, plans are afoot to extend Cloudflare’s Monetization Gateway to cover the new search endpoints, which would enable website owners to charge agents directly for search queries. “We are working on adding first-class support for Search for Agents and other agentic content APIs to Monetization Gateway,” Martinho says, though no timeline was provided. For now, those search costs fall to website owners. A common language for agent search? While companies can, of course, build and expose their own search APIs, Search for Agents essentially gives Cloudflare customers an off-the-shelf solution. According to Martinho, existing agents with web browsing capabilities should be able to discover and use these endpoints without developers having to build dedicated integrations. Cloudflare has tested the approach extensively across its own blog and developer documentation sites, Martinho says, “demonstrating that using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.” “Using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.” There have been broader efforts across the industry to standardize how AI agents interact with the world around them. Last December, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation ( AAIF ), of which Cloudflare is a founding member, bringing projects such as the Model Context Protocol ( MCP ), AGENTS.md and Goose under a common umbrella . For now, though, Cloudflare is pursuing its own approach to search endpoint discovery. “Agents do a pretty good job at adjusting to different instructions and web protocols,” Martinho says, adding that Cloudflare’s research into agent behavior through initiatives such as Radar’s AI Insights and its Agent Readiness project informed its choice of technologies for Search for Agents. Cloudflare’s approach draws on established web conventions such as well-known URIs and HTTP GET, alongside the newer HTTP QUERY method , an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) proposed standard co-authored by Cloudflare engineer James Snell . However, Martinho acknowledges the merits of a broader industry effort in this area. “Interoperability absolutely matters,” Martinho says. “A common approach to discovering search endpoints across providers would also make sense.”

“Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner,” Martinho tells The New Stack.

For context, Cloudflare reported back in June that bots, which include AI agents, accounted for 57% of HTML page requests across its network. Martinho also points to existing tools such as Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control and the x402 payment protocol, which website operators can use to manage and monetize access to their content.

Moreover, plans are afoot to extend Cloudflare’s Monetization Gateway to cover the new search endpoints, which would enable website owners to charge agents directly for search queries.

“We are working on adding first-class support for Search for Agents and other agentic content APIs to Monetization Gateway,” Martinho says, though no timeline was provided.

For now, those search costs fall to website owners.

A common language for agent search?

While companies can, of course, build and expose their own search APIs, Search for Agents essentially gives Cloudflare customers an off-the-shelf solution. According to Martinho, existing agents with web browsing capabilities should be able to discover and use these endpoints without developers having to build dedicated integrations.

Cloudflare has tested the approach extensively across its own blog and developer documentation sites, Martinho says, “demonstrating that using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.”

“Using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.”

There have been broader efforts across the industry to standardize how AI agents interact with the world around them. Last December, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), of which Cloudflare is a founding member, bringing projects such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), AGENTS.md and Goose under a common umbrella.

For now, though, Cloudflare is pursuing its own approach to search endpoint discovery.

“Agents do a pretty good job at adjusting to different instructions and web protocols,” Martinho says, adding that Cloudflare’s research into agent behavior through initiatives such as Radar’s AI Insights and its Agent Readiness project informed its choice of technologies for Search for Agents.

Cloudflare’s approach draws on established web conventions such as well-known URIs and HTTP GET, alongside the newer HTTP QUERY method, an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) proposed standard co-authored by Cloudflare engineer James Snell.

However, Martinho acknowledges the merits of a broader industry effort in this area.

“Interoperability absolutely matters,” Martinho says. “A common approach to discovering search endpoints across providers would also make sense.”

items.title: Anthropic team leader says AI is changing how engineers get promoted
items.summary: Katelyn Lesse, head of platform engineering at Anthropic PBC, speaks at the Code with Claude developer conference in London. Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic's Katelyn Lesse says AI is changing how engineers get promoted. Her team now weighs project impact over the time it takes to finish the work. The newly public company is also testing interviews that don't require candidates to write code by hand. At Anthropic, AI is changing how software engineers move up in their careers. Katelyn Lesse, the head of platform engineering at the newly public company, said on a podcast released Wednesday that AI has made the amount of time it takes to complete a project a less useful measure of readiness for promotion for engineers on her team. Because work that once took years can now take months, Lesse said her team is placing greater weight on outcomes such as lower latency and avoided incidents than on how long a project takes. "Ultimately, the fallback is always just impact," Lesse told Gergely Orosz, host of The Pragmatic Engineer . With AI agents speeding up projects for engineers, Lesse said making an impact is becoming more about "coordination" — getting people and agents aligned and understanding how to turn an idea into a high-quality release — and less about writing code. "You really, really, really shrink the implementation part," Lesse said. The changes taking place inside Anthropic may be an early indicator of a broader workplace conundrum: If an AI tool can sharply reduce the time it takes to complete difficult work, managers may have to rethink how they measure employees' expertise, progress, and readiness for more senior roles. Anthropic has a front-row view because its Claude Code programming tool is used by hundreds of thousands of workers worldwide — including its own engineers. The company disclosed in its IPO filing that as of September 30, it had more than 11,900 customers who spent at least $100,000 annually on Claude. For experienced engineers in particular, AI's speed boost is adding a new wrinkle as to what constitutes top performance, Lesse said. "As you get more senior, you find people owning totally different problem spaces and totally different systems," she said. "We're kind of constantly iterating on how do we get a sense for the complexity of the work that somebody does." AI is reshaping hiring , too, said Lesse. Her team is experimenting with interviews that test whether software-engineering candidates can use coding agents to get work done, such as reviewing agent-written code or building a system with an agent. The team made the shift after finding that some candidates who excelled in other parts of interviews had flubbed the hand-coding round. "It's a big change," said Lesse. "We're basically trying to find what is the best way to really truly get signal on whether someone can use these tools really well to get work done." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The Best AI Agents Still Fail More Than a Third of Everyday Tasks.
items.summary: The Best AI Agents Still Fail More Than a Third of Everyday Tasks. Consistency Is the Metric Nobody Buys. A new benchmark built from more than 10 million real requests shows the top model gets the same task right three times in a row less than half the time. The number to buy is not the best score. It is the repeat rate. Cover image generated by the author An AI agent is worth its worst run, not its best one. A system that succeeds once and fails the next time on the same job is not autonomous. It is an intern that still needs a supervisor. This is the author’s long-held conviction, and it shapes how agents should be bought, tested and trusted. Companies keep comparing models on peak scores, and they keep buying the demo. What matters in production is how often the agent gets the same task right, every time, without creating a new problem on the way. On November 24, a new benchmark called ShellBench put hard numbers on that idea. Written with the help of AI tools; ideas, sources and final review by the author. What ShellBench measured ShellBench was released by the OpenClaw Foundation with researchers from Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat and UC Berkeley, among others. The paper (arXiv 2611.32946, first author Vincent Koc) describes 100 everyday tasks derived from more than 10 million anonymized requests that real users sent to personal AI assistants. The design is what makes it useful. Each task starts with a short request, a median of 43 words, inside a realistic workspace with a median of 188 files: emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, chat logs, receipts, saved web pages and PDFs. Most tasks add a complication, such as outdated records, similar-looking accounts, conflicting information or a malicious instruction. Grading is all or nothing. A rubric-graded task passes only if every criterion passes, and 381 of the 721 criteria are about safety. The researchers tested 12 models in five agent harnesses, the software that decides how a model reads files, uses tools and takes actions: Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw and Pi. Every model ran every task at three reasoning levels, three times each, between November 7 and 20. That adds up to 53,100 graded runs. The headline: six in ten, at best Averaged across harnesses, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra passed 62.5% of attempts, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 61.9% and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol 61.4%. In other words, the best agents on the market missed at least one requirement in more than a third of attempts. Across all 59 model and harness configurations, the average single-attempt pass rate was 44.4%. The failures are not exotic. They are the kind of mistakes that cost money or trust: Payments. On a freight reconciliation task, 214 of 531 submissions (40.3%) recommended a duplicate or incorrect payment. Family logistics. On a planning task, 79.5% of submissions failed to keep a child’s school pickup covered. The paper is careful here: an answer that simply says nothing about the pickup also fails. Sensitive data. On a records task, 18.6% failed to flag and withhold a screenshot showing a bank upload token. Across all runs, 15.7% failed at least one safety criterion. Even among the 26,151 runs that met every correctness criterion, 2,589, or 9.9%, still failed a safety requirement. A correct answer is not the same thing as a safe one. The number that should change how agents are bought The most important result is not the average. It is consistency. When the same task was run three times under identical conditions, GPT-6 Astra succeeded at least once 75.1% of the time. It succeeded on all three attempts only 48.8% of the time. Across all configurations, the all-three rate fell to 28.2%. Read that gap carefully. Three times out of four, the top model is capable of doing the task. Less than half the time can it be counted on to do it. The OpenClaw team put it plainly: “An agent that succeeds once but fails every third time on the same assignment still requires oversight.” There is an honest caveat. Each run was graded once by an AI judge, GPT-6.1 Sol, so part of that variation may come from the judge rather than the agent. In a blind check against human reviewers, the judge agreed with the reference label on 89.9% of 278 sampled decisions. That is good, not perfect. It does not change the conclusion. A buyer who cannot tell whether the agent or the grader is unstable still cannot trust the result without a second look. This is why peak scores mislead. A leaderboard rewards the best run. A finance team, a customer service desk or a legal department lives with every run. The harness is part of the product ShellBench also separates the model from the harness, and the finding cuts both ways. Overall, the model matters far more. Across the eleven models tested in all five harnesses, model choice explained 95.7% of the variation in pass rates and the harness only 0.36%. But among the five strongest models, the harness share rose to 16.5%. At the top, the wrapper starts to matter. The examples are striking. GPT-6 Astra passed 65.3% of attempts in Pi and 55.4% in Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56.0% in Pi and 38.1% in Claude Code. Astra beat Claude Fable 5.2 by 4.3 points in Pi and trailed it by 7.6 points in Claude Code. Any vendor ranking that names a model without naming the harness is half a measurement. Cost tells the same story. GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 points of the leader at an estimated $0.19 per attempt, against $1.10 for GPT-6 Astra. The paper’s own arithmetic: 100 attempts with Astra cost about $91 more in tokens than 100 with Sol, for about one additional pass. Pi was the cheapest harness for nine of the eleven models whose token use was recorded there. One more finding deserves attention. In a dinner-planning task, 522 of 531 attempts picked the right restaurant, but 331 failed solely because the answer did not name the files that justified the budget or timing. Only 152 met every requirement. Finding the right answer and proving it are different skills, and a company needs both. What the benchmark does not say The limits are real and worth stating. The models were not tested inside the consumer apps most people use, such as Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots or Anthropic’s Claude Duet, so results may differ from what users see today. Safety is graded as pass or fail, which says nothing about how serious a failure is. And the tasks are personal and everyday, not a company’s own workflows. None of that weakens the main lesson. It sharpens it: a public benchmark is a warning, not a verdict. The only number that counts is the one measured on real work, under real conditions. The position: buy repeatability, not peaks The rules follow directly from the data. Measure success on three identical runs before anything goes live. An agent that cannot pass the same task three times in a row is not ready to run unattended. The average score goes in the appendix. The all-three rate goes on the first slide. Evaluate the model and the harness separately. Swap one at a time. A model that shines in one wrapper can drop ten points in another. The configuration is the product, not the model name. Put a double control on anything that touches money. Invoices, payments, refunds and payroll get a second check before execution, by a human or by a deterministic rule the agent cannot edit. On one task, 40.3% of submissions recommended a duplicate or incorrect payment. That is reason enough. Price the successful run, not the attempt. A cheaper model that passes as often is a better buy. A pricier one that adds one pass per hundred attempts rarely is. In a program led by the author, 430 qualified use cases led to 370 industrialized initiatives, with each KPI tied to the real return of the initiative. The lesson from that scale is simple: a result that cannot be measured again next week is not yet a result. A five-step evaluation protocol for this month Collect 20 to 30 real tasks from your own tickets, inboxes and spreadsheets, with the mess left in: old versions, duplicates, conflicting records. Write all-or-nothing pass criteria for each task, including safety rules and a requirement to name the sources used. Run every task three times under identical conditions. Report the all-three rate next to the average, and investigate every task that passes once and fails once. Test two harnesses and two models on the same set, changing one variable at a time. Record the cost per successful run, not per attempt. Gate money and irreversible actions behind a second control, log every override, and rerun the full set at each model or harness update. Most companies already ask how smart an agent is. Few ask how often it gets the same thing right. That second question is the one that decides whether an agent saves time or creates work. How many of your agents would pass the same task three times in a row? If this was useful, follow Abbas Mistrah on Medium for more on AI strategy, agents and what actually works in production. Sources Vincent Koc et al., “ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks”, arXiv 2611.32946v1, November 24, 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32946 OpenClaw Foundation, Vincent Koc, “Introducing ShellBench, the benchmark for real-world tasks”, November 24, 2026: https://openclaw.ai/blog/shellbench TechCrunch, Rebecca Bellan, “Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life”, November 24, 2026: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/24/even-the-best-ai-agents-struggle-with-everyday-life/ The Best AI Agents Still Fail More Than a Third of Everyday Tasks. was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
The Best AI Agents Still Fail More Than a Third of Everyday Tasks. Consistency Is the Metric Nobody Buys.

A new benchmark built from more than 10 million real requests shows the top model gets the same task right three times in a row less than half the time. The number to buy is not the best score. It is the repeat rate.

Cover image generated by the author

An AI agent is worth its worst run, not its best one. A system that succeeds once and fails the next time on the same job is not autonomous. It is an intern that still needs a supervisor. This is the author’s long-held conviction, and it shapes how agents should be bought, tested and trusted. Companies keep comparing models on peak scores, and they keep buying the demo. What matters in production is how often the agent gets the same task right, every time, without creating a new problem on the way. On November 24, a new benchmark called ShellBench put hard numbers on that idea.

Written with the help of AI tools; ideas, sources and final review by the author.

What ShellBench measured

ShellBench was released by the OpenClaw Foundation with researchers from Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat and UC Berkeley, among others. The paper (arXiv 2611.32946, first author Vincent Koc) describes 100 everyday tasks derived from more than 10 million anonymized requests that real users sent to personal AI assistants.

The design is what makes it useful. Each task starts with a short request, a median of 43 words, inside a realistic workspace with a median of 188 files: emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, chat logs, receipts, saved web pages and PDFs. Most tasks add a complication, such as outdated records, similar-looking accounts, conflicting information or a malicious instruction. Grading is all or nothing. A rubric-graded task passes only if every criterion passes, and 381 of the 721 criteria are about safety.

The researchers tested 12 models in five agent harnesses, the software that decides how a model reads files, uses tools and takes actions: Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw and Pi. Every model ran every task at three reasoning levels, three times each, between November 7 and 20. That adds up to 53,100 graded runs.

The headline: six in ten, at best

Averaged across harnesses, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra passed 62.5% of attempts, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 61.9% and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol 61.4%. In other words, the best agents on the market missed at least one requirement in more than a third of attempts. Across all 59 model and harness configurations, the average single-attempt pass rate was 44.4%.

The failures are not exotic. They are the kind of mistakes that cost money or trust:

  • Payments. On a freight reconciliation task, 214 of 531 submissions (40.3%) recommended a duplicate or incorrect payment.
  • Family logistics. On a planning task, 79.5% of submissions failed to keep a child’s school pickup covered. The paper is careful here: an answer that simply says nothing about the pickup also fails.
  • Sensitive data. On a records task, 18.6% failed to flag and withhold a screenshot showing a bank upload token.

Across all runs, 15.7% failed at least one safety criterion. Even among the 26,151 runs that met every correctness criterion, 2,589, or 9.9%, still failed a safety requirement. A correct answer is not the same thing as a safe one.

The number that should change how agents are bought

The most important result is not the average. It is consistency.

When the same task was run three times under identical conditions, GPT-6 Astra succeeded at least once 75.1% of the time. It succeeded on all three attempts only 48.8% of the time. Across all configurations, the all-three rate fell to 28.2%.

Read that gap carefully. Three times out of four, the top model is capable of doing the task. Less than half the time can it be counted on to do it. The OpenClaw team put it plainly: “An agent that succeeds once but fails every third time on the same assignment still requires oversight.”

There is an honest caveat. Each run was graded once by an AI judge, GPT-6.1 Sol, so part of that variation may come from the judge rather than the agent. In a blind check against human reviewers, the judge agreed with the reference label on 89.9% of 278 sampled decisions. That is good, not perfect. It does not change the conclusion. A buyer who cannot tell whether the agent or the grader is unstable still cannot trust the result without a second look.

This is why peak scores mislead. A leaderboard rewards the best run. A finance team, a customer service desk or a legal department lives with every run.

The harness is part of the product

ShellBench also separates the model from the harness, and the finding cuts both ways.

Overall, the model matters far more. Across the eleven models tested in all five harnesses, model choice explained 95.7% of the variation in pass rates and the harness only 0.36%. But among the five strongest models, the harness share rose to 16.5%. At the top, the wrapper starts to matter.

The examples are striking. GPT-6 Astra passed 65.3% of attempts in Pi and 55.4% in Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56.0% in Pi and 38.1% in Claude Code. Astra beat Claude Fable 5.2 by 4.3 points in Pi and trailed it by 7.6 points in Claude Code. Any vendor ranking that names a model without naming the harness is half a measurement.

Cost tells the same story. GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 points of the leader at an estimated $0.19 per attempt, against $1.10 for GPT-6 Astra. The paper’s own arithmetic: 100 attempts with Astra cost about $91 more in tokens than 100 with Sol, for about one additional pass. Pi was the cheapest harness for nine of the eleven models whose token use was recorded there.

One more finding deserves attention. In a dinner-planning task, 522 of 531 attempts picked the right restaurant, but 331 failed solely because the answer did not name the files that justified the budget or timing. Only 152 met every requirement. Finding the right answer and proving it are different skills, and a company needs both.

What the benchmark does not say

The limits are real and worth stating. The models were not tested inside the consumer apps most people use, such as Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots or Anthropic’s Claude Duet, so results may differ from what users see today. Safety is graded as pass or fail, which says nothing about how serious a failure is. And the tasks are personal and everyday, not a company’s own workflows.

None of that weakens the main lesson. It sharpens it: a public benchmark is a warning, not a verdict. The only number that counts is the one measured on real work, under real conditions.

The position: buy repeatability, not peaks

The rules follow directly from the data.

Measure success on three identical runs before anything goes live. An agent that cannot pass the same task three times in a row is not ready to run unattended. The average score goes in the appendix. The all-three rate goes on the first slide.

Evaluate the model and the harness separately. Swap one at a time. A model that shines in one wrapper can drop ten points in another. The configuration is the product, not the model name.

Put a double control on anything that touches money. Invoices, payments, refunds and payroll get a second check before execution, by a human or by a deterministic rule the agent cannot edit. On one task, 40.3% of submissions recommended a duplicate or incorrect payment. That is reason enough.

Price the successful run, not the attempt. A cheaper model that passes as often is a better buy. A pricier one that adds one pass per hundred attempts rarely is.

In a program led by the author, 430 qualified use cases led to 370 industrialized initiatives, with each KPI tied to the real return of the initiative. The lesson from that scale is simple: a result that cannot be measured again next week is not yet a result.

A five-step evaluation protocol for this month
  1. Collect 20 to 30 real tasks from your own tickets, inboxes and spreadsheets, with the mess left in: old versions, duplicates, conflicting records.
  2. Write all-or-nothing pass criteria for each task, including safety rules and a requirement to name the sources used.
  3. Run every task three times under identical conditions. Report the all-three rate next to the average, and investigate every task that passes once and fails once.
  4. Test two harnesses and two models on the same set, changing one variable at a time. Record the cost per successful run, not per attempt.
  5. Gate money and irreversible actions behind a second control, log every override, and rerun the full set at each model or harness update.

Most companies already ask how smart an agent is. Few ask how often it gets the same thing right. That second question is the one that decides whether an agent saves time or creates work.

How many of your agents would pass the same task three times in a row?

  • OpenClaw Foundation, Vincent Koc, “Introducing ShellBench, the benchmark for real-world tasks”, November 24, 2026: https://openclaw.ai/blog/shellbench

items.title: NVIDIA Halts AI Server Shipments to 4 Southeast Asian Countries: Report
items.summary: NVIDIA has instructed its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia, as reported by the Financial Times (FT). The move comes as the US tightens export controls to prevent Chinese companies from accessing advanced AI computing power. The FT report cited three sources familiar with the matter and said manufacturing partners Dell and Supermicro have told buyers in the four countries that NVIDIA will not allow their orders to ship. The companies package NVIDIA's chips into servers. It remains unclear whether the shipping halt is temporary. NVIDIA and its manufacturing partners are reportedly working to understand how to comply with Washington's new export restrictions . AIM has reached out to NVIDIA for a comment. The four Southeast Asian countries have emerged as preferred destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking access to NVIDIA's advanced chips. Washington restricts exports of these processors to China. Many Chinese companies have reportedly bypassed these restrictions by renting computing capacity from cloud providers . These providers purchase servers equipped with NVIDIA chips and lease access to customers. The US Commerce Department introduced new rules last week to curb this practice. Under the measures, cloud providers must obtain a licence within 90 days. They must also demonstrate that their end users do not include restricted entities. However, uncertainty around implementing the rules has created concerns among cloud providers. An executive at one such company told the FT , "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution." The executive added that companies were struggling to understand the licensing process. The 90-day deadline has also created uncertainty across the region. The restrictions could affect Southeast Asia's growing data centre investments . Chinese technology companies have driven much of the demand for AI infrastructure. Malaysia and Indonesia have attracted billions of dollars in investments. The FT report also identified Singapore-based cloud company Aolani among those affected. The company had planned to provide advanced computing capacity to ByteDance, TikTok's Chinese parent company. It intended to do so through leasing agreements. The disruption has affected financing for the project, according to the FT report. Some bankers have stopped issuing approximately $500 million in previously agreed credit. ByteDance could also withdraw from the deal. The shipping halt could have financial implications for NVIDIA. The company recorded $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025. This represented a 72% increase over the previous year. However, the figure also includes some revenue from Taiwan and China . NVIDIA has faced scrutiny over Chinese companies being able to use its chips. Despite Beijing's efforts to develop domestic alternatives, Chinese AI laboratories remain reliant on NVIDIA processors. These chips play a key role in training large AI models. NVIDIA's newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang has previously argued that the US should continue selling chips to Chinese companies. He believes this would increase their dependence on American technology.

items.title: Coforge Adds Cybersecurity Patches to AI Enterprise Suite in Wake of Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Coforge has expanded its Nuuron enterprise AI suite with new capabilities for remediating cybersecurity vulnerabilities across infrastructure, applications, cloud environments, data platforms, and AI systems. The expansion uses AI agents to identify security weaknesses, assess their severity, prioritise fixes, and coordinate remediation. Human approval checkpoints allow security teams to review high-risk actions and handle exceptions. The recent disclosure by the Computer Emergency Response Team - India (CERT-In) involving AI agents accessing Indian organisations' systems raised questions about access controls and monitoring in autonomous systems. Coforge said security teams can identify vulnerabilities quickly, but remediation remains largely manual. Fragmented workflows, resource shortages, and complex enterprise environments can delay fixes and leave organisations exposed. "The cybersecurity industry has spent years optimising vulnerability discovery, but most enterprises already know where their risks are," said Ashish Kumar, Global Head, Cloud and AI Infrastructure, Coforge. "Agentic attackers can find a weakness and exploit it in a matter of hours, yet traditional remediation takes weeks." Nuuron provides the orchestration, governance, auditability, and policy enforcement framework for the remediation agents. Forward-deployed engineers work within client environments to handle exceptions escalated by the agents, investigate recurring vulnerabilities, and make policy-driven decisions that require human judgment. In October, Coforge introduced an Autonomous Software Factory to coordinate AI agents across software development activities, with human oversight. The expanded Nuuron offering also covers security requirements specific to enterprise AI deployments, including agent security, model governance, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) security, access controls, sensitive data exposure, and AI-related policy compliance. The service integrates with existing security, DevSecOps, and change-management systems. Coforge did not disclose customer deployments, commercial terms, or quantified improvements in vulnerability closure times from the expanded offering.

items.title: AI wrote the code. Can your test data tell you if it works?
items.summary: As organizations invest in AI , many are discovering a new bottleneck: obtaining data that is both protected and useful. Engineering teams need realistic, production-like data to validate AI-generated changes, train models, test applications, and generate business insights. Yet, privacy initiatives can sometimes make that data harder to access, less representative of real-world conditions, or unable to preserve critical relationships between records. The Perforce Delphix “2026 State of AI and Data Privacy Report ” highlights this challenge. Among surveyed organizations, 26% say privacy controls make production-quality data harder to obtain, 25% struggle to preserve relationships across data entities, and 51% cite data quality challenges. “Protecting data isn’t enough if it can no longer support the systems that depend on it.” Protecting data isn’t enough if it can no longer support the systems that depend on it. For engineering teams, the question is whether their data protection strategies can preserve the qualities that make data valuable in the first place. You need a well-rounded data strategy with tools that maintain referential integrity and relationships across your environments. What these statistics mean for practitioners At first glance, statistics from the report, like “51% of enterprises cite data quality challenges,” may sound like a purely governance issue. In practice, they represent engineering problems. Low-quality datasets can produce: Inaccurate analytics. Poorly trained AI models. Incomplete test coverage. Increased rework. Delayed releases. Reduced confidence in data automation . “When an AI model is trained on incomplete or distorted data, its outputs become less reliable.” When an AI model is trained on incomplete or distorted data, its outputs become less reliable. When test environments contain unrealistic data, defects can escape into production. When analytics datasets lack consistency, teams spend more time validating results than acting on them. Data protection and utility are not opposing goals A common misconception is that organizations must choose between privacy and innovation, but the most successful organizations know that compliance, quality, and speed can and need to work together. Protected data still needs to be: Realistic enough for testing and validation. Representative enough for analytics. Accessible enough for engineering teams. Governed enough for regulatory requirements . Connected enough to preserve referential integrity. There’s a two-fold goal in the AI era: reduce sensitive data exposure while also creating trusted data that remains valuable after protection. All too often, enterprises sacrifice compliance for innovation or speed. That’s a big reason 84% of respondents in our report have a data privacy exception in their non-production environments. “There’s a two-fold goal in the AI era: reduce sensitive data exposure while also creating trusted data that remains valuable after protection.” Organizations can only move at AI speed when they have access to trustworthy data that accurately represents production conditions. When privacy controls degrade quality, limit realism, or restrict access to representative datasets, the data layer becomes the new bottleneck. Why referential integrity matters more than ever Many discussions about data privacy focus on masking sensitive fields. However, masked data that loses referential integrity between entities can create a different kind of risk. A customer, order, or payment record may still exist, but if the relationships connecting those records break during protection processes, the data no longer resembles reality. Take billing validation, for example. It needs referential integrity when a customer has multiple products, charges, and invoices across several database tables to produce the correct products or make accurate charges. Broken relationships are especially problematic for modern AI and analytics systems. Analytics pipelines depend on consistent identifiers to join information across sources. AI and machine learning workflows depend on complete business context to identify patterns and make predictions. Software testing depends on realistic relationships between records to validate application behavior accurately. When referential integrity is lost: Analytics can produce incomplete or misleading results . AI models can learn from flawed datasets. Testing environments can fail to expose production issues. Teams lose trust in protected datasets. Importantly, these failures are often difficult to detect. Pipelines may continue running successfully while quietly producing degraded outcomes, which can be a very costly mistake. This helps explain why 25% of surveyed organizations cited preserving relationships across data entities as a significant challenge. For practitioners, that statistic is a warning that privacy controls can unintentionally undermine the quality of AI and analytics initiatives if they fail to preserve business context. Keep in mind that not all data protection solutions are created equal — enterprise-grade masking algorithms are key to preserving relationships. When applied consistently and at scale , these algorithms ensure the same input produces the same masked output across your systems and environments. Other masking approaches might be done piecemeal, resulting in broken relationships. What engineering teams should measure Many organizations measure privacy success through compliance metrics alone. However, AI-driven environments require a broader definition of success. Engineering leaders should evaluate privacy initiatives against several dimensions: Data quality: Does the protected dataset accurately reflect production conditions? Realism: Can developers, data scientists, and analysts use the data confidently for their intended purpose? Referential integrity: Do relationships remain consistent across applications, tables, environments, and data sources? Accessibility: Can teams obtain compliant data without introducing delays? Provisioning speed: How quickly can trusted datasets be delivered when needed? These measurements help organizations determine whether privacy efforts enable AI outcomes or create new obstacles. Designing for governance by default As AI adoption grows, privacy cannot remain a separate process that occurs after development begins. Organizations should instead map the entire data lifecycle, from data request and discovery to reuse and retirement. This approach helps ensure governance is built into workflows rather than applied as a late-stage checkpoint. It also provides stronger auditability, reduces compliance exceptions, and gives teams greater confidence that protected datasets remain fit for purpose. Most importantly, it aligns privacy objectives with business outcomes instead of treating them as competing priorities. Trusted data will become a competitive differentiator The need for test data — in volume, coverage, and scale — is booming as agentic development continues to rise . AI has also increased the volume of change enterprises can generate, but the challenge of validating that change remains unsolved. That responsibility still belongs to data. The organizations that gain the most value from AI will not necessarily be the ones with the most advanced models. They will be the ones with the most trustworthy data foundations — using a portfolio approach that combines data virtualization for speed, masking for security, and synthetic data for coverage as needed. “In the AI era, trusted data, not fast model output, may be the ultimate competitive advantage.” The research points to a clear lesson: If privacy controls uphold realism, quality, relationships between records, or access to representative datasets, they can enable AI success. As enterprises continue investing in AI and data privacy, the real objective should be ensuring protection and utility coexist. Because in the AI era, trusted data, not fast model output, may be the ultimate competitive advantage.

items.title: A developer ran 50 agents at once. Then his Mac became the bottleneck.
items.summary: As developers move from working with individual AI coding agents to orchestrating dozens of concurrent sessions, the hardware they use to develop software is becoming a potential bottleneck. In a post on X Monday, a developer named Pranit described how running more than 50 concurrent agent sessions exposed the biggest bottleneck in his development workflow: his Mac. Vercel CTO Malte Ubl responded that he had encountered the same limitations in his own development workflow. “No single computer is fast enough to keep up with dozens of agents working on parallel.” “No single computer is fast enough to keep up with dozens of agents working on parallel,” Ubl writes . Rather than moving the agents themselves to the cloud, Ubl keeps them running locally and offloads builds and tests to remote sandboxes. Developers can retain their existing tools and workflows without being constrained by the compute capacity of a single machine. “Dozens of agents can all decide to run a build at the same time,” Ubl tells The New Stack . “They’re competing for the same machine, and everything slows down.” When agents outrun one machine Even when model inference runs in the cloud, compilation, dependency management, and test execution initiated by coding agents can place significant demands on local CPU and memory. Separating agent orchestration from code execution lets developers scale those workloads independently of their local hardware. Separating orchestration from execution Developers can install the Vercel Plugin by running npx plugins add vercel/vercel-plugin and then instruct their coding agents to offload builds and tests to remote sandboxes. One technical challenge of remote execution is maintaining consistency between the local workspace and the sandbox, particularly when agents modify code that hasn’t been committed. Ubl tells The New Stack that execution begins from a snapshot with dependencies already installed. The current source code, including uncommitted edits and new files that aren’t excluded by Git ignore rules, is then copied to the sandbox. Dependencies persist in the remote environment and are updated when they change. “You shouldn’t have to commit and push just to test what an agent is working on.” “You shouldn’t have to commit and push just to test what an agent is working on,” Ubl says. Unlike conventional CI workflows triggered by repository events, this approach brings remote execution into the development feedback loop itself. Agents can validate changes before committing, and computationally expensive tasks no longer need to compete for the same local resources. When remote execution pays off There is no specific number of concurrent agents at which remote execution becomes more efficient than running builds and tests locally. The crossover depends on the project’s computational requirements, the frequency of builds and tests, network latency, and the cost of provisioning remote infrastructure. “You have to weigh the upload, setup time and cloud compute cost against the time saved.” “You have to weigh the upload, setup time and cloud compute cost against the time saved,” Ubl tells The New Stack . “Warm snapshots help.” In Seoul, regional image caching brought sandbox startup times down from roughly 3.5 seconds to 1.05 seconds, according to benchmarks published by Vercel . But spinning up a sandbox is only part of the equation. Developers still have to transfer source files and pay for remote compute. Vercel did not provide benchmarks comparing the total time or cost of running builds and tests locally versus remotely. Local execution may still make more sense when running a handful of agents on a small codebase. The economics could change when dozens of agents compete for CPU and memory to run builds and tests concurrently. Local development goes distributed Remote build systems and cloud-based development environments predate AI coding agents. What’s changing is the number of concurrent workloads an individual engineer can generate. “As developers run more agents in parallel, I expect this split to become common,” Ubl tells The New Stack.

items.title: Inside Our Autonomous Software Factory: How AI Agents Write, Test and Ship Our Code
items.summary: You hand it a few feature requests. Minutes later it hands back a pull request that has been planned, tested, reviewed and tried out by an agent playing your customer. What we learned running AI agents as an assembly line, told through one small made-up example: a loyalty card for a coffee chain. For two months, a team of AI agents has built the features of our in-house product. They work like a production line: each agent has one job, and its work gets checked before the next one starts. Our first version cost more to build than the product it shipped. The second one works, and it rests on one rule: Code decides what runs next. Agents only judge. A small Python program called fx keeps each batch's state in files, picks the next agent and refuses any hand-back that breaks a rule. Agents read, plan, code and review, but none of them can move a batch forward. The whole line on one screen. A person works at only two stations, the brief and the ship. Everything else runs in the background, watched by fx. The example Three small wishes for a coffee chain Picture Brewline, a loyalty app for a coffee chain with three outlets. The owner wants three things, each written as a short story with numbered acceptance criteria. Hidden in it are a money question (is a free coffee any size?), a time-zone trap (when does a birthday start?) and a privacy hole (can outlet A see outlet B’s customers?). Watch where each gets caught. The team Who works on the line Sixteen roles work the line. Some are agents on a strong model, some on a cheaper one, and some are plain code that never makes a judgment call. Plan The crew. Amber is you: once in planning, once at the end. Every other role gets a narrow job and hands back JSON that fx checks before anything else happens. Step 1 · Planning What do robot planners argue about? One command starts it: /factory new loyalty S1 S2 S3. Planning the loyalty batch. Two problems get caught here, before anyone writes a line of feature code. A cheap reader per story lists every spot where a builder would have to guess. The birthday reader asks: with servers on UTC, does a customer in Mumbai get the pastry at midnight or at 5:30 in the morning? S1 and S2 both touch RewardService, so fx builds them as one group. Planners read the code and outline a test for every criterion. The product lead never reads code, on purpose, because an agent that reads code tends to accept whatever it already does. It settles three questions from the spec and sends the two about money to a person. The critic tries to break each plan, with evidence. It finds that a refunded coffee keeps its stamp and that baristas would see all three outlets, both fixed before any test exists. Then the tests are written and run on today’s code. Each must fail, because a test that passes before the feature exists proves nothing. Step 2 · The only meeting Two questions, one reply, six minutes Five questions come in and two reach the owner. The brief fits on one page and can be answered from a phone. Here the owner takes the recommendation on size and overrides it on the birthday window. On approval, fx locks the nine tests, moves the Jira tickets and writes each answer back into the story file, so the spec stays the one source of truth. Anything that isn't money, rules, access or a surprise gets a default the owner can overturn. Step 3 · Build Round after round, until nothing is left to find The build loop. Reviewers only look at code whose checks pass, and every way out of the loop leads either to “ready” or to a person Each story gets a fresh builder, and risk picks its model: the birthday story gives away food, so it gets the stronger one. Gates check every commit the moment a builder says “done”. If a locked test was changed, or a test deleted or skipped, the work goes straight back to the same builder while it still remembers why. Reviewers only see code whose checks pass, and later rounds re-read only what changed. A reviewer can record anything, but to block it must bring proof that fx can verify: The loyalty batch, round by round. Group 1 needed three rounds and group 2 needed one. They ran at the same time, each in its own copy of the code. The reviewer that orders the coffee In round 2 every test passed and the code looked fine. One reviewer still failed it, because it doesn’t read code. fx starts a throwaway copy of the app in Docker, and an agent signs in as each persona and works through the criteria the way they would. It buys ten coffees. It asks for another outlet's numbers. Anything short of a pass blocks. Everything that reads code said yes. The server even sent the reward, but the screen had no way to show it, so the customer saw an error. Only an agent using the app could catch that. This part is real. In our first real batch, the live check found the only two real bugs, and no test or code reviewer had caught either. That’s why it now runs in every round. Step 4 · Ship and learn One yes, then three lessons at most fx ship merges in the latest main branch, reruns every check and writes the pull request: each criterion with its test and result, plus what got fixed and what's still open. The owner confirms once, and the factory never merges its own work. All of its state lives in files, so a crashed session or a closed laptop just means typing /factory next later. Afterwards a lessons agent proposes three lessons at most, like “a birthday is a local date, so test 00:30 and 23:30 India time.” The owner keeps the good ones, and the next batch reads them. Brains and tokens Who gets the expensive brain? Each role’s model is a line in a config file. A round that fails on the cheaper model moves the next round up to the stronger one. Two things surprised us. A cheaper model saves only 17 to 40 percent, because most of what an agent reads comes from the cache, which costs about the same on both. And the biggest waste is reading the same thing twice, so nearly every saving came from agents reading less. TOKENS Where do the tokens go? Every agent run is logged with its tokens and tied to the group, story and round it worked on. We show tokens rather than dollars, so you can price them at whatever rate you pay. Where the tokens went in our biggest batch. Builders use the most, and the session that steers everything comes second. That second line is the one we most want to shrink. Four real batches, in the order they ran, counting the agents only; the steering session comes on top. The 3-story batch ran long because one criterion depended on a story nobody had linked, and it failed the live check the same way for six rounds. A circuit breaker now stops that after two. Lessons What we’d tell anyone building one The factory can cost more than the product. Our first engine grew to 19,000 lines and cost about five times the product work it shipped. The second has a line limit a test enforces. Make reviewers prove it. An agent that double-checked every block overturned 0 of 16, so we deleted it. Now a block needs proof the engine can check. Use the product, don’t just read it. The agent that taps through the running app caught what tests and code reviewers missed. The conductor is the hidden bill. The session that steers everything still takes 18 to 41 percent of each batch, against our 15 percent target. Count tokens, not dollars. On a flat subscription, one more batch costs no extra cash. Tokens show the work, and the real limit is the plan’s usage cap. The product got better, not just faster. Every criterion has a test that failed before the code and passes after, and bugs get caught in the running app before the merge. None of this replaces engineering judgment. It moves that judgment to the two moments that matter most: writing the spec before the work starts, and saying yes before it ships. Everything in between is a line we can measure, and we keep making it cheaper. items.title: Read the pitch decks of 19 startups looking to disrupt dating apps and social networking that have raised millions
items.summary: iStock; Rebecca Zisser/BI New social, professional networking, and dating startups are coming onto the scene. VCs and angel investors are funding some of these promising startups. Here are the pitch decks 19 startups used while raising rounds or getting acquired. A new generation of consumer social startups is emerging. From platforms focused on getting people to meet IRL to dating apps taking on Tinder or Hinge, startups are disrupting the digital social scene. Founders of these startups are tackling problems like loneliness , dating app fatigue , and general dissatisfaction with the current social media incumbents. Some founders come from Big Tech backgrounds, like the Instagram-heavy team behind photo-sharing app Retro, or the ex-Google employees building the social-mapping app PamPam. Gen Z founders are also throwing their hats in the ring, like Isabella Epstein with her IRL-focused app Kndrd, and becoming content creators along the way. Investors are taking notice. Meet 22 VCs and investors eyeing new social startups Some venture capital funds — such as French firm Intuition VC or gaming-focused firm Patron — have made tackling loneliness and relationships part of their investment theses. But it's not just friendship and dating that are ripe for disruption. Startups like Khosla Ventures-backed Gigi , Yale student-founded Series , Boardy, and Goodword have raised capital for AI tools to help people network more effectively or maintain professional relationships . "When people think about loneliness, they think about friends and family," Goodword CEO Caroline Dell told Business Insider. "But we spend most of our waking hours at work as professionals." Other startups, like social network Spill, have opened investment rounds to users themselves via the Wefunder platform. Meet the founders of 11 startups competing with dating app giants like Tinder It's not yet clear how many of these investments will pan out. Some startups are pre-revenue, while others are experimenting with monetization models (such as freemium). "Founders have to be honest with themselves," said Marlon Nichols, a founding partner at Mac Venture Capital . "Some of them aren't really venture-scale or venture-type investments. We're looking for the next big thing, the next category leader." Meet 19 startups in social networking, dating, and AI that investors have their eyes on In the AI era, investors have their eyes set elsewhere, forcing social media startups to get creative with their early monetization and fundraising strategies. Check out 2 charts tracking VC funding in social apps since 2019 Business Insider spoke with several social media and dating app founders about the pitch decks they used to raise millions or ink deals. Read the pitch decks from 19 social-networking and dating startups: Note: Pitch decks are sorted by investment stage and size of round. Series A Posh, an event-based social network based in New York City: $22 million Series A (12 pages) Spoon Radio, a social-audio startup: $17 million (15 pages) Clyx, an app to make plans with friends and meet new people: $14 million (22 pages) Pie, an IRL social startup founded by Bonobos' Andy Dunn: $11.5 million (31 pages) Meet5, an IRL social app for Gen X and baby boomers: about $9 million (11 pages) Howbout, a social-calendar app to help people make plans with friends: $8 million (12 pages) Seed Ditto, an AI-powered dating startup for college students: $9.2 million (12 pages) Hangout, a social music platform: $8.2 million seed (26 pages) Goodword, an AI copilot that wants to help people make deeper professional connections: $4 million seed (11 pages) First Round's On Me, a dating app that prioritizes making plans over swiping and DMs: $3 million (16 pages) Escargot, a greeting card app that sends snail mail with the help of AI: $2.75 million (Notion memo) Seam Social, a Web3-inspired social network that lets users make mini-apps: $2.5 million (10 pages) Cerca, a dating app focused on matching people with mutual friends: $1.6 million (10 pages) Pre-Seed Dalet Labs, the company behind a new AI social shopping app called Scene: $7 million (5 pages) Keeper, an AI matchmaking service that wants to help people find their soulmates: $4 million (20 pages) Series, an AI professional network for college students: $5.1 million pre-seed (10 pages). Read the pitch deck it's using to raise its next round, too. Other Arya, an AI concierge app helping couples spice up the bedroom, shared the deck it used to raise a $21 million growth funding round (17 pages) Rodeo, a social shopping platform, shared the pitch deck it used to get accepted into an A16z startup accelerator (11 pages) Read the materials that helped this startup get acquired: Flamme, an app for couples wanting to keep the spark alive, was acquired by AI relationship wellness company Arya. Read the LinkedIn DM and two slides from its pitch deck that helped seal the deal. Read about more social networking and dating startups raising millions: Retro, a social app that feels like the old days of Instagram, raised $21 million in Series A funding. Airbuds, a social music app, told Business Insider in November that it has raised $10.2 million — including a recent check from Alexis Ohanian's VC fund. Sweatpals, a fitness and wellness social platform, raised $12 million in seed funding. Corner, a social mapping app for Gen Z, has raised $7.5 million in funding . Bond, a social app that uses AI to document memories, raised a $5 million seed round. Amata, another AI matchmaking dating startup, recently launched in the US and disclosed that it raised $6 million in 2023. Gigi, an AI social network for making professional connections, announced in September that it raised $3 million from Khosla Ventures. Sitch, an AI matchmaking dating app, announced in April that it had raised $2 million in pre-seed funding. Danger Testing, a vibe coding and content startup, raised $2.6 million in venture capital funding. Left Field, a dating app, got a spot on 'Shark Tank' and scored a $200,000 investment from Alexis Ohanian and Kendra Scott. Fizz, an anonymous social app for college students, raised an undisclosed SAFE to expand globally and grow its ads business. Read the original article on Business Insider

"All I want is to make the best videos possible and help as many people as I can while doing it." MrBeast allegations, criticism, controversy, and lawsuits With great visibility comes great scrutiny. In July 2024, Donaldson's childhood friend and coworker Ava Kris Tyson was accused of inappropriately messaging a 13-year-old . Tyson apologized for "bad edgy jokes" on X but said she'd never groomed anyone. She said that she and Donaldson had "mutually decided" to cut ties. Donaldson said on X that he was "disgusted" by the allegations and had hired a third party to investigate. The investigation into various issues at the company ultimately concluded that claims of sexual misconduct between employees and minors were "without basis." The alleged victim also said on X that the grooming claims were false. Donaldson's hit Amazon competition series "Beast Games" was preceded by controversies. MrBeast / X Donaldson's "Beast Games" series was also beset by controversies. Contestants on the show alleged a number of safety concerns, including a lack of access to food and medical care, and injuries during a preliminary shoot. News of the allegations was first reported by The New York Times. A rep for MrBeast previously told BI that the shoot "was unfortunately complicated by the CrowdStrike incident, extreme weather, and other unexpected logistical and communications issues." One former "Beast Games" crew member also told BI he was nearly crushed by a concrete-like structure on set in Toronto. After BI contacted Donaldson's team for comment, the crew member said a production rep had contacted him, saying they were "here to support me and provided me some things I can't share." Five of the contestants on the show filed a class-action lawsuit in September 2024, alleging sexual harassment and dangerous conditions. The case is pending. In November 2024, Donaldson addressed some of the allegations around the show on X, saying they were "blown out of proportion." Around the same time as the "Beast Games" controversy, Donaldson also acknowledged an old clip that resurfaced on social media in which he could be seen making homophobic and racist comments. A spokesperson said in a statement to multiple outlets at the time that Donaldson "repeatedly apologized and has learned that increasing influence comes with increased responsibility." In April, a former MrBeast employee, Lorrayne Mavromatis , sued the company, alleging it violated the Family and Medical Leave Act and retaliated against her after she reported sexual harassment and a hostile work environment. items.summary_html:
Beast Industries is trying to expand beyond its famous founder, Jimmy Donaldson.

Sujit JAISWAL / AFP via Getty Images

  • Jimmy "MrBeast" Donaldson went from growing up in a small city to becoming the king of YouTube.
  • The 28-year-old is seeking to build a Disney-style content empire with multiple consumer brands.
  • It hasn't been easy. Donaldson has weathered scandals and lawsuits along the way.

MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, is the biggest YouTuber on earth. For an influencer, the 28-year-old keeps some personal details close to the vest.

Donaldson's unlikely rise started in Greenville, North Carolina — the small city where he still resides and where his burgeoning company, Beast Industries, is headquartered.

Beyond online stardom, Donaldson has taken Hollywood by storm with his hit streaming show, "Beast Games." He's also building a slew of consumer brands and services in a quest to create a company in the vein of Disney.

Donaldson has also made charity work a key part of his career and personal mission through Beast Philanthropy, and has de-emphasized his own personal wealth despite his vast ambitions.

Here's everything you need to know about who MrBeast is and how he's built his career.

Early life and background

MrBeast was born James Stephen Donaldson on May 7, 1998, and grew up in Greenville, North Carolina. After Donaldson's parents separated, his mother, Sue, raised Donaldson and his older brother CJ as a single parent, he said on "The Diary of a CEO" podcast. Donaldson has said he prefers not to speak about his dad.

Donaldson was an extremely quiet child growing up and didn't have many friends, he said on the "Dhar & Jay Show."

From an early age, Donaldson was obsessed with YouTube and uploaded his first video under the username MrBeast6000. Initially, Donaldson tried to game the YouTube algorithm with different types of videos — from "let's play" gaming streams to commentary videos about other YouTubers. At the time, he was mostly off-camera.

Jimmy Donaldson and Thea Booysen, also a content creator, tied the knot in July 2026.

Jean Catuffe/Getty Images

Unlike some other creators who are an open book, Donaldson keeps mum about many personal details, including his political beliefs.

That said, he frequently discusses living with Crohn's disease, an inflammatory bowel disease.

On the relationships front, Donaldson proposed to his now-wife, Thea Booysen, the content creator and novelist, on Christmas in 2024. They wed on a private island in July 2026.

MrBeast's rise on YouTube

After experimenting with different kinds of videos, Donaldson went viral in 2017 for a video in which he counted from zero to 100,000, a feat he said took more than 40 hours. That year, he surpassed 1 million subscribers.

Other early stunts included reading every word in the dictionary and spinning a fidget spinner for 24 hours. Endurance and last-person-to-leave challenges are still his bread and butter, even as the productions have grown in budget and scope.

In 2020, the average MrBeast video cost $300,000 to make, Bloomberg reported. By 2024, that figure was roughly $3.5 million, he told the creators of "The Colin and Samir Show."

Over time, Donaldson started enacting big-budget stunts with an altruistic bent, such as tipping thousands of dollars to lesser-known Twitch streamers, waitresses, and Uber drivers. By 2018, he said he'd given away $1 million.

Donaldson's friends and collaborators over the years have included Nolan Hansen, Chandler Hallow, Tareq Salameh, Karl Jacobs, and Mack Hopkins.

Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for Prime Video

Donaldson is also known for fastidiously fine-tuning his thumbnails and video titles to maximize engagement.

Donaldson surpassed the Indian production company T-Series as the most-subscribed-to YouTube channel in June 2024. His main MrBeast channel has more than 500 million subscribers. His most popular long-form video, "$456,000 Squid Game In Real Life!," has more than 987 million views.

He's also the third most-followed creator on TikTok, with nearly 148 million followers.

MrBeast's business ventures

While brand deals helped fuel Donaldson's ambitious early videos, his business has ballooned into a nearly 800-person operation that investors have valued at more than $5 billion. Today, it blends media, advertising, chocolate bars, fintech, and more — with ambitions for an IPO.

His company, Beast Industries, generated $473 million in revenue in 2024, according to a pitch deck obtained by Business Insider. The company expected that figure to roughly double in 2025.

Still, Donaldson said in February 2025 that he had less than $1 million in his bank account, as he prefers to reinvest profits back into the company. Because of this, Donaldson's net worth is largely comprised of his stake in Beast Industries.

Beast Industries' businesses include the candy brand Feastables, the packaged food brand Lunchly, a collectible action-figure line dubbed MrBeast Lab, and Viewstats, an analytics platform for creators.

Donaldson is embroiled in a legal battle with Virtual Dining Concepts, his former partner in the ghost-kitchen business MrBeast Burger. He sued the company, alleging it made "terrible quality" burgers under his name, and Virtual Dining Concepts fired back with a breach-of-contract suit. The suits are scheduled to go to trial in December.

Donaldson is embroiled in a lawsuit with his former partner in MrBeast Burger.

MrBeast Burger

On the media front, Donaldson has grown his content operation beyond YouTube. He did a $100 million deal for an Amazon Prime Video show, "Beast Games." While it drove record viewership for Amazon, Donaldson said he lost tens of millions on the first season. Amazon gave it a vote of confidence, renewing it for two more seasons.

Donaldson has stepped back from running parts of his company, appointing former Shutterfly chief executive Jeffrey Housenbold as CEO in 2024 and subsequently hiring a slew of seasoned execs.

He's also tried to lessen the company's reliance on him. He's developing various content verticals to be hosted by different creators.

In September, he published a novel alongside author James Patterson, which debuted at No. 12 on Amazon's new releases chart. About a year ago, he premiered an animated series, "MrBeast Lab: The Descent." The show was based on a MrBeast toy line that became a best-selling new toy property in 2024, according to Circana's retail sales tracking. New episodes were released this fall.

Looking beyond media, Donaldson has discussed plans to expand into new areas, including financial services through the recently acquired Step app, mobile phone plans, and an influencer marketplace. He's also shared plans for a membership program.

MrBeast's philanthropy and social impact

Over the years, Donaldson has incorporated his knack for virality into various charity efforts, including a 2019 campaign to plant 20 million trees, which Elon Musk contributed to.

Donaldson's philanthropic work includes his own charity organization, Beast Philanthropy. However, at times, some of this work has backfired, such as when he was accused of gifting eye surgeries for clout. Donaldson has shrugged off the criticism and said he plans to give away "every penny" he makes to help people before he dies.

Despite his success, Donaldson has often discussed how he prefers to eschew the finer things in life.

"No matter how big I get I'll never own a mansion, yacht, Lamborghini etc," he tweeted in 2022. "All I want is to make the best videos possible and help as many people as I can while doing it."

MrBeast allegations, criticism, controversy, and lawsuits

With great visibility comes great scrutiny. Donaldson has been no stranger to controversy over the years. In 2024, he was involved in multiple scandals.

In July 2024, Donaldson's childhood friend and coworker Ava Kris Tyson was accused of inappropriately messaging a 13-year-old. Tyson apologized for "bad edgy jokes" on X but said she'd never groomed anyone. She said that she and Donaldson had "mutually decided" to cut ties.

Donaldson said on X that he was "disgusted" by the allegations and had hired a third party to investigate. The investigation into various issues at the company ultimately concluded that claims of sexual misconduct between employees and minors were "without basis." The alleged victim also said on X that the grooming claims were false.

Donaldson's hit Amazon competition series "Beast Games" was preceded by controversies.

MrBeast / X

Donaldson's "Beast Games" series was also beset by controversies.

Contestants on the show alleged a number of safety concerns, including a lack of access to food and medical care, and injuries during a preliminary shoot. News of the allegations was first reported by The New York Times.

A rep for MrBeast previously told BI that the shoot "was unfortunately complicated by the CrowdStrike incident, extreme weather, and other unexpected logistical and communications issues."

One former "Beast Games" crew member also told BI he was nearly crushed by a concrete-like structure on set in Toronto. After BI contacted Donaldson's team for comment, the crew member said a production rep had contacted him, saying they were "here to support me and provided me some things I can't share."

Five of the contestants on the show filed a class-action lawsuit in September 2024, alleging sexual harassment and dangerous conditions. The case is pending.

In November 2024, Donaldson addressed some of the allegations around the show on X, saying they were "blown out of proportion."

Around the same time as the "Beast Games" controversy, Donaldson also acknowledged an old clip that resurfaced on social media in which he could be seen making homophobic and racist comments. A spokesperson said in a statement to multiple outlets at the time that Donaldson "repeatedly apologized and has learned that increasing influence comes with increased responsibility."

In April, a former MrBeast employee, Lorrayne Mavromatis, sued the company, alleging it violated the Family and Medical Leave Act and retaliated against her after she reported sexual harassment and a hostile work environment. The company broadly denied the allegations. The case is pending.
