items.title: Google's AI Mode Can Now Read Your Wallet, With Drive Coming Next
items.summary: Google is letting its AI Mode in Search
items.summary_html:
Google is letting its AI Mode in Search read more of users' personal data. Personal Intelligence in AI Mode can now connect to Google Wallet, and support for Google Drive will follow in the coming weeks.

Personal Intelligence arrived in AI Mode earlier this year. It pulls information from a user's Google apps to personalize answers. Google says the new connections are strictly opt-in: users have to turn them on manually, and can turn them off again later.

What AI Mode Can Do With Wallet and Drive

Robby Stein, Google's VP for Search, said a more connected Search can give users insights into their digital life. With Wallet connected, Google says AI Mode can:

  • track financial "milestones"
  • offer advice on ways to improve spending
  • help users get the most out of the benefits of the credit cards saved in Wallet

Google stresses that AI Mode can read financial data from a user's accounts, but cannot move, manage or invest money on their behalf.

Once Drive support arrives, AI Mode will be able to scan PDFs, documents and other files stored in Google Drive to add context to answers and suggest ideas.

Gemini and AI Mode Share Context

Google is also linking its two AI products more closely. In the coming weeks, users will be able to start a conversation in the Gemini app and continue it in AI Mode in Search, or the other way around.

Users could already connect their Search history to Personal Intelligence in the Gemini app. Now they will also be able to connect Gemini to AI Mode. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode will also give more personalized answers based on a user's recent search context.

The changes coming to AI Mode:

  • Now: Google Wallet can be connected to Personal Intelligence
  • Coming weeks: Google Drive support
  • Coming weeks: conversations that move between the Gemini app and AI Mode
Privacy Considerations

The features are designed to make Search more useful, but they also give Google's AI direct access to financial information and personal documents. Users who care about privacy should think about which apps they connect.

Since everything is opt-in, nothing changes for users who do not turn the connections on. Those who try them can disconnect Wallet or Drive at a later date if they change their mind.

The move is part of Google's push to turn Search into a personal assistant built around AI Mode, even though Google has acknowledged on its latest earnings call that AI Mode still earns less money than traditional search.

items.title: What to do if your Thanksgiving flight is delayed or canceled due to weather
items.summary: Here's what to do if you get caught up in holiday travel chaos. Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Storms are expected to bring heavy rainfall across the US on Thanksgiving. Weather is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies. Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled. Holiday travelers have begun to experience some flight delays and cancellations on Thanksgiving as a series of storms hit the US . If you're wondering what your options are if the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, weather or an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. It was the same situation during the five-hour nationwide ground stop on November 13 that led to over 12,000 flight cancellations. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due weather or other non-controllable factor would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted. 1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the US Airline passengers have some customer rights in the US. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: 1-602-333-5925 JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers . Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as Chase's Sapphire Reserve and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs. Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). items.summary_html:
Here's what to do if you get caught up in holiday travel chaos.

Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images

  • Storms are expected to bring heavy rainfall across the US on Thanksgiving.
  • Weather is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies.
  • Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled.

Holiday travelers have begun to experience some flight delays and cancellations on Thanksgiving as a series of storms hit the US.

If you're wondering what your options are if the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out.

According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, weather or an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions.

That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. It was the same situation during the five-hour nationwide ground stop on November 13 that led to over 12,000 flight cancellations.

Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard, which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due weather or other non-controllable factor would not fall under crew scheduling.

Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card.

Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted.

1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the USAirline passengers have some customer rights in the US.

Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images

According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events.

The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats.

If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control.

The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations.

2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking optionsMost airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online.

Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images

When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog.

Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person.

If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night.

Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent.

Here are the phone numbers for each airline:

  • Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008
  • Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888
  • American: 1-800-433-7300
  • Avelo: 1-346-616-9500
  • Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger.
  • Delta: 1-800-221-1212
  • Frontier: 1-602-333-5925
  • JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583
  • Southwest: 1-800-435-9792
  • United: 1-800-864-8331
3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucherThe Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport.

: Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers. 

Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard.

Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher.

For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask.

It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier.

4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insuranceAmerican Express and Chase have travel credit cards.

Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images

Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance, such as Chase's Sapphire Reserve and American Express' Platinum Card. Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit.

For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US.

However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs. 

Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim.

5. Know when to walk awayConsider renting a car or taking the train.

Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images

Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance).

If you are stuck in another city and have no other option but to stay in a hotel or wait at the airport, decide how you want to spend your time and make a plan.

items.title: Elon Musk floats a truly wild figure for SpaceX's potential value: $128 quintillion
items.summary: Elon Musk says SpaceX could be worth an astonishing sum in the future. Jae C. Hong/AP Elon Musk says SpaceX could be worth around $128 quintillion, or 75 million times its value today. It would have to colonize other planets and harness a tiny fraction of the Sun's energy, he said. "I recommend holding on to your shares," Musk posted on X. Elon Musk is going galactic with his latest claim of what SpaceX might be worth one day: $128 quintillion. That's 128 billion billions, or 128 trillion millions, or 128 followed by 18 zeros: 128,000,000,000,000,000,000. "If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun's energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy," Musk said in an early morning X post on Thursday. The IMF puts the value of the world economy at around $128 trillion. Musk's post suggests SpaceX could be worth a million times that much, or $128 quintillion. That would be a roughly 75 million-fold increase from its $1.7 trillion market capitalization as of Wednesday's close. "These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them," Musk wrote. "I recommend holding on to your shares." If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy. These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them. I recommend holding on to your shares. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026 Musk's post implies that a single SpaceX share, worth around $127 at Wednesday's close, could one day be worth $9.5 billion or so, assuming no dilution. The world's wealthiest man is no stranger to making wild, unfounded claims about SpaceX's potential value. He posted in October that the maker of Starlink, Starship, Grok, and X could eventually be worth " orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy." Musk later posted that wasn't a "statement of extreme confidence," but a belief that "there is such a path and the probability of achieving it is not zero." SpaceX generated $14.6 billion of revenue last quarter , up 161% from the same period last year, and swung from a $1.1 billion net loss to a $4.4 billion net income. Musk posted in October that SpaceX hitting $1 trillion in annual revenue in 2028 was " no longer impossible ." Even if it reaches that mark, then grows revenue another 1,000-fold to $1 quadrillion, that would still be less than 1% of $128 quintillion. He made his latest claim about SpaceX's potential price tag after pledging to match the company's gift of one share to every active Trump Account. The rocket maker said it was part of his commitment to give one of his SpaceX shares to " every kid in America " next year. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.summary: Welcome to Runtime. Ed Targett stepping in today for Tom Krazit , because we miserable Brits don't know what Thanksgiving is. Not already spending quality time with family, or need an escape from them already? We're here in your hour of need. Let's lock in. In today's newsletter, we mull the decisions of Uber's engineers; note that Cloudflare's were ahead of the curve with Code Mode; implore Nutanix not to hire CJ Desai (jokes); revisit a stock exchange CTO's views on AI economics, and read some juicy Microsoft research. Skills for skills for prompts for work Not every workflow – let's just call it a task – needs to be a call-and-response between an engineer and a choir of agents singing back. Uber – briefly headline-grabbing earlier this year for its CTO going "whoops, where did the AI budget disappear to again?"; less headline-grabbing for actually being militantly focused on impressively improving profitability and free cash flow, mostly by giving drivers less money – has learned this the fast and furious way, it appears , after over its staff added over 5,000 homegrown "skills" to a homegrown skills marketplace. “Code is cheaper, easier to test, and has better outcomes for deterministic work than LLMs” Uber's engineers this week Vendors, it has learned – like others – design MCP servers to expose full product capabilities because they can't anticipate specific customer usage. If you don't do some early wrenching to avoid exposing them to a model each time you call it and you end up with... voluminous token use. Welcome to Runtime. Ed Targett stepping in today for Tom Krazit, because we miserable Brits don't know what Thanksgiving is.

Not already spending quality time with family, or need an escape from them already? We're here in your hour of need. Let's lock in.

In today's newsletter, we mull the decisions of Uber's engineers; note that Cloudflare's were ahead of the curve with Code Mode; implore Nutanix not to hire CJ Desai (jokes); revisit a stock exchange CTO's views on AI economics, and read some juicy Microsoft research. Read on.

If Runtime was forwarded to you, you can sign up here for free.

Skills for skills for prompts for work

Not every workflow – let's just call it a task – needs to be a call-and-response between an engineer and a choir of agents singing back.

Uber – briefly headline-grabbing earlier this year for its CTO going "whoops, where did the AI budget disappear to again?"; less headline-grabbing for actually being militantly focused on impressively improving profitability and free cash flow, mostly by giving drivers less money – has learned this the fast and furious way, it appears, after over its staff added over 5,000 homegrown "skills" to a homegrown skills marketplace.

“Code is cheaper, easier to test, and has better outcomes for deterministic work than LLMs” Uber's engineers this week

Vendors, it has learned – like others – design MCP servers to expose full product capabilities because they can't anticipate specific customer usage. If you don't do some early wrenching to avoid exposing them to a model each time you call it and you end up with... voluminous token use.

The below, loosely, is where many organisations are converging...

Your models are gorging on pointless instructions. Anthropic, Cloudflare, Uber have converged on a solution
Ye Olde Fashioned software engineering solves a lot of AI economics problems…
Who wants Rajiv's job?

Nutanix's softly spoken, engineer-turned-CEO Rajiv Ramswami is off to pastures as-yet unknown. Also, as-yet unknown, is who will replace him.

The hyperconverged single pane of glass-flinger is hiring.

Throw your hat into the ring? (Paging Mike McKee.)

Nutanix's CEO wobbles show succession is hard. Ask MongoDB
Rajiv Ramaswami will leave Nutanix by April at the latest, it has been announced. There's no heir apparent, nor an interim.

Side note and side quest; The above was written by new guy on the team, Adam, who we are putting through a journalism scholarship, because, well, most old tech journalists are burned out and most young ones really just want to write about football or celebrities or wars. Adam's already done the writing about football thing and isn't burned out yet. (Give us time...) He does a day per week with us whilst in training. From February, he's full time and you will be seeing a lot more of him.

We'll be doing this again – paying for a talented youngster to do an intensive six-month multimedia journalism diploma in London then giving them a paid six-month placement with the possibility to make it permanent. If you're mulling a career change and this is a bit of you (hey, Rajiv, it doesn't pay as well but it's pretty fun?) then get in touch,

The rest of The Stack

Real money: Dell's doing its server-buyer diligence, it insists.

Dell Q3 earnings release shows $132bn AI server backlog
Dell has pooh-poohed fears that customers behind its titanic AI server orderbook may not be able to pay up.

Big ones: Apropos Tom Krazit's recent interview with Matt Garman and given it is a quiet week – bar the ongoing global awakening that the internet is held together with duct tape, you should probably pull everything off it, patching mainframes under pressure is scary, etc. - I thought I'd resurface some recent interviews.

Trade this: Here's the London Stock Exchange Group's CTO Ken Beinert on AI unit economics, innovation, and P&L for tokenomics.

LSEG CTO on AI unit economics, innovation, and P&L for tokenomics
“We want to develop the right evals to measure accuracy, quality, latency, feel and experience as well as cost.”

Roaches: Here's Cockroach Labs CEO Spencer Kimball on the rise of Bring Your Own Cloud. the economics of agentic traffic, and “bastardised” Postgres wrappers.

The Big Interview: Cockroach Labs CEO Spencer Kimball
On BYOC, the economics of agentic traffic, and “bastardised” Postgres wrappers

Factory reset: Here's Nestle's Group CIO on the perils of getting all cheerful about the cool stuff you can do with digital twins based on telemetry from your factories when everyone wants to hack you (I paraphrase.) Plus a lot more

The Big Interview: Nestlé Group Group CDIO, Chris Wright
270,000+ staff, 335 factories, 7,000 applications, 30 "billionaire" brands; a lot of spinning plates.

Finally, in partnership with decision intelligence firm Quantexa:

“Too often, sovereignty is reduced to a question of nationality. In reality, what matters is control... A domestic black box is still a black box, while a foreign-built system that is fully auditable and transferable may provide far greater sovereign control.”
Buy the plumbing, keep the keys: new rules for sovereign AI procurement
Best-of-breed vs build it vs sovereign?

All that and more on the homepage.

Quote of the week
"The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa." Levent Alpöge.
We're also reading...
  • "How much do coding agents over-edit, and why? An empirical study of unneeded edits in repository-level agent patches." Via Microsoft.
  • "US economics outlook: The end of the inflation shocks." Via Goldman Sachs.
  • HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT: Via Scott Aaronson.

Enjoy Thanksgiving, those of you celebrating.

Hope to see many of our readers at re:Invent.

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people. The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.title: FCC clears SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites for orbital AI data centers by 2040
items.summary: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites to process AI data as orbital data centers. SpaceX is targeting its first launches in 2027, and the full constellation is set to be operating by 2040. Google and Blue Origin are also working on AI infrastructure in space, but Boston Consulting Group estimates costs will stay well above ground-based data centers for now. items.title: The US Navy wants drones to work alongside warships. Sometimes they're better off on their own, defense analysts say.
items.summary: A new report analyzes the US Navy's plans for the future fleet and offers several key takeaways. US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Andrew Langholf Pairing drones with warships isn't always the best approach, defense analysts say. Drones operating separately from crewed ships could be more flexible and effective. The approach could shape how the US uses drones to counter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. The US Navy wants naval drones to help its crewed warships do more, but a new report argues that making them work together might not always be the best approach. Sometimes, drones might prove more useful on their own, defense analysts wrote. The US military has experimented with crewed-uncrewed teaming for years, focusing on how uncrewed systems can complement crewed naval elements by extending reach, sensing, and firepower. But forced manned-unmanned teaming can limit their biggest advantages, specifically their flexibility and the ability to take risks that humans can't. In a new report from the Hudson Institute think tank, authors Bryan Clark, David Byrd, and Dan Patt analyze the Navy's plan to grow the fleet, proposing a more affordable design and structure that adapts to new threats and embraces emerging technologies. Discussing a new theory of victory for the Navy, the authors argue that pairing crewed and uncrewed platforms "tend to suboptimize both the manned and unmanned components of the team and fail to exploit the advantages of each." For example, uncrewed ships could carry additional munitions for crewed vessels, but limitations in speed, range, and protection could demand more frequent refueling and the use of defensive escorts, potentially defeating the purpose of using a naval drone in the first place. Furthermore, drones that aren't equally low-observable could compromise nearby stealthier platforms, while fixing that could get expensive, sacrificing their affordability. Meanwhile, deploying drones alongside crewed warships could undermine the ability to quickly modify and adapt the uncrewed systems. "Manned platforms cannot change sensors, EW [electronic warfare] systems, C2 [command and control] software, or weapons quickly because engineers need to assess the impact on safety and other systems," the report says. Autonomous systems can be modified much faster but could be subject to the same limitations if operating nearby. Clark, Byrd, and Patt provided several real-world examples that demonstrate how uncrewed technologies can operate as independent units. Over the past year, for instance, Ukrainian troops have expanded their use of uncrewed ground vehicles (UGVs) for logistics and medical evacuations, as well as engineering and fire support. Ukraine has increased its employment of ground robots throughout this year, especially for logistics operations and medical evacuations. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images "These operations deliberately use unmanned systems for operations or in places where the Ukrainian commanders do not want to risk human troops, increasingly producing a human-free front line," the authors write. In less-contested environments, soldiers and ground robots can work together, but communications problems, difficult terrain, and the need to refuel and repair robots can complicate operations, potentially putting accompanying troops at risk. The authors argue that the more hands-off approach to uncrewed systems could help the US military counter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. According to the Hudson report, recent Navy Integrated Battle Problems examining a potential Chinese invasion have experimented with using autonomous systems in ways that draw on lessons from Ukrainian, Iranian, and Houthi operations. "By attacking troop transports and their escorts with drone boats, undersea vehicles, and loitering munitions, a force of mostly RAS [robotics and autonomous systems] could slow or disrupt the invasion. This would give US and allied forces targeting information and time to destroy PLA [People's Liberation Army] ships with long-range missiles and torpedo fires," the authors write. US military officials have also explored using large numbers of drones to disrupt Chinese invasion forces in the Taiwan Strait. Adm. Samuel Paparo, the head of US Pacific Command, has referred to it as an "unmanned hellscape" that would effectively act as a first line of defense and buy US, allied, and partner forces time to respond. Clark, Byrd, and Patt's observations come as the US military figures out the roles of uncrewed systems and autonomy and when it's better to use them together with crewed assets or independently. The Navy has looked at drone boats for port security and also used them for rescue and attack missions in the Middle East. The Hudson report's argument isn't that drones should never work alongside crewed ships, but the Navy could get more out of them by giving them missions that take advantage of what they can do on their own. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: “Just ask the model for translation”
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on Rtask, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

You can read the original post in its original format on Rtask website by ThinkR here: “Just ask the model for translation”

I was recently in charge of ensuring the migration from a piece of code that translated text with a translation API to a setup where only LLMs were available. When I asked how to set up the translation, I was told to “just ask the model for translation”. I wish it was that simple

Side note: this blogpost wasn’t written by an LLM, and to prove it, here is a picture of me writing it:

But yes, Claude proof-read it, given that, you know, I’m a French guy writing in English. And fun fact: the French translation was performed by Claude, but that’s easier as I’m able to re-read it 🫣

Context

(Yep, the real client context is not that one but I kept confidentiality)

The product is a Shiny app that allows you to search for a metal band, get the list of available albums, and print the lyrics of all the songs inside a web page. You can then download a pdf of the lyrics on your laptop. The content is stored inside the app as YAML files, where entries are in markdown.

We display on the page both an entry with the band bio (very simple, just {band} is a {style} band from {country}), and the lyrics, in their original language, and a translation in a handful of other languages. Given that these are metal lyrics, the topics can be very specific, and contain names that need to be kept in their original language, and other specificity like places, references, etc.

The content arrives in R as a list of markdown strings, so that it can be both displayed on the page and written to pdf with Quarto. Yes, there might be better solutions to do that, but we’re not here to discuss that. We’re here to talk about the transition from sending this R list of markdown strings to the Google Translation API, to sending it to an LLM.

The issue with LLM translation

Notes: for the sake of demonstration, the code in this section is just a prompt to the API with the model version and “Translate the following text from English to French.”

Notes bis: the outputs below are illustrative.

LLMs are non-deterministic

You can ask them twice the same thing, they might not respond the same. Which is not what we want for our use case, both because of the content and because of the technical format:

  • The markdown should always be kept as is so that it’s rendered correctly,
  • Some parts of the text should stay as is. For example, we might not want the lyrics of “We Are Motörhead” to translate the “Motörhead” part.

For example, here is a long sentence, passed twice to the same model:

> translate(
     "The manager told the developer that she had to review the report with her team before the deadline,
      so the client waiting by the bank asked whether he could bring his own light.",
     model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
 ) |> extract()
[1] "Le manager a dit à la développeuse qu'elle devait revoir le rapport avec son équipe avant la date limite, alors le client qui attendait près de la banque a demandé s'il pouvait apporter sa propre lumière."
> translate(
     "The manager told the developer that she had to review the report with her team before the deadline,
      so the client waiting by the bank asked whether he could bring his own light.",
     model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
) |> extract()
[1] "Le responsable a dit à la développeuse qu'elle devait revoir le rapport avec son équipe avant la date limite, donc le client attendant près de la banque a demandé s'il pouvait apporter sa propre lumière."

See? “manager” is translated “manager” the first time, and “responsable” the second time, and “so” “alors” then “donc”.

Another example that is crucial to what I was trying to do: the output might return a json object with names that vary:

# First time
> translate_section(
     "Hello world."
)
$text
[1] "Bonjour le monde"

# Second time
> translate_section(
     "Hello world."
)
$translation
[1] "Bonjour le monde"

Which makes it, well, hard to handle in R because when receiving the JSON and converting it to a list, we want the structure to always be the same.

All models are not made equal

Some LLMs can determine that something is ambiguous. Others don’t. Let’s play with the sentence: “I saw her duck”, which is ambiguous by design. Depending on the model you call, you’ll get one version (the animal), or the other (the action), or a large text stating that this is ambiguous.

With Claude Haiku 5.5 
> translate(
+     "I saw her duck.",
+     model = "claude-haiku-5-5"
+   ) |> extract()
[1] "J'ai vu son canard."
With Claude Sonnet 5.5 
> translate(
+     "I saw her duck.",
+     model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
+   ) |> extract()
[1] "Je l'ai vu se baisser."
With Claude Opus 5.5 
> translate(
+   "I saw her duck.",
+    model = "claude-opus-5-5"
+ ) %>% cat()
Possible translations:

- **Je l'ai vue se baisser.** — if "duck" means *lower her head/body*.
- **J'ai vu son canard.** — if "duck" means the animal belonging to her.

The fact that we receive different translations, for now, is fine: this is the behaviour we could have from a standard translation service. But getting the results from the last call is a bit more problematic.

LLM can add elements in their answers

One known issue with LLMs is that they can add context to a sentence, or just noise, like “sure”, or “here is”. That’s what “claude-haiku-5-5” did:

> translate(
+     "Hello",
+     model = "claude-haiku-5-5"
+   ) |> extract()
[1] "Hello can be translated to French as \"Bonjour.\""

Which is not what we want in a translation function. Another, subtle element, but most models will add punctuation if you send it a sentence without a final dot.

> translate(
+     "I see here dog",
+     model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
+   ) |> extract()
[1] "Je vois son chien."
Output might not be predictable

Another issue that extends from the previous section: I found a case where asking for JSON returned the markdown fences:

> translate(
+     "I see here dog",
+     model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
+   ) |> extract()
[1] "```json {'result':''..."
So, what do we do?

We would expect from a generative service to get different answers. I mean, we’re kind of used to the idea that if we ask Claude “generate me lyrics for a death metal song”, we’ll get a different answer.

But that’s not what we want from a translator: we need the response to be, if not fully predictable, at least structured, and constrained enough so that it can go through the rest of the pipeline (markdown rendering, Quarto, PDF) without anything breaking.

Spoiler: nothing below makes the model deterministic. It only shrinks what the model is allowed to answer, and detects when it goes out of bounds anyway.

Structured output

The first thing we need to be sure of: the output has a predictable structure, so that it can be handled in R without any problem.

The output of the LLM will be a string, so we need to be sure we use a structured, interoperable format. In other words, we need a JSON string, with fixed names. You can prompt your model all you want (“answer with a JSON object with a translation key”), you’ll get translation today, text tomorrow, and a JSON wrapped in markdown fences the day after. This is a real challenge, and Claude offers what is called structured outputs: you send a JSON schema with your request, and the API constrains the generation to match it. The documentation is here: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

The schema is deliberately boring: one key, one string.

translation_schema <- list(
  type = "object",
  properties = list(
    translation = list(
      type = "string"
    )
  ),
  required = list(
    "translation"
  ),
  additionalProperties = FALSE
)

translate_text <- function(
  text,
  system_prompt,
  model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
) {
  # ...
  httr2::req_body_json(
    list(
      model = model,
      max_tokens = 4096,
      system = system_prompt,
      messages = list(
        list(
          role = "user",
          content = text
        )
      ),
      output_config = list(
        format = list(
          type = "json_schema",
          schema = translation_schema
        )
      )
    )
  )
  # ...
}

That way, the output Claude returns will be constrained to the given schema: a valid JSON with a translation key, in the text block of the response (content[[1]]$text in R), ready to be parsed with jsonlite::fromJSON().

Engineering the prompt to enforce things

A precise prompt can’t guarantee anything, but it removes most of the annoying behaviours we’ve seen above:

system_prompt <- paste(
  c(
    "You are a professional translator from English into French.",
    "Return only the translation: no comment, no explanation, no alternative.",
    "If the text is ambiguous, pick the most likely reading without mentioning it.",
    "Keep the Markdown syntax as is (**bold**, _italic_, links) and translate the text inside it.",
    "Do not add or remove punctuation.",
    "Keep every [[KEEP_n]] token unchanged.",
    "Always translate 'manager' as 'responsable'."
  ),
  collapse = "\n"
)

The fun part was iterating over the model, sending things to be translated, and getting the error from it, so that I could enrich the prompt.

As you can see, each rule answers one failure from the previous section: “Hello can be translated to French as…” (rule 2), the “Possible translations” answer (rule 3), the missing final dot of “I see here dog” (rule 5), and the manager/responsable flip-flop (the last one: a mini glossary, for terms that must always be translated the same way).

Keeping some terms as they are

Remember “We Are Motörhead”? Telling the model “don’t translate band names” works most of the time anyway, but again, we rely on the model to guess them. The app already knows the band name and the album titles, so instead of asking the model to remember them, I take them out of the text before the call, as tokens ([[KEEP_1]], [[KEEP_2]]…), and put them back after, with a small dictionary:

|key   | value    |
|---   |---       |
|KEEP_1| Motörhead|
Checking what comes back

A prompt is a request, not a guarantee. So the last piece is a function that compares the source that is sent, and the translation that comes back: same number of markdown tokens, and all [[KEEP_n]] still there. I tried to make word count work as a metric, but the app actually has languages like german, in which the size can vary a lot compared to english.

Of course, this is a purely syntactical check, and won’t see wrong meanings. For that, we need the human eye anyway.

Why not translate once?

We could imagine a translation for the content for each combination of band/language/song and store it in the app. But of course, the real use case is a bit more complicated, and storing is practically impossible, given that the user can input text in the application that are included in the translation.

Conclusion

“Just ask the model for translation.”

Yes, that’s doable, but not as easy as it sounds. You can’t just throw a translation request at a model and expect things to work, and that’s inherently linked to the way LLMs work.

So I did my best, so that, you know, we can be “Motörhead” worldwide.

This post is better presented on its original ThinkR website here: “Just ask the model for translation”

items.title: The Download: Better bionic hands and AI’s natural-gas boom
items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one’s hand. Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he’s the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system. Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel . —Jessica Hamzelou How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom — Casey Crownhart In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas . Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s been proven right. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. Meanwhile, Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s. Across the US, natural gas has become the default to meet exploding power demand. Here’s what that means for the future of the grid . This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 SpaceX has won approval to launch 1 million data center satellites The FCC says they’ll help meet AI computing demand. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 The US Army just blew up nearly five tons of unstable explosives The EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following the detonation. ( Verge ) + Scientists are now testing soil and water for contamination. ( Wired $) + Officials were criticized for poor communication beforehand. ( Axios ) 3 Earth just had its first six-day streak above 2°C Scientists say it’s an early warning of what’s to come. ( Guardian ) 4 Ukraine has claimed the first-ever laser takedown of a jet drone Its Blysk laser downed a Russian kamikaze drone. ( Bloomberg $) 5 Neuralink has won approval for a brain-implant trial in ALS patients It’s the final stage of testing before seeking market clearance. ( Gizmodo ) + China is racing to catch up in brain-computer interfaces. ( SCMP ) + A BCI gave a man with ALS his voice back. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Hackers have breached the US Treasury’s financial crime watchdog It’s taken systems used to report money laundering offline. ( FT $) 7 Bankrupt startup Character.ai wants to sell millions of user chats 42 attorneys general are trying to block the sale. ( TechCrunch ) 8 The hunt for dark matter is getting weirder Scientists are using levitating magnets and nuclear clocks. ( Quanta ) + Dark matter’s hiding places keep growing. ( MIT Technology Review ) 9 Scientists used seabird spies to track ships that had gone dark Recorders on the birds detected ships with trackers off. ( 404 Media ) 10 This Thanksgiving, AI is becoming a popular sous-chef But food bloggers say its recipes are often “total nonsense.” ( Axios ) Quote of the day “Hey, by the way, this might be the last time we see each other—potentially, probably not, but maybe—because of AI.” —Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and author of the “AI 2027” forecast, tells The New York Times how he plans to bring up AI extinction risks with his wife’s family this Thanksgiving. One more thing VINCENT KILBRIDE AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better? Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly. In late 2024, even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some could solve them nearly perfectly. But puzzles do more than highlight AI’s progress. Seeing where models succeed and fail, and where humans still beat them, offers a window into the technology’s strengths and weaknesses. We’ve gathered seven puzzles that have stumped models. Try them yourself to find out whether you can outsmart AI . —Grace Huckins We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Fly across the universe in this interactive map of space . + A film industry analyst has produced a fascinating, data-driven look at movie shots and cuts. + They say F1 cars corner like they’re on rails, so Red Bull Racing put one on an actual railway line . + Travel like 007 with License to Locate , which maps every James Bond filming location, from Jamaica to Venice.
items.summary_html:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one’s hand.

Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he’s the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system.

Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel.

—Jessica Hamzelou

How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

— Casey Crownhart

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s been proven right.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. Meanwhile, Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s.

Across the US, natural gas has become the default to meet exploding power demand. Here’s what that means for the future of the grid.

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 SpaceX has won approval to launch 1 million data center satellites
The FCC says they’ll help meet AI computing demand. (Reuters $)
+ But they could overcrowd the orbit and obscure the stars. (Bloomberg $)
+ SpaceX must start deploying them by 2033 under its license. (BBC)
+ Europe has opened a megafactory to build a Starlink rival. (CNBC)
+ Can data centers really work in orbit? (MIT Technology Review)

2 The US Army just blew up nearly five tons of unstable explosives
The EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following the detonation. (Verge)
 + Scientists are now testing soil and water for contamination. (Wired $)
 + Officials were criticized for poor communication beforehand. (Axios)

3 Earth just had its first six-day streak above 2°C
Scientists say it’s an early warning of what’s to come. (Guardian)

4 Ukraine has claimed the first-ever laser takedown of a jet drone
Its Blysk laser downed a Russian kamikaze drone. (Bloomberg $)

5 Neuralink has won approval for a brain-implant trial in ALS patients
It’s the final stage of testing before seeking market clearance. (Gizmodo)
+ China is racing to catch up in brain-computer interfaces. (SCMP)
+ A BCI gave a man with ALS his voice back. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Hackers have breached the US Treasury’s financial crime watchdog
It’s taken systems used to report money laundering offline. (FT $)

7 Bankrupt startup Character.ai wants to sell millions of user chats
42 attorneys general are trying to block the sale. (TechCrunch)

8 The hunt for dark matter is getting weirder
Scientists are using levitating magnets and nuclear clocks. (Quanta)
+ Dark matter’s hiding places keep growing. (MIT Technology Review)

9 Scientists used seabird spies to track ships that had gone dark
Recorders on the birds detected ships with trackers off. (404 Media)

10 This Thanksgiving, AI is becoming a popular sous-chef
But food bloggers say its recipes are often “total nonsense.” (Axios)

Quote of the day

“Hey, by the way, this might be the last time we see each other—potentially, probably not, but maybe—because of AI.”

—Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and author of the “AI 2027” forecast, tells The New York Times how he plans to bring up AI extinction risks with his wife’s family this Thanksgiving.

One more thing

VINCENT KILBRIDE

AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?


Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly. In late 2024, even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some could solve them nearly perfectly.

But puzzles do more than highlight AI’s progress. Seeing where models succeed and fail, and where humans still beat them, offers a window into the technology’s strengths and weaknesses.

We’ve gathered seven puzzles that have stumped models. Try them yourself to find out whether you can outsmart AI. 

—Grace Huckins

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Fly across the universe in this interactive map of space.
+ A film industry analyst has produced a fascinating, data-driven look at movie shots and cuts.
+ They say F1 cars corner like they’re on rails, so Red Bull Racing put one on an actual railway line.
+ Travel like 007 with License to Locate, which maps every James Bond filming location, from Jamaica to Venice.

items.title: Threatened by SaaSpocalypse, 9 Bets Defined Indian IT’s AI Strategy in 2026
items.summary: Earlier this year, Indian IT companies were spooked by the prospect of autonomous agents replacing both SaaS tools and outsourced services. On February 3, Anthropic rolled out 11 open-source plugins for Claude Cowork that could read files, draft documents, review contracts, and execute tasks spanning domains like legal, sales, and finance—threatening downstream IT services specialised in implementing these tasks. So followed the “SaaSpocalypse” phenomenon. The next day, Indian IT stocks suffered a sharp selloff. Infosys nosedived over 7%. Mid-cap stocks mirrored the panic. Nifty IT index saw a correction of 6.3% and lost 19.5% over the month, wiping about $62.8 billion (about ₹5.81 lakh crore) in market value. Now, IT companies have struck a Faustian bargain with the AI companies, often onboarding the same products and tools that once threatened their operating model. Infosys partnered with Anthropic merely days after the stock bloodbath. Anthropic has since become one of the most prominent partners for Indian IT firms. Its Claude Partner Network, launched in March with an initial investment of $100 million (about ₹925 crore), offers training, technical support and joint marketing. The partnerships reflect three pressures on the sector: a scramble for forward-deployed engineers , the need to furnish AI revenue, and the possibility that AI labs could become competitors. The Anthropic Cluster 1. TCS x Anthropic TCS became a Global Premier Partner in the Claude Partner Network. It plans to equip 50,000 employees with Claude , establish a business unit, and develop offerings for regulated sectors such as financial services, healthcare, and telecom. Also, Diligenta, TCS's UK life and pensions business, which serves more than 22 million customers, plans to use Claude for customer experience and process transformation. An internal business that doubles as a reference customer is a stronger sales asset than a licence count. 2. HCLTech x Anthropic HCLTech also signed a Global Premier partnership with Anthropic. It will establish an Anthropic Business Unit and a Centre of Excellence (CoE), where FDEs can build secure sandbox environments for client deployments. Its software arm, HCLSoftware, became an independent software vendor (ISV) partner and will embed Claude and Claude Code in select products. Claude will also be integrated into AI Force, HCLTech's engineering platform, and across IT support, code remediation, and digital employee services. Few Indian peers sell both services and software. This deal puts Claude into each. 3. Cognizant x Anthropic Cognizant expanded its relationship with Anthropic and became a Global Premier Partner. Claude is now integrated into its Flowsource, Neuro AI Engineering and Neuro IT Ops platforms. More than 44,000 associates had completed Claude training by November. The proof point is a client. In May, Cognizant and travel technology company Travelport had collaborated to deploy Claude across Travelport's engineering organisation, with Cognizant leading implementation. Cognizant then committed 25,000 professionals to Claude delivery through a global capability group and introduced managed services. It swore by client deployments that cut downtime and compressed troubleshooting. 4. LTM x Anthropic LTM is integrating Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork into its BlueVerse AI Delivery Fabric and establishing a Claude CoE. Its AI1000 programme will train and deploy Claude-certified architects and FDEs. The initial focus is on banking and financial services, high-tech, consumer, and manufacturing clients, with joint go-to-market plans. LTM has more to gain from a frontier lab's sales reach. Its partnership will be a useful test of whether this model can work beyond the largest IT services firms. OpenAI Enters the Picture 5. Infosys x OpenAI Infosys paired Codex with its Topaz Fabric platform. The initial use cases include legacy modernisation, DevOps automation, code review, and vulnerability detection. Infosys has already put OpenAI models into production across 10 enterprise engagements. 6. TCS x OpenAI Announced in February at the India AI Impact Summit, this deal has two layers. TCS will use Codex to improve software engineering and position itself as a primary enterprise integrator for OpenAI in India. Several thousand Tata Group employees will also get access to ChatGPT Enterprise. OpenAI became the first customer of HyperVault, TCS's data centre business. The initial agreement covers 100 megawatts (MW) of capacity, with an option to scale to one gigawatt (GW). Beyond Frontier Labs 7. TCS x Mistral On May 28, TCS became the first global systems integrator partner for Mistral Forge, the platform of Paris-based AI startup Mistral. Forge lets enterprises build models using their own data. TCS will establish a CoE, get early access to Mistral's beta models and target banking, manufacturing, healthcare, and public sector clients across North America, Europe, the UK, and Asia-Pacific. Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said TCS's global scale and contextual industry knowledge make it an ideal partner. For TCS, the arrangement adds custom model development to its enterprise AI portfolio. 8. Wipro x ServiceNow Wipro expanded its partnership with enterprise workflow software provider ServiceNow, building on a collaboration first established in 2024. Wipro Intelligence, its suite of AI platforms, integrates with the ServiceNow AI Platform to run agentic workflows across IT, HR, procurement, and cybersecurity. The first offerings include the AI-powered procurement automation solution SmartProcure, Telco Autonomous Networks that modernises networks and service management, and the cybersecurity operations solution Cyber Transform. 9. Wipro x Palo Alto Networks Wipro also expanded its partnership with cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks to offer AI-driven managed detection and response. The service combines Palo Alto's Cortex XSIAM platform with Wipro's managed security services across cloud, network and security transformation.

items.title: Cognition’s new engineers aren’t even downloading code anymore — they build entirely through Devin
items.summary: Some engineers joining Cognition no longer set up local development environments . Instead, Devin has become their primary interface for software development. Speaking to Patrick O’Shaughnessy on Tuesday’s episode of Invest Like the Best , Cognition co-founder and CEO Scott Wu describes how the company’s internal engineering practices have changed as coding agents have become more capable. No terminal, no download “The funniest moment for me, I would say, was actually around like four or five months ago when we started to realize that new engineers that joined our team just didn’t even download the code on their computer,” Wu says. “Like they didn’t pull up a terminal. They didn’t run a command line or anything.” “new engineers that joined our team just didn’t even download the code on their computer … They didn’t run a command line or anything.” Over roughly a year, Cognition doubled its engineering headcount while increasing its rate of merged pull requests 20-fold, Wu says. That amounts to approximately ten times as many merged pull requests per engineer, despite the company’s already extensive use of AI coding tools a year earlier. Perhaps more significant, Wu estimates, is that approximately 90% of Cognition’s internal Devin usage is now automated in some form. When Devin runs itself Wu cites incident response as an example of Cognition’s automated Devin workflows, where an error can trigger an investigation before an on-call engineer intervenes. “It doesn’t involve a human saying, ‘Hey, Devin, I need you to go work on this thing’ to kick it off.” “It doesn’t involve a human saying, ‘Hey, Devin, I need you to go work on this thing’ to kick it off,” Wu says. Although Wu does not specify whether the 90% figure represents session count, token consumption, or another metric, automated execution has implications for compute provisioning and budget allocation as inference demand becomes less dependent on individual developer activity. Cognition has already introduced hierarchical budgets for Devin , which give enterprises spending controls across organizational levels. 250,000 pull requests monthly Wu says one of Cognition’s largest banking customers was on track to merge 250,000 pull requests with Devin in October. Until a few months earlier, the entire organization had been merging approximately 400,000 pull requests per month. The bank has approximately 80,000 engineering personnel, according to Wu, and only a fraction of the organization had been fully onboarded to Devin at the time of the interview. Separately, Citi CEO Jane Fraser says during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call that 14,000 engineers use Devin. Neither Cognition’s internal figures nor the banking customer’s projected PR volume account for the complexity of individual changes. Wu does not provide corresponding data on change failure rates or review workloads , metrics that would help establish whether the rest of the SDLC has kept pace with implementation. The disparity between implementation and review capacity has already prompted vendors such as CodeRabbit to expand into agentic change management . Wu argues that enterprise adoption also requires engineering leaders to reconsider their roadmaps and organizational structures to accommodate additional implementation capacity. Watching the agent swarms The shift from individual background agents to swarms is a particular concern for Wu because monitoring becomes more difficult when multiple agents work together. Cognition has been exploring this execution model with its recently introduced Devin Bots , persistent agents that manage other agents’ work. Wu stresses the need to catch unintended agent behavior early and limit what agents can access, especially when workflows run without an engineer supervising them. The engineering skill ceiling hasn’t changed “The barrier to entry has for sure gotten a lot lower,” Wu says. “However, I think the skill ceiling and, you know, a lot of the particular skill sets that you need are still very much the same as they always have been.” “I think people who can do that really well have always been valuable and now they’re just 10 times more valuable.” For Wu, writing code is only one part of software engineering. Engineers still have to figure out what an incomplete or ambiguous specification actually means and make architectural decisions that could affect the business for years, even if an agent handles the implementation. “I think people who can do that really well have always been valuable and now they’re just 10 times more valuable,” Wu says.

items.title: All the Worst Government GTA Memes from Around the World
items.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI is a true monocultural event . Every news channel is covering it, anyone with a passing interest in video games is playing it, and it’s made almost $4 billion in less than a week. Desperate to connect with constituents, governments around the world have tried to capitalize on GTA’s popularity by releasing some of the worst AI-generated memes I’ve ever seen. The pictures of politicians in the hyper-real cartoon pink-tinted style of GTA 6 are so awful they even caused a minor political scandal in Scotland. Let’s begin in the United States, where Vice President JD Vance, the White House, and several other government-run X accounts attempted to capture the cultural zeitgeist by quickly churning out AI-generated meme garbage. items.title: Microsoft details how state-backed hackers use the ARTEX AI framework to automate cyberattacks
items.summary: Microsoft has published the technical architecture of ARTEX, an AI framework in wide use since July 2026 that runs cyberattacks with specialized agents and almost no human involvement. State-backed groups from China and North Korea, along with criminal organizations, are already using the system. Microsoft recommends deception techniques like honeypots and faked success signals as defenses, but how long those will hold up against agents that learn and adapt remains an open question. Meta has rolled out its Muse AI assistant, which can be tasked with shopping, booking tickets and carrying out negotiations on a user’s behalf, across countries including the UK, US, Canada, Australia and Japan. The AI agent needs the customer’s permission to go out and make purchases, connect to apps, use bank details or send emails autonomously. However, the possibility of employees connecting their Muse assistant to their work emails and databases is a concern for companies and their clients.

items.title: AIhub coffee corner: “Rogue AI”
items.summary: The AIhub coffee corner captures the musings of AI experts over a short conversation. Joining the conversation this time are: Rina Dechter (University of California, Irvine), Tom Dietterich (Oregon State University), Sabine Hauert (University of Bristol), Hadi Hosseini (Penn State University) and Marija Slavkovik (University of Bergen). Lucy Smith: Today’s topic is so-called “rogue AI”, prompted by the attempted OpenAI model hack of Hugging Face. How concerned should we be about these models, and is the anthropomorphised framing of them as rogue agents justified? Tom Dietterich: Well, I think they should be considered rogue AI in some sense. We’ve all had the experience of having a program run that we weren’t able to kill before it did some damage to our file system. I believe there are still old computer viruses out there that have not been completely exterminated from the internet. They’re just running out of old hardware that no one has retired. New computers are immune to them. And so it seems absolutely possible to have AI systems build such things and have them persist forever. So in that sense, we will lose control of those things. I guess a key difference right now is that with the AI-based models, if they actually have to call out to an LLM, that gives us a point of control because we can shut down their access. But there are a lot of problems that need to be solved before we can do that. For instance, we need every agent to have a cryptographic identity so we know who they are and we can shut them down. And right now they don’t have any identities, they just carry around API keys. So that’s a big issue. Whether you can call it rogue or not depends on what you mean by rogue. But uncontrolled, unstoppable, it is. An obvious failure is that OpenAI didn’t have very good monitoring on what these systems are doing and certainly wasn’t properly structured as an organization. As some of you know, I worry a lot about safety-critical applications. And the lesson there for decades has been that there is no such thing as automation, in the sense that there’s nothing that you can really let go completely autonomously. You always have to build a human organization around the so-called automation to monitor it, and to find its failure modes before they cause big trouble. One lesson to take away from all this is that you can’t let your agents run unmonitored. You have to think about what the human organization is that’s going to be doing the monitoring. We see this for all the software engineers who are using AI to do programming for them. They’re spending all their time monitoring. We saw this for Waymo. It turned out they needed to hire a bunch of human monitors. And it’s the same story over and over again. The pipe dream that we could have fully autonomous agents doing our bidding for us and watching out for us is not going to happen. I think that end consumers are not going to like agents very much because they are not going to want to pay that monitoring price. That is a lesson to take away from this: we have to think really carefully about how we do monitoring, and it is part of the price of running these systems. Rina Dechter: One of the questions that resonated with me was, how come there were thousands of these hacking incidents? Why, after the first one, didn’t they do anything to stop it? I mean, anybody who is building a product in biology, for example, as soon as they see the first unsafe phenomenon, they will take it back and revise and so on. So this is puzzling. Marija Slavkovik: We have since graduated from hacking Hugging Face to hacking the Australian government. The statements were that it wasn’t just the Australian government that was hacked, but the rest of them didn’t speak up. So this is an issue. It seems to me that there is a very large consensus in the academic environment asking why nobody is being punished for this. It’s like rogue agents are deemed to be a new entity in the legislative world. And to me, it seems like that term is just being used to escape the fact that somebody brought an untrainable dog with a weak leash to the playground that bit a kid and then argued, “but the dog is so wild”. This situation of rogue agents is presented as new because it involves agents. But in reality, there are people who did not design the environment properly, and did not design the agent properly. It seems that you can get away with hacking the Australian government. This government is just going to ask the company to be better, but there are governments that are not going to react that way if they are hacked. Hadi Hosseini: I really like the idea that Tom mentioned about agents having an identity so we can identify what these agents are and, more importantly, who they are working for. I think that is a new world that we are getting into, that we need to know who this software belongs to. In the old world, or pre-generative AI, we had a very clear definition of these things. It was clear who built the software. Of course you tried to put in guardrails and wanted to make sure that the software was properly tested. I think this word agent is being misused. Thinking in a very philosophical way, what is agency? I mean, we are attaching this agency to software. I’m really trying to understand, from a philosophical perspective, whether we can actually attach agency to these software agents themselves, or is it because we designed something that was not properly designed or properly vetted? This is not a new conversation. In philosophy, people have been thinking about agency, where it comes from, going back to Albert Bandura’s work about how to define intentionality all the way back to Aristotle’s work. What is an agent? What is it that you’re trying to do? I think this is something that the academic community understands, but industry has become a bit distanced from this question. Who is responsible for these, let’s call them, rogue agents . It’s not like the rogue agent decided by itself. It’s a rogue agent designed by a company who didn’t do it very well. They didn’t test it. They didn’t make sure that this is safe to be put out there. It’s very complex. Marija: I mean, we are seeing the testing. The testing is being done live. That’s the problem. Rina: But didn’t OpenAI and Anthropic already admit that they are responsible? So we know who to blame. Marija: Yeah, and then what happened? Nobody’s blaming them. Tom: Nobody’s taking them to court, yet. Sabine Hauert: The robotic side is interesting because these agents, when embedded in a physical body, have a different kind of impact. Something I’ve been wondering about from the swarm perspective and the multi-agent perspective is that for a very long time, we’ve had limited agents by design, because that’s how our robots were built, or that’s how we could build our programs. And so we spent years figuring out how we made these agents cooperate in a way where they did things together in a beneficial way. And I think one of the challenges that we see in the AI space is that they’re letting these very generalist agents, without any constraints on the individual level, figure out how to cooperate to do things. And as a result, you get the expected strange outputs that you’d get from any crowd of people if you don’t restrict both the agent and their ability to cooperate towards a common incentive. I think we need to pull back those lessons from the past years of research into the way agents are being designed. Let’s not invent things from scratch and go to town with the capabilities of individual agents, but build on what we know already. Marija: One problem is that if there is a punishment for AI companies then they will not admit when something has gone wrong. And I’m not sure we have a good way to test that they have done something wrong. It’s something we need the cybersecurity community to tell us – how good are we at detecting hacking or intrusions by AI agents? And that’s the thing, the only motivation to not punish the perpetrators is if you want to incentivize them to admit to the wrongdoing. Sabine: Like a near miss in a biology lab. Tom: It seems that they didn’t really test their containment at all. Another lesson is when we build complex systems, there are always unknown failure modes that we didn’t anticipate. I mean, software engineers spend their whole lives trying to anticipate everything that will go wrong, but we fail. And so I think the fact that these systems were able to hack their way out of their containment is a sign of future problems like that. If they’re clever enough and they have enough computer resources, they’ll probably find a way out, unless we design them very, very carefully. We need truly air-gapped systems and so on. We do have some experience with containing other kinds of information in high security government settings. Again, there usually are leaks, but they’re human-caused. Marija: One point we can discuss is how badly they have designed the containment. Tom: Right. They should be liable if they design a bad system. Marija: Remember, pharmaceutical companies, who very much wanted to regulate themselves in the 50s, argued there is no such thing as a perfectly safe drug. Fair, we accept, but then there are funds that compensate the people who are harmed. So, we can argue that containment is very difficult and they did the best they could, but there is still some damage that can leak out. Tom: Yeah, I mean, the fact that it’s hard is no excuse. Marija: Right. I mean, put up the money to compensate. Tom: It should be a standard of testing and you have to show that you’ve built a system that at least certain reference agents cannot escape from. You could imagine a whole testing regime there. Rina: Gary Marcus is suggesting an FDA-like system. In the same way that the FDA screens all the drugs, we should have some FDA-type organization for AI systems, which I thought is interesting. Hadi: We’ve talked mostly about the legal framework and who is responsible and I think that’s a very important topic. But another topic is around how these companies can ensure that their software agents are safe. One idea that I’ve been hearing a lot about is auditing, trying to create frameworks where you have an agent and you can audit this agent depending on the task it’s doing, or in general. Maybe sometimes there are agents who need to do something that is good in environment A, but maybe very harmful in environment B. This is something that auditing can actually tell us. And then we can profile these agents by saying that this agent is safe if you’re using it the following way. `In the same way that the drug companies, as Marija was saying, are profiling their drugs. I think that’s a very good conversation to have.
