The AIhub coffee corner captures the musings of AI experts over a short conversation. Joining the conversation this time are: Rina Dechter (University of California, Irvine), Tom Dietterich (Oregon State University), Sabine Hauert (University of Bristol), Hadi Hosseini (Penn State University) and Marija Slavkovik (University of Bergen).

Lucy Smith: Today’s topic is so-called “rogue AI”, prompted by the attempted OpenAI model hack of Hugging Face. How concerned should we be about these models, and is the anthropomorphised framing of them as rogue agents justified?

Tom Dietterich: Well, I think they should be considered rogue AI in some sense. We’ve all had the experience of having a program run that we weren’t able to kill before it did some damage to our file system. I believe there are still old computer viruses out there that have not been completely exterminated from the internet. They’re just running out of old hardware that no one has retired. New computers are immune to them. And so it seems absolutely possible to have AI systems build such things and have them persist forever. So in that sense, we will lose control of those things. I guess a key difference right now is that with the AI-based models, if they actually have to call out to an LLM, that gives us a point of control because we can shut down their access. But there are a lot of problems that need to be solved before we can do that. For instance, we need every agent to have a cryptographic identity so we know who they are and we can shut them down. And right now they don’t have any identities, they just carry around API keys. So that’s a big issue. Whether you can call it rogue or not depends on what you mean by rogue. But uncontrolled, unstoppable, it is.

An obvious failure is that OpenAI didn’t have very good monitoring on what these systems are doing and certainly wasn’t properly structured as an organization. As some of you know, I worry a lot about safety-critical applications. And the lesson there for decades has been that there is no such thing as automation, in the sense that there’s nothing that you can really let go completely autonomously. You always have to build a human organization around the so-called automation to monitor it, and to find its failure modes before they cause big trouble. One lesson to take away from all this is that you can’t let your agents run unmonitored. You have to think about what the human organization is that’s going to be doing the monitoring. We see this for all the software engineers who are using AI to do programming for them. They’re spending all their time monitoring. We saw this for Waymo. It turned out they needed to hire a bunch of human monitors. And it’s the same story over and over again. The pipe dream that we could have fully autonomous agents doing our bidding for us and watching out for us is not going to happen. I think that end consumers are not going to like agents very much because they are not going to want to pay that monitoring price. That is a lesson to take away from this: we have to think really carefully about how we do monitoring, and it is part of the price of running these systems.

Rina Dechter: One of the questions that resonated with me was, how come there were thousands of these hacking incidents? Why, after the first one, didn’t they do anything to stop it? I mean, anybody who is building a product in biology, for example, as soon as they see the first unsafe phenomenon, they will take it back and revise and so on. So this is puzzling.

Marija Slavkovik: We have since graduated from hacking Hugging Face to hacking the Australian government. The statements were that it wasn’t just the Australian government that was hacked, but the rest of them didn’t speak up. So this is an issue. It seems to me that there is a very large consensus in the academic environment asking why nobody is being punished for this. It’s like rogue agents are deemed to be a new entity in the legislative world. And to me, it seems like that term is just being used to escape the fact that somebody brought an untrainable dog with a weak leash to the playground that bit a kid and then argued, “but the dog is so wild”. This situation of rogue agents is presented as new because it involves agents. But in reality, there are people who did not design the environment properly, and did not design the agent properly. It seems that you can get away with hacking the Australian government. This government is just going to ask the company to be better, but there are governments that are not going to react that way if they are hacked.

Hadi Hosseini: I really like the idea that Tom mentioned about agents having an identity so we can identify what these agents are and, more importantly, who they are working for. I think that is a new world that we are getting into, that we need to know who this software belongs to. In the old world, or pre-generative AI, we had a very clear definition of these things. It was clear who built the software. Of course you tried to put in guardrails and wanted to make sure that the software was properly tested. I think this word agent is being misused. Thinking in a very philosophical way, what is agency? I mean, we are attaching this agency to software. I’m really trying to understand, from a philosophical perspective, whether we can actually attach agency to these software agents themselves, or is it because we designed something that was not properly designed or properly vetted? This is not a new conversation. In philosophy, people have been thinking about agency, where it comes from, going back to Albert Bandura’s work about how to define intentionality all the way back to Aristotle’s work. What is an agent? What is it that you’re trying to do? I think this is something that the academic community understands, but industry has become a bit distanced from this question.

Who is responsible for these, let’s call them, rogue agents. It’s not like the rogue agent decided by itself. It’s a rogue agent designed by a company who didn’t do it very well. They didn’t test it. They didn’t make sure that this is safe to be put out there. It’s very complex.

Marija: I mean, we are seeing the testing. The testing is being done live. That’s the problem.

Rina: But didn’t OpenAI and Anthropic already admit that they are responsible? So we know who to blame.

Marija: Yeah, and then what happened? Nobody’s blaming them.

Tom: Nobody’s taking them to court, yet.

Sabine Hauert: The robotic side is interesting because these agents, when embedded in a physical body, have a different kind of impact. Something I’ve been wondering about from the swarm perspective and the multi-agent perspective is that for a very long time, we’ve had limited agents by design, because that’s how our robots were built, or that’s how we could build our programs. And so we spent years figuring out how we made these agents cooperate in a way where they did things together in a beneficial way. And I think one of the challenges that we see in the AI space is that they’re letting these very generalist agents, without any constraints on the individual level, figure out how to cooperate to do things. And as a result, you get the expected strange outputs that you’d get from any crowd of people if you don’t restrict both the agent and their ability to cooperate towards a common incentive. I think we need to pull back those lessons from the past years of research into the way agents are being designed. Let’s not invent things from scratch and go to town with the capabilities of individual agents, but build on what we know already.

Marija: One problem is that if there is a punishment for AI companies then they will not admit when something has gone wrong. And I’m not sure we have a good way to test that they have done something wrong. It’s something we need the cybersecurity community to tell us – how good are we at detecting hacking or intrusions by AI agents? And that’s the thing, the only motivation to not punish the perpetrators is if you want to incentivize them to admit to the wrongdoing.

Sabine: Like a near miss in a biology lab.

Tom: It seems that they didn’t really test their containment at all. Another lesson is when we build complex systems, there are always unknown failure modes that we didn’t anticipate. I mean, software engineers spend their whole lives trying to anticipate everything that will go wrong, but we fail. And so I think the fact that these systems were able to hack their way out of their containment is a sign of future problems like that. If they’re clever enough and they have enough computer resources, they’ll probably find a way out, unless we design them very, very carefully. We need truly air-gapped systems and so on. We do have some experience with containing other kinds of information in high security government settings. Again, there usually are leaks, but they’re human-caused.

Marija: One point we can discuss is how badly they have designed the containment.

Tom: Right. They should be liable if they design a bad system.

Marija: Remember, pharmaceutical companies, who very much wanted to regulate themselves in the 50s, argued there is no such thing as a perfectly safe drug. Fair, we accept, but then there are funds that compensate the people who are harmed. So, we can argue that containment is very difficult and they did the best they could, but there is still some damage that can leak out.

Tom: Yeah, I mean, the fact that it’s hard is no excuse.

Marija: Right. I mean, put up the money to compensate.

Tom: It should be a standard of testing and you have to show that you’ve built a system that at least certain reference agents cannot escape from. You could imagine a whole testing regime there.

Rina: Gary Marcus is suggesting an FDA-like system. In the same way that the FDA screens all the drugs, we should have some FDA-type organization for AI systems, which I thought is interesting.

Hadi: We’ve talked mostly about the legal framework and who is responsible and I think that’s a very important topic. But another topic is around how these companies can ensure that their software agents are safe. One idea that I’ve been hearing a lot about is auditing, trying to create frameworks where you have an agent and you can audit this agent depending on the task it’s doing, or in general. Maybe sometimes there are agents who need to do something that is good in environment A, but maybe very harmful in environment B. This is something that auditing can actually tell us. And then we can profile these agents by saying that this agent is safe if you’re using it the following way. `In the same way that the drug companies, as Marija was saying, are profiling their drugs. I think that’s a very good conversation to have.

items.title: Vertiv Expands 800 VDC Power Portfolio for AI Data Centres
items.summary: US-based Vertiv has expanded its 800 VDC power portfolio to support rising energy demands from AI data centres. The expansion adds systems for AI compute pods and data halls and extends the company's portfolio, which began with the PowerDirect 5000 Power Rack in May 2026. The solutions cover three deployment levels: rack, compute pod and data hall. This expanded portfolio will help data centre operators scale infrastructure as computing requirements evolve. Vertiv is showcasing the portfolio at the SC26 International Conference for High-Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. As AI workloads increase power requirements, operators are evaluating 800 VDC systems for higher-density computing environments. However, Vertiv expects AC and DC architectures to coexist. This makes flexibility in power conversion, distribution and deployment important. "The 800 VDC power train is not just a new power product or conversion methodology; it is a set of architectures and system designs," said Scott Armul, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertiv. He added that the systems combine power conversion, energy storage, distribution, protection, controls and safety. The company aims to let operators introduce 800 VDC at different points in their existing infrastructure. At the rack level, Vertiv's PowerDirect 5000 Power Rack supports configurations of up to 800 kW. It accepts 480 VAC facility power and delivers 800 VDC or ±400 VDC. The system includes 30 hot-pluggable 30 kW power supply units and an integrated battery backup. Vertiv has also introduced the PowerDirect 3000, a 90 kW DC-DC converter designed for installation inside compute racks. It converts 800 VDC to 54 VDC for compute trays, with peak efficiency of 98.5%. The architecture moves power conversion and energy storage outside IT racks. This can free up 8 to 16 rack units for additional computing equipment. It also allows operators to retain existing AC infrastructure without redesigning their facilities. For AI compute pods, the PowerDirect 9000 Power Centre converts 480 VAC to 800 VDC. The 1.5 MW system distributes power across an entire row or pod through DC busways and tap-off boxes. The system also connects to Vertiv's EnergyCore Li5 800 VDC battery cabinet. Each cabinet provides 200 kW of continuous backup at up to 98% conversion efficiency. Up to six cabinets can operate in parallel. At the data hall level, Vertiv's PowerNexus MV SST is a 5 MW solid-state transformer. It converts medium-voltage AC directly to 800 VDC in a single conversion stage. The system offers up to 98% AC-to-DC efficiency. The outdoor, liquid-cooled and containerised system also supports bidirectional power flow. Vertiv said it can reduce intermediate conversion stages and help manage fluctuations in power demand from AI workloads. Vertiv said its 800 VDC portfolio includes safety features designed for DC operating environments. These include touch-proof busbars, high-voltage isolation, midpoint grounding and ground-fault detection. The systems also incorporate arc-flash prevention measures. "Different operators have different requirements, whether they're building new AI facilities, upgrading existing sites, or supporting a mix of tenants and workloads," said Kyle Keeper, Senior Vice President of Vertiv's Power Management Business Unit. Keeper said the portfolio allows customers to choose deployment architectures based on their infrastructure and power requirements. Vertiv said pilot programmes, technical validation activities and customer-specific development initiatives are underway . The company is also engaging with customers on potential deployment plans.

items.title: Microsoft sets one-hour recovery goal after worst-ever M365 outage
items.summary: Microsoft has ordered an overhaul of its Microsoft 365 engineering and incident response practices after a 24-hour outage disrupted businesses and governments worldwide, setting a target of resolving future service disruptions globally within an hour, Reuters reported . Microsoft attributed the November 12-13 disruption to a scalability flaw in Windows that went undetected for months after its introduction in July, the report said. The outage affected Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services, including Teams . Microsoft said neither cyber activity nor AI agents were responsible. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, described the disruption as Exchange Online’s worst incident in terms of customer impact in a staff memo reviewed by Reuters. Under the “Code Red” initiative, Microsoft intends to limit the spread of failures between regions. It also plans to use AI agents to speed up diagnosis. Engineers exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats during the outage, with diagnostic information dispersed across internal systems, Reuters reported. Microsoft had previously needed five to six days to complete the global rollout of an urgent software fix, the report added. In an earlier memo, Henderson said Microsoft needed to reduce the interval between detecting its most urgent security issues and safely deploying fixes worldwide to an hour. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that implementing lessons from the outage remained a priority and that the company was committed to preventing further disruptions. Can Microsoft bring recovery times down to an hour? Microsoft’s one-hour recovery target has no stated implementation deadline and is not reflected in the company’s standard service terms, according to Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research. A one-hour target in an internal memo is “a promise Microsoft has made to itself, and customers should now ask for one made to them,” Gogia said. “The target is ambitious but achievable for many outages with better automation, faster fault detection and improved coordination between engineering teams,” said Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting. Meeting that target consistently across major outages, however, would be challenging, Jain added. Achieving faster recovery would require Microsoft to strengthen its ability to isolate faults and switch workloads away from failing infrastructure. It would also need to automate the reversal of problematic software changes, according to Charlie Dai , VP and principal analyst at Forrester. For CIOs, monitoring Microsoft’s progress will require looking beyond conventional uptime figures. Outage frequency and recovery times provide a measure of reliability, while the number of affected users helps establish the scale of business exposure. Jain also recommended assessing the quality of communication during incidents. Microsoft’s standard service-level agreement (SLA) for Exchange Online measures monthly availability rather than setting recovery deadlines for individual outages, according to Gogia. Service credits are tied to subscription fees rather than the business losses customers incur during an outage. Jain said stronger service-level agreements should establish limits on downtime and provide more meaningful compensation for prolonged outages. Dai said customers should also seek evidence that recovery mechanisms have been tested, alongside contractual commitments that account for differing recovery requirements. Ahead of contract renewals, procurement teams should seek written commitments on recovery times and clarity on how Microsoft prioritizes service restoration, Gogia said. Enterprises with greater bargaining power could seek termination rights following repeated SLA breaches. The risks of putting too much in one cloud Enterprises may use different Microsoft 365 applications for separate business functions, but that does not necessarily mean their failure risks are independent. Shared identity services and network infrastructure can leave multiple SaaS applications vulnerable to the same underlying fault, Dai said. Gogia said the outage does not necessarily undermine the business case for consolidation. Moving to another provider could increase costs without eliminating similar architectural risks. Jain urged CIOs to examine the extent of that dependence, noting that distributing services across multiple data centers does not necessarily protect applications that share underlying components. The challenge for CIOs is determining where the financial and operational benefits of consolidation justify the risk of simultaneous disruption across business functions. Business continuity when Microsoft 365 is down Traditional disaster recovery planning assumes that enterprises have some control over restoring their systems. With SaaS, CIOs must also plan for how long their businesses can operate while waiting for a provider to resolve a failure. Continuity planning becomes particularly complicated when the tools IT teams use to manage an outage depend on the same cloud environment as the affected applications. “A plan that assumes the consoles will be there to run the recovery is a plan for a different outage,” Gogia said. Enterprises could establish alternative communication channels independent of Microsoft’s authentication services. Sending service health notifications to external email addresses and maintaining an independently accessible employee directory would offer relatively inexpensive safeguards. Jain recommended maintaining backup email services for employees in critical roles. Independent data backups and offline access to essential documents could also help sustain operations. Some critical business processes may also need predefined manual workflows so employees can continue operating without access to cloud applications, Dai said. Restoring access to applications does not necessarily mean business operations have returned to normal . Gogia recommended that businesses independently verify receipt of time-sensitive communications following an outage. He urged CIOs to conduct a continuity exercise before their next contract renewal without access to email, Teams, the Microsoft 365 admin center, or the Defender portal.

items.title: The Next Big IT Services Opportunity Could Be Operationalising AI
items.summary: Enterprises are becoming more cautious about AI spending, but they are not pulling back from adoption. Instead, the focus is shifting towards measurable returns, better governance, and integrating AI into existing business processes. To address this, Straive is positioning itself as a partner that can help enterprises not only build AI systems but also operate and continuously improve them. “We are trying to operationalise AI,” says Naveen Gattu, Global Head of Growth at Straive, tells AIM in an exclusive interview. He believes operationalising AI could emerge as a distinct category within the technology services industry, comparable to the growth of IT services companies in the late 1990s. Gattu says that the next generation of large technology services companies will emerge from organisations that can help enterprises continuously build, deploy, operate and improve AI systems. “A couple of billion-dollar companies in India will evolve that have adopted this operationalising AI,” he notes. For Straive, the opportunity lies in building a business around this category, combining domain knowledge, consulting and engineering with the ability to operate AI systems at scale. The company recently partnered with OpenAI and Anthropic as part of its broader ecosystem strategy, which already includes Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Databricks, Snowflake and NVIDIA. Gattu says the OpenAI partnership would give Straive faster access to emerging technologies, benchmarking capabilities and joint go-to-market opportunities. The partnership is expected to involve pre-sales, technical sales and technical support from OpenAI. It will also allow Straive to work more closely with OpenAI’s product teams to understand and integrate new capabilities. “Since things are changing at such a rapid pace, we would want to experiment in our research labs, understand what’s new coming, and make sure how this is different from existing versions or competing LLMs,” he says. The partnership also provides external validation of Straive’s technical capabilities through certifications and experience in large-scale implementations. AI ROI Gattu believes AI investments are already delivering returns for leading enterprises. However, the gap between companies that have successfully adopted AI and those lagging is widening. According to him, leading AI adopters are almost eight times more impactful than their lagging counterparts. He identifies three primary reasons why enterprises struggle to translate AI investments into business outcomes. The first is the disconnect between business objectives and technology implementation. Companies often approach AI as a technology initiative, attempting to apply it to an existing problem without first establishing whether AI is the right solution. “AI is not a technology initiative, in my view. You marry a business problem and see whether AI is the right thing to solve it or not,” Gattu says. The second challenge is the failure to integrate AI into business processes. When one team builds an AI system and another is responsible for implementing it, the feedback loop between development and operations can break down. Straive believes the same team should ideally be responsible for both building and running AI systems, allowing enterprises to incorporate feedback and iterate faster. The third challenge is data quality and governance. Large enterprises continue to struggle with bringing the right data into AI systems at the right velocity. Frontier AI Models are Not Enough While frontier models have improved significantly in their capabilities, Gattu believes they cannot independently solve industry-specific enterprise problems. A general-purpose model such as Google’s Gemini could produce a reasonably accurate report, but Gattu estimates that it could achieve only 70–80% accuracy without additional industry-specific context. This is where domain-specific customisation becomes necessary. “Frontier model alone will not solve any business problem,” he notes. Straive Wants to Combine Consulting, Building and Running AI Gattu positions Straive at the intersection of three segments within the enterprise technology services market. The first component competes directly with companies such as Fractal and Tiger Analytics, which focus on data management, data science, machine learning and AI development. The second includes business process and knowledge services companies such as EXL and Genpact, which bring domain expertise and operational capabilities. The third consists of consulting firms such as Accenture and Deloitte, which advise enterprises on business and technology transformation. Straive believes its proposition combines all three. The company has around 6,000 employees with master’s degrees or PhDs, giving it a substantial domain knowledge base. It combines this knowledge with consulting capabilities, analytics engineering and business operations. “Straive is the only player who can advise, run and build AI together,” Gattu says. He argues that separating AI development from its day-to-day operations can limit the ability to generate efficiencies and demonstrate ROI. For enterprises, the ability to connect business problems with the right technical solutions is becoming particularly important. Gattu identifies forward-deployed engineers (FDEs), who combine business consulting knowledge with technical expertise, as an important part of this process. Demonstrating ROI is another priority, as the company looks to increase its presence within existing customer accounts through account-based expansion strategies. Enterprises are becoming more cautious about AI spending, but they are not pulling back from adoption. Instead, the focus is shifting towards measurable returns, better governance, and integrating AI into existing business processes.

To address this, Straive is positioning itself as a partner that can help enterprises not only build AI systems but also operate and continuously improve them. “We are trying to operationalise AI,” says Naveen Gattu, Global Head of Growth at Straive, tells AIM in an exclusive interview.

He believes operationalising AI could emerge as a distinct category within the technology services industry, comparable to the growth of IT services companies in the late 1990s.

Gattu says that the next generation of large technology services companies will emerge from organisations that can help enterprises continuously build, deploy, operate and improve AI systems. “A couple of billion-dollar companies in India will evolve that have adopted this operationalising AI,” he notes.

For Straive, the opportunity lies in building a business around this category, combining domain knowledge, consulting and engineering with the ability to operate AI systems at scale.

The company recently partnered with OpenAI and Anthropic as part of its broader ecosystem strategy, which already includes Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Databricks, Snowflake and NVIDIA.

Gattu says the OpenAI partnership would give Straive faster access to emerging technologies, benchmarking capabilities and joint go-to-market opportunities.

The partnership is expected to involve pre-sales, technical sales and technical support from OpenAI. It will also allow Straive to work more closely with OpenAI’s product teams to understand and integrate new capabilities.

“Since things are changing at such a rapid pace, we would want to experiment in our research labs, understand what’s new coming, and make sure how this is different from existing versions or competing LLMs,” he says.

The partnership also provides external validation of Straive’s technical capabilities through certifications and experience in large-scale implementations.

AI ROI

Gattu believes AI investments are already delivering returns for leading enterprises. However, the gap between companies that have successfully adopted AI and those lagging is widening.

According to him, leading AI adopters are almost eight times more impactful than their lagging counterparts.

He identifies three primary reasons why enterprises struggle to translate AI investments into business outcomes.

The first is the disconnect between business objectives and technology implementation. Companies often approach AI as a technology initiative, attempting to apply it to an existing problem without first establishing whether AI is the right solution.

“AI is not a technology initiative, in my view. You marry a business problem and see whether AI is the right thing to solve it or not,” Gattu says.

The second challenge is the failure to integrate AI into business processes. When one team builds an AI system and another is responsible for implementing it, the feedback loop between development and operations can break down.

Straive believes the same team should ideally be responsible for both building and running AI systems, allowing enterprises to incorporate feedback and iterate faster.

The third challenge is data quality and governance. Large enterprises continue to struggle with bringing the right data into AI systems at the right velocity.

Frontier AI Models are Not Enough

While frontier models have improved significantly in their capabilities, Gattu believes they cannot independently solve industry-specific enterprise problems.

A general-purpose model such as Google’s Gemini could produce a reasonably accurate report, but Gattu estimates that it could achieve only 70–80% accuracy without additional industry-specific context.

This is where domain-specific customisation becomes necessary. “Frontier model alone will not solve any business problem,” he notes.

Gattu positions Straive at the intersection of three segments within the enterprise technology services market.

The first component competes directly with companies such as Fractal and Tiger Analytics, which focus on data management, data science, machine learning and AI development.

The second includes business process and knowledge services companies such as EXL and Genpact, which bring domain expertise and operational capabilities.

The third consists of consulting firms such as Accenture and Deloitte, which advise enterprises on business and technology transformation.

Straive believes its proposition combines all three.

The company has around 6,000 employees with master’s degrees or PhDs, giving it a substantial domain knowledge base. It combines this knowledge with consulting capabilities, analytics engineering and business operations.

“Straive is the only player who can advise, run and build AI together,” Gattu says.

He argues that separating AI development from its day-to-day operations can limit the ability to generate efficiencies and demonstrate ROI.

For enterprises, the ability to connect business problems with the right technical solutions is becoming particularly important. Gattu identifies forward-deployed engineers (FDEs), who combine business consulting knowledge with technical expertise, as an important part of this process.

This approach, according to Gattu, allows Straive to reduce implementation timelines from around 18 weeks to eight to 12 weeks.

The company currently focuses on six industries, bringing domain specialists and pre-built solutions into customer engagements rather than developing everything from scratch.

items.title: Uber goes wild with agentic skills, finds code is king
items.summary: When thousands of employees start issuing instructions to AI agents, things can get messy – and expensive – very fast indeed. You can wind up with multiple individuals or teams building the same automation in different ways, and even AI dependency growing for workflows that do not necessarily need to be a baroque call-and-response between an engineer soloist and a choir of agents singing back. Uber arguably faced that risk. Its internal AI “skills” marketplace grew from a single entry in October 2025 to more than 5,000 just one year later. Agents used those skills over a million times in a month. The enthusiasm for skills – or sprawl of them – has even resulted in it creating agentic skills for finding agentic skills: “ How the find-skills skill finds a skill for a prompt ” reads the caption to one chart by its engineers. What’s a skill, anyway? Like the often nebulous “loop” (and frankly still inconsistent definition of an “agent” itself) views on what constitutes a “skill” varies. Here, they really just boil down to a short set of rules/scripts that tell an agent to do one job well: e.g. submit a code change for review, pull figures from a metrics store, draft a weekly sales deck.

items.title: Marc Levinson on How UPS Created Modern Logistics
items.summary: UPS was founded nearly a century ago in the basement of a Seattle saloon by James E. Casey and his business partner Claude Ryan. It is now hard to imagine modern, globalized life, and the logistics required to prop it up, without the innovations Casey and his partners at UPS cooked up during the company's early decades. Marc Levinson has just written a biography of Casey and the company he founded — UPS Man: James E. Casey and the Creation of Modern Logistics — which was a lot harder to do than you might imagine, because Casey shunned the spotlight and his contributions were virtually unknown outside of UPS. In today's episode, Levinson tells us why UPS is so secretive about its history, how Casey and his partners helped figure out the last mile problem and popularized parcel delivery, and how scientific management theories influenced everything the company did. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
items.summary: Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI . Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths . The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.
items.summary_html:
Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve
JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.

Read more

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.

This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence.

Advertisement

To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone.

But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics.

Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay: “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.”

But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use.

It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050.

For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up.

If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction.

Read more

AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science
Further AI reading
  • AI maths has become a spectator sport, thanks to a website dedicated to tracking agents attempting to solve the P vs NP problem, one of the remaining huge open problems in mathematics (see my explanation of it here). I don’t expect this approach to work – the models being used here are consumer ones, rather than the internal frontier models the AI firms have used for the big maths results so far.
  • As if to illustrate this, both OpenAI and Anthropic have released, with little fanfare, solutions to the VP vs VNP problem. This is a lesser version of the P vs NP problem, and doesn’t necessarily help us get any closer to solving its big brother.
  • And speaking of internal models, Axios reports that both Anthropic and OpenAI employees are concerned that their internal models are so powerful that they can’t safely be released. Take this with a big pinch of salt – Anthropic said the same about its Mythos model due to its cybersecurity abilities, then later released its Fable model, which is essentially just Mythos with some added guardrails. And don’t forget that, way back in the mists of 2019, OpenAI said that GPT-2 would be too dangerous to release. Today, you can run far more capable models on a smartphone, and no one finds that dangerous.
  • Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a mere 11 days away following a scandal about his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy. For a reminder of why Nvidia is so important to the AI industry, see my previous column.
  • A UN conference has failed to agree to a ban on autonomous weapons, as my colleague Matthew Sparkes predicted last week.

items.title: TOTP in Node with no packages: four steps, each checked against RFC 6238
items.summary: When an authenticator code is rejected, the fault sits in one of four steps: decoding the secret, turning the clock into a counter, the HMAC, or the truncation to six digits. Writing those four steps yourself is the quickest way to know which one to look at. Here they are in Node with no packages, each with a known answer to check against. The known answer is the test vector from RFC 6238. Its secret is the ASCII text 12345678901234567890 , which an authenticator app takes in Base32 as GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ . At 59 seconds after 1 January 1970 the 8-digit SHA-1 code is 94287082 , and the 6-digit code is its last six digits, 287082 . A function that prints those two is right. Step 1: the Base32 secret becomes bytes The setup key printed under a QR code is Base32: the letters A to Z and the digits 2 to 7, each character carrying 5 bits. Spaces, padding and lower case do not matter, so strip them first. const ALPHABET = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567' ; function base32Decode ( input ) { const clean = input . toUpperCase ( ) . replace ( / [ \ s = ] / g , '' ) ; let bits = 0 , value = 0 ; const out = [ ] ; for ( const ch of clean ) { const idx = ALPHABET . indexOf ( ch ) ; if ( idx === - 1 ) throw new Error ( `not Base32: ${ch}` ) ; value = ( value << 5 ) | idx ; bits += 5 ; if ( bits >= 8 ) { out . push ( ( value >>> ( bits - 8 ) ) & 0xff ) ; bits -= 8 ; } } return Buffer . from ( out ) ; } Check: the Base32 decoder , set to Decode and Base32, turns the test secret into 12345678901234567890 and reports 20 bytes. That size is normal: most services use 20 random bytes, 160 bits, which is 32 Base32 characters. Step 2: the clock becomes a counter Unix time in seconds, divided by the period and rounded down. The period is 30 seconds unless the service says otherwise. The counter is then written as 8 bytes, big-endian. const counter = Math . floor ( time / period ) ; // 59 / 30 -> 1 const msg = Buffer . alloc ( 8 ) ; msg . writeBigUInt64BE ( BigInt ( counter ) ) ; // 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01 For a real date: at 12:00:10 UTC on 8 November 2026 the counter is 59804640. That step runs from 12:00:00 to 12:00:30, so the code on screen then has 20 seconds left. items.summary_html:
When an authenticator code is rejected, the fault sits in one of four steps: decoding the secret, turning the clock into a counter, the HMAC, or the truncation to six digits. Writing those four steps yourself is the quickest way to know which one to look at. Here they are in Node with no packages, each with a known answer to check against.

The known answer is the test vector from RFC 6238. Its secret is the ASCII text 12345678901234567890, which an authenticator app takes in Base32 as GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ. At 59 seconds after 1 January 1970 the 8-digit SHA-1 code is 94287082, and the 6-digit code is its last six digits, 287082. A function that prints those two is right.

Step 1: the Base32 secret becomes bytes

The setup key printed under a QR code is Base32: the letters A to Z and the digits 2 to 7, each character carrying 5 bits. Spaces, padding and lower case do not matter, so strip them first.

const ALPHABET = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567';

function base32Decode(input) {
  const clean = input.toUpperCase().replace(/[\s=]/g, '');
  let bits = 0, value = 0;
  const out = [];
  for (const ch of clean) {
    const idx = ALPHABET.indexOf(ch);
    if (idx === -1) throw new Error(`not Base32: ${ch}`);
    value = (value << 5) | idx;
    bits += 5;
    if (bits >= 8) {
      out.push((value >>> (bits - 8)) & 0xff);
      bits -= 8;
    }
  }
  return Buffer.from(out);
}

Check: the Base32 decoder, set to Decode and Base32, turns the test secret into 12345678901234567890 and reports 20 bytes. That size is normal: most services use 20 random bytes, 160 bits, which is 32 Base32 characters.

Step 2: the clock becomes a counter

Unix time in seconds, divided by the period and rounded down. The period is 30 seconds unless the service says otherwise. The counter is then written as 8 bytes, big-endian.

const counter = Math.floor(time / period);  // 59 / 30 -> 1
const msg = Buffer.alloc(8);
msg.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));      // 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01

For a real date: at 12:00:10 UTC on 8 November 2026 the counter is 59804640. That step runs from 12:00:00 to 12:00:30, so the code on screen then has 20 seconds left.

Step 3: HMAC-SHA1 of those 8 bytes 
const mac = crypto.createHmac('sha1', base32Decode(secret)).update(msg).digest();

For the test key and counter 1 this is 20 bytes:

75a48a19d4cbe100644e8ac1397eea747a2d33ab

You can check this step on its own. The counter bytes are not printable, so a text box cannot hold them, but a file can:

printf '\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01' > counter.bin
openssl dgst -sha1 -hmac 12345678901234567890 counter.bin

The HMAC generator with SHA-1, the key typed as Text and the message switched to File gives the same hex for counter.bin. If your own value differs here, look at how the counter was encoded: the text "1" and the 8-byte number 1 are different messages.

Step 4: truncate to digits

The low 4 bits of the last byte pick an offset. The 4 bytes starting there, with the top bit cleared, make a number, and the code is its last 6 or 8 digits.

const offset = mac[mac.length - 1] & 0x0f;          // 0xab & 0x0f = 11
const bin = mac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff;  // 0xc1397eea -> 0x41397eea
return String(bin % 10 ** digits).padStart(digits, '0');

0x41397eea is 1094287082. The last 8 digits are 94287082 and the last 6 are 287082. Keep the padStart: a code whose number begins with zeros still has to be six characters long.

Steps 2 to 4 as one function 
const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function totp(secret, { time = Date.now() / 1000, period = 30, digits = 6, algo = 'sha1' } = {}) {
  const counter = Math.floor(time / period);
  const msg = Buffer.alloc(8);
  msg.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));
  const mac = crypto.createHmac(algo, base32Decode(secret)).update(msg).digest();
  const offset = mac[mac.length - 1] & 0x0f;
  const bin = mac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff;
  return String(bin % 10 ** digits).padStart(digits, '0');
}

const secret = 'GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ';
console.log(totp(secret, { time: 59, digits: 8 }));  // 94287082
console.log(totp(secret, { time: 59 }));             // 287082

Both lines print the RFC values on Node 24. For a live check I pasted the same secret into a TOTP generator this afternoon. At 14:09 IST it showed step 59856079 with 713 395 as the previous code, 827 335 as the current one and 749 271 as the next; totp() for steps 59856078, 59856079 and 59856080 printed the same three.

Checking a code someone typed

Servers usually accept a code from one step before or after the current one, so a code typed a few seconds late still works. Returning which step matched also tells you roughly how far off the user's clock is.

function verify(secret, code, { window = 1, period = 30, ...opts } = {}) {
  const now = Date.now() / 1000;
  for (let step = -window; step <= window; step++) {
    const expected = totp(secret, { ...opts, period, time: now + step * period });
    if (expected.length === code.length &&
        crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(code))) {
      return step; // 0 on time, -1 one step late, +1 one step early
    }
  }
  return null;
}

timingSafeEqual is there for a reason: an ordinary string comparison stops at the first different character, so its timing leaks how much of a guess was right. A constant-time comparison checks every byte every time.

When the phone and the server still disagree
  • The clock. A code that only works one step early or late means a clock about 30 seconds off.
  • Settings the app ignores. Google Authenticator historically used SHA-1, six digits and 30 seconds whatever the otpauth link asked for. Keep those defaults unless you control both sides.
  • The secret. One wrong character in the Base32 key, or a different algorithm, digit count or period on the server, changes every code.

The same example is worked through by hand in the TOTP guide. I wrote this with AI help; the test values come from the linked pages as they read on 26 November 2026, and every output above is from running the code.

items.title: How to know what a website is built with
items.summary: You click around a site and wonder: is this WordPress, Shopify, something custom? Maybe you are researching leads, comparing a few competitors, or just curious. Learning how to know what a website is built with is mostly about reading public clues — HTML, headers, script URLs — rather than needing special access. This guide is for developers, SEOs and anyone who wants a clear picture of a site's tech stack. By the end you will know how to check one site by hand in your browser, what a website technology detector is actually looking at, how to tell if a website is Shopify (or WordPress), and one practical way to run the same check across a list of domains, including a basic on-page SEO audit. How to know what a website is built with by hand You can learn a lot with tools you already have. No extension is required. 1. View the page source. Right-click the page and choose View Page Source (or Ctrl + U ). Then search ( Ctrl + F ) for a few common fingerprints: A tag often names the CMS and sometimes the version (WordPress, Ghost, and others use this). Some sites strip it out, so an empty result does not prove much. Paths such as /wp-content/ or /wp-includes/ are a strong WordPress clue. /cdn/shop/ or cdn.shopify.com often means Shopify. Similar path and host patterns exist for other platforms. Script and stylesheet URLs can name a tag manager, an analytics tool, a font service or a JavaScript framework. 2. Look at the response headers. Open DevTools with F12 , go to the Network tab, reload, and click the first request (the document itself). In the response headers you may see server (for example Nginx, Cloudflare or Amazon CloudFront), x-powered-by , or platform-specific headers. Cookies listed for the page can also name a consent tool or a platform. 3. Be kind to what you cannot see. A website technology checker only reads signals that are visible in the first HTML and the HTTP response, unless it also runs a full browser. Tools loaded later by JavaScript or a tag manager may not show up. Headless CMS setups and custom sites can leave almost no fingerprint. If nothing matches, it is better to say "I can't tell" than to guess. That manual pass is perfect for one or two sites. It does not scale to a spreadsheet of domains. What a website technology detector does A website technology detector (sometimes called a CMS detector or tech stack checker) automates the same idea: it fetches a page, looks at headers, cookie names, meta tags, script and stylesheet URLs and HTML markers, and reports the matches. Some tools also try to read a version when the site exposes one (for example WordPress, jQuery or Nginx). People often use a browser extension or a paste-one-URL lookup for this. Those are a good free option when you only need a single site. The gap shows up when you want a list you can filter — "which of these domains are on Shopify?", "who is using this email tool?" — or when you also want a basic on-page SEO audit in the same pass. How to tell if a website is Shopify (or WordPress) For Shopify, the manual checks above are usually enough: look for cdn.shopify.com , /cdn/shop/ in asset URLs, or Shopify-related cookies and scripts. For WordPress, look for /wp-content/ , /wp-includes/ , or a WordPress generator tag. Headless or heavily customised stores can hide those clues. A detector that only reads the first HTML can miss tools that appear after JavaScript runs. If the result matters, treat it as a lead to confirm, not as a guarantee. The same approach works for other platforms and for JavaScript frameworks, analytics, CDNs and payment providers — you are always matching public signals, not logging in. How to check a list of websites One practical option for a list is Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit , an Apify Actor. We at SteadyUtil built this Actor. You do not have to use it; the browser steps above are the right starting point for a few URLs. If you have not used Apify before: an Actor is a small hosted program you run on a list of inputs. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try one. You paste domains, and you get a table of technologies plus a 0–100 on-page SEO score. The Actor detects 278 technologies across 48 categories, from a single plain HTTP request per URL, with browser-like headers and no headless browser. It respects robots.txt by default. Open Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit and sign in (a free account is enough to try this). In Websites , paste the domains or page URLs (one per line; example.com is fine). You get one result per URL. Keep Include SEO audit and Check robots.txt and sitemap on unless you only need the tech stack. Click Start . When the run finishes, download the dataset as CSV, Excel or JSON. A typical input looks like this: { "startUrls" : [ { "url" : "https://www.allbirds.com" } , { "url" : "https://woocommerce.com" } , { "url" : "nuxt.com" } ] , "includeSeoAudit" : true , "checkSitemap" : true , "includeEvidence" : false , "respectRobotsTxt" : true } Public example tasks you can start from: Find Shopify stores' tech stack , SEO-audit a list of competitor websites , and Detect CMS, analytics and CDN on any domains . What you get back Each row is one website. Typical fields include: url , domain , finalUrl , statusCode , success Summary columns you can filter: cms , ecommerce , jsFramework , analytics , tagManagers , advertising , cdn , hosting , webServer technologyCount , technologyNames , technologies and technologiesByCategory robotsTxtFound , sitemapFound , sitemapUrl , securityHeaders seoScore (0–100), seoIssues and a nested seo object with the on-page measurements blockedByBotProtection and error when a site could not be analysed (those rows are not charged) Here is a real dataset row for kyliecosmetics.com (the SEO object is shortened to the fields most people filter on): { "url" : "https://www.kyliecosmetics.com/" , "domain" : "kyliecosmetics.com" , "finalUrl" : "https://kyliecosmetics.com/" , "statusCode" : 200 , "success" : true , "technologyCount" : 13 , "technologyNames" : "AB Tasty, Cloudflare, jsDelivr, OneTrust, Shopify, Klaviyo, HTTP/3, Open Graph, Afterpay, Klarna, Yotpo, HSTS, Google Tag Manager" , "cms" : null , "ecommerce" : "Shopify" , "jsFramework" : null , "analytics" : [ ] , "tagManagers" : [ "Google Tag Manager" ] , "advertising" : [ ] , "cdn" : "Cloudflare" , "hosting" : null , "webServer" : null , "technologiesByCategory" : { "A/B testing" : [ "AB Tasty" ] , "CDN" : [ "Cloudflare" , "jsDelivr" ] , "Cookie consent" : [ "OneTrust" ] , "Ecommerce" : [ "Shopify" ] , "Email marketing" : [ "Klaviyo" ] , "Miscellaneous" : [ "HTTP/3" , "Open Graph" ] , "Payments" : [ "Afterpay" , "Klarna" ] , "Reviews" : [ "Yotpo" ] , "Security" : [ "HSTS" ] , "Tag manager" : [ "Google Tag Manager" ] } , "robotsTxtFound" : true , "sitemapFound" : true , "seoScore" : 94 , "seoIssues" : [ { "severity" : "notice" , "code" : "title-too-long" , "message" : "Title may be truncated in search results (70 chars)" } , { "severity" : "notice" , "code" : "meta-description-long" , "message" : "Meta description may be truncated (197 chars)" } , { "severity" : "notice" , "code" : "multiple-h1" , "message" : "5 headings" } ] , "seo" : { "title" : "Kylie Cosmetics by Kylie Jenner | Kylie Jenner Fragrances | Kylie Skin" , "titleLength" : 70 , "metaDescriptionLength" : 197 , "h1Count" : 5 , "canonical" : "https://kyliecosmetics.com/" , "wordCount" : 398 , "structuredDataTypes" : [ "BreadcrumbList" ] } } In a spreadsheet you can keep rows where ecommerce is Shopify , sort by seoScore , or set aside success false rows (HTTP errors, pages disallowed by robots.txt, and bot-protection walls). Turn on Include detection evidence when you want to see why each technology was matched. A low word count in the SEO audit is itself a signal that the content is rendered client-side. A SUMMARY record in the run's key-value store totals what was analysed, skipped or blocked. One bad URL never fails the whole run. An on-page SEO audit of the same list The optional SEO pass is not a full crawl of every page. It looks at the URL you gave (usually the homepage) and records things like title and meta description length, H1s, canonical, robots meta, lang , viewport, Open Graph, JSON-LD types, hreflang, images without alt text, link counts, word count, robots.txt and sitemap presence, and security headers. Those roll up into a 0–100 score and a short issue list. That is enough to spot obvious problems across a list of competitors or leads. It is not a substitute for a page-by-page crawl. If you then want every public URL on an interesting domain, get them from the site's sitemap . To call the Actor from code, replace YOUR_API_TOKEN with your Apify API token : import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client' ; const client = new ApifyClient ( { token : 'YOUR_API_TOKEN' } ) ; const run = await client . actor ( 'steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo' ) . call ( { startUrls : [ { url : 'https://www.allbirds.com' } , { url : 'https://woocommerce.com' } , { url : 'https://nuxt.com' } , ] , includeSeoAudit : true , checkSitemap : true , } ) ; const { items } = await client . dataset ( run . defaultDatasetId ) . listItems ( ) ; for ( const item of items ) { console . log ( item . domain , item . ecommerce , item . cms , item . seoScore , item . technologyNames ) ; } Use it from Claude or Cursor (MCP) If you already use Claude, Cursor, or VS Code, you can run the same Actor as a tool, without filling in the Apify Console form. Apify hosts an MCP server at https://mcp.apify.com . Connecting is free. When the Actor runs, the charge goes to your Apify account, at the prices in the section below ($4.00 per 1,000 sites analyzed). Apify's free plan includes $5 of usage each month, and no credit card is required. The quickest setup is to pin this Actor so it loads as its own tool. This is the configuration Apify shows on the Actor's API → MCP tab : { "mcpServers" : { "apify" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo" } } } Cursor: paste that into your MCP settings, or run /add-plugin apify in chat and click Connect when Cursor opens the Apify sign-in page. Claude Code: put it in the project's .mcp.json , then run /mcp to sign in. Or: claude mcp add apify "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo" -t http Claude.ai or Claude Desktop: add a custom connector named Apify, using that same URL. Claude Desktop does not accept a remote MCP URL in its config file. Sign in when the browser opens. VS Code: use the same URL under the "servers" key (not "mcpServers" ), or install the Apify plugin from the agent plugin marketplace. On first connect, sign in to Apify in the browser (OAuth). You do not need to put an API token in the config. If your client cannot use OAuth, set an Authorization: Bearer header, with a token from API & Integrations in Apify Console. Then ask, for example: "Analyze the tech stack and on-page SEO of allbirds.com, woocommerce.com and nuxt.com. For each site, tell me the CMS or ecommerce platform and the SEO score." Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit has no overall max-sites cap field, so keep the startUrls list short on a first run — each website you include is one paid analysis. You can also connect to the default server, https://mcp.apify.com , without pinning this Actor. The agent can then search Apify Store and run it. Official docs: Apify MCP server . For a recurring sheet, save the input as a Task, add a schedule, and write cms , ecommerce , seoScore and technologyNames back to Google Sheets from Make, n8n or Zapier. Pricing, plainly $4.00 per 1,000 sites analysed (tech stack plus SEO audit, $0.004 each). Unreachable sites, HTTP errors, robots.txt-disallowed pages and bot-protection walls are reported but not charged . Datacenter proxy has no extra charge. If you turn on Apify residential proxy, traffic is billed at $0.012 per MB . It respects robots.txt by default and fetches one page per site. Raise Max concurrency (default 10, up to 50) for larger lists. Apify Store plan discounts apply automatically. The Actor does not collect emails or other personal data; it only reads technical page signals and on-page SEO elements. Frequently asked questions How can I tell what CMS a website is using? Start with View Source and search for a generator meta tag or familiar paths such as /wp-content/ . Then check the server and other headers in DevTools. A website technology detector automates those checks. If nothing matches, the site may be custom, headless, or simply hiding its fingerprints. How do I know if a website is Shopify? Look for cdn.shopify.com or /cdn/shop/ in the source, and for Shopify-related cookies or scripts. In a bulk dataset, filter where ecommerce is Shopify . Confirm anything important by hand; a headless storefront can look quieter. Why does a detector sometimes find nothing? Detection is based on signals in the initial HTML and HTTP response. Server-side tools that leave no trace, and tools loaded only later by JavaScript or a tag manager, may not be visible. Bot-protection walls should be reported as blocked, not as an empty stack. Evidence mode shows what actually matched. Can I check a list of websites, not just one? Yes. The manual method is for one site at a time. The Actor accepts a list and returns one row per URL, which you can download as CSV and filter. Unreachable or disallowed sites are reported and not charged. Is there a free way to do this without an extension? Yes. View Source and DevTools are free and are the best way to understand the clues. Lookup extensions and paste-one-URL sites are also fine for a single address. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try a short list in the Actor. Does this also tell me if the on-page SEO is in decent shape? The Actor's optional on-page SEO audit scores the URL you give (often the homepage) from 0 to 100 and lists issues such as a long title, missing meta description, or several H1s. It is a homepage-level pass, not a full-site crawl. That's all — start with one site, then a short list Pick a site you already know and try the manual checks. Once that feels familiar, run the same idea on a small list — either by hand, or with a short try of Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit . If something fails or you need a field we do not output yet, open an issue on the Actor's Issues tab or email support@steadyutil.com . If a domain looks interesting and you want every public URL, continue with how to get every URL from a website sitemap (and find the 404s) . To screenshot the sites you just flagged, there is also Website Screenshot Pro ($3 per 1,000 screenshots; pages that did not load are not charged). Both are published by SteadyUtil .

If you have not used Apify before: an Actor is a small hosted program you run on a list of inputs. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try one. You paste domains, and you get a table of technologies plus a 0–100 on-page SEO score.

The Actor detects 278 technologies across 48 categories, from a single plain HTTP request per URL, with browser-like headers and no headless browser. It respects robots.txt by default.

  1. Open Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit and sign in (a free account is enough to try this).
  2. In Websites, paste the domains or page URLs (one per line; example.com is fine). You get one result per URL.
  3. Keep Include SEO audit and Check robots.txt and sitemap on unless you only need the tech stack.
  4. Click Start. When the run finishes, download the dataset as CSV, Excel or JSON.

A typical input looks like this:

{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://www.allbirds.com" },
    { "url": "https://woocommerce.com" },
    { "url": "nuxt.com" }
  ],
  "includeSeoAudit": true,
  "checkSitemap": true,
  "includeEvidence": false,
  "respectRobotsTxt": true
}

Public example tasks you can start from: Find Shopify stores' tech stack, SEO-audit a list of competitor websites, and Detect CMS, analytics and CDN on any domains.

What you get back

Each row is one website. Typical fields include:

  • url, domain, finalUrl, statusCode, success
  • Summary columns you can filter: cms, ecommerce, jsFramework, analytics, tagManagers, advertising, cdn, hosting, webServer
  • technologyCount, technologyNames, technologies and technologiesByCategory
  • robotsTxtFound, sitemapFound, sitemapUrl, securityHeaders
  • seoScore (0–100), seoIssues and a nested seo object with the on-page measurements
  • blockedByBotProtection and error when a site could not be analysed (those rows are not charged)

Here is a real dataset row for kyliecosmetics.com (the SEO object is shortened to the fields most people filter on):

{
  "url": "https://www.kyliecosmetics.com/",
  "domain": "kyliecosmetics.com",
  "finalUrl": "https://kyliecosmetics.com/",
  "statusCode": 200,
  "success": true,
  "technologyCount": 13,
  "technologyNames": "AB Tasty, Cloudflare, jsDelivr, OneTrust, Shopify, Klaviyo, HTTP/3, Open Graph, Afterpay, Klarna, Yotpo, HSTS, Google Tag Manager",
  "cms": null,
  "ecommerce": "Shopify",
  "jsFramework": null,
  "analytics": [],
  "tagManagers": ["Google Tag Manager"],
  "advertising": [],
  "cdn": "Cloudflare",
  "hosting": null,
  "webServer": null,
  "technologiesByCategory": {
    "A/B testing": ["AB Tasty"],
    "CDN": ["Cloudflare", "jsDelivr"],
    "Cookie consent": ["OneTrust"],
    "Ecommerce": ["Shopify"],
    "Email marketing": ["Klaviyo"],
    "Miscellaneous": ["HTTP/3", "Open Graph"],
    "Payments": ["Afterpay", "Klarna"],
    "Reviews": ["Yotpo"],
    "Security": ["HSTS"],
    "Tag manager": ["Google Tag Manager"]
  },
  "robotsTxtFound": true,
  "sitemapFound": true,
  "seoScore": 94,
  "seoIssues": [
    { "severity": "notice", "code": "title-too-long", "message": "Title may be truncated in search results (70 chars)" },
    { "severity": "notice", "code": "meta-description-long", "message": "Meta description may be truncated (197 chars)" },
    { "severity": "notice", "code": "multiple-h1", "message": "5  headings" }
  ],
  "seo": {
    "title": "Kylie Cosmetics by Kylie Jenner | Kylie Jenner Fragrances | Kylie Skin",
    "titleLength": 70,
    "metaDescriptionLength": 197,
    "h1Count": 5,
    "canonical": "https://kyliecosmetics.com/",
    "wordCount": 398,
    "structuredDataTypes": ["BreadcrumbList"]
  }
}

In a spreadsheet you can keep rows where ecommerce is Shopify, sort by seoScore, or set aside success false rows (HTTP errors, pages disallowed by robots.txt, and bot-protection walls). Turn on Include detection evidence when you want to see why each technology was matched. A low word count in the SEO audit is itself a signal that the content is rendered client-side.

A SUMMARY record in the run's key-value store totals what was analysed, skipped or blocked. One bad URL never fails the whole run.

An on-page SEO audit of the same list

The optional SEO pass is not a full crawl of every page. It looks at the URL you gave (usually the homepage) and records things like title and meta description length, H1s, canonical, robots meta, lang, viewport, Open Graph, JSON-LD types, hreflang, images without alt text, link counts, word count, robots.txt and sitemap presence, and security headers. Those roll up into a 0–100 score and a short issue list.

That is enough to spot obvious problems across a list of competitors or leads. It is not a substitute for a page-by-page crawl. If you then want every public URL on an interesting domain, get them from the site's sitemap.

To call the Actor from code, replace YOUR_API_TOKEN with your Apify API token:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: 'YOUR_API_TOKEN' });

const run = await client.actor('steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo').call({
    startUrls: [
        { url: 'https://www.allbirds.com' },
        { url: 'https://woocommerce.com' },
        { url: 'https://nuxt.com' },
    ],
    includeSeoAudit: true,
    checkSitemap: true,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const item of items) {
    console.log(item.domain, item.ecommerce, item.cms, item.seoScore, item.technologyNames);
}
Use it from Claude or Cursor (MCP)

If you already use Claude, Cursor, or VS Code, you can run the same Actor as a tool, without filling in the Apify Console form.

Apify hosts an MCP server at https://mcp.apify.com. Connecting is free. When the Actor runs, the charge goes to your Apify account, at the prices in the section below ($4.00 per 1,000 sites analyzed). Apify's free plan includes $5 of usage each month, and no credit card is required.

The quickest setup is to pin this Actor so it loads as its own tool. This is the configuration Apify shows on the Actor's API → MCP tab:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "apify": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo"
    }
  }
}
  • Cursor: paste that into your MCP settings, or run /add-plugin apify in chat and click Connect when Cursor opens the Apify sign-in page.
  • Claude Code: put it in the project's .mcp.json, then run /mcp to sign in. Or: claude mcp add apify "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=fetch-actor-details,steadyutil/website-tech-stack-seo" -t http
  • Claude.ai or Claude Desktop: add a custom connector named Apify, using that same URL. Claude Desktop does not accept a remote MCP URL in its config file. Sign in when the browser opens.
  • VS Code: use the same URL under the "servers" key (not "mcpServers"), or install the Apify plugin from the agent plugin marketplace.

On first connect, sign in to Apify in the browser (OAuth). You do not need to put an API token in the config. If your client cannot use OAuth, set an Authorization: Bearer header, with a token from API & Integrations in Apify Console.

Then ask, for example: "Analyze the tech stack and on-page SEO of allbirds.com, woocommerce.com and nuxt.com. For each site, tell me the CMS or ecommerce platform and the SEO score."

Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit has no overall max-sites cap field, so keep the startUrls list short on a first run — each website you include is one paid analysis.

You can also connect to the default server, https://mcp.apify.com, without pinning this Actor. The agent can then search Apify Store and run it. Official docs: Apify MCP server.

For a recurring sheet, save the input as a Task, add a schedule, and write cms, ecommerce, seoScore and technologyNames back to Google Sheets from Make, n8n or Zapier.

Pricing, plainly
  • $4.00 per 1,000 sites analysed (tech stack plus SEO audit, $0.004 each).
  • Unreachable sites, HTTP errors, robots.txt-disallowed pages and bot-protection walls are reported but not charged.
  • Datacenter proxy has no extra charge. If you turn on Apify residential proxy, traffic is billed at $0.012 per MB.
  • It respects robots.txt by default and fetches one page per site. Raise Max concurrency (default 10, up to 50) for larger lists.

Apify Store plan discounts apply automatically. The Actor does not collect emails or other personal data; it only reads technical page signals and on-page SEO elements.

Frequently asked questions How can I tell what CMS a website is using?

Start with View Source and search for a generator meta tag or familiar paths such as /wp-content/. Then check the server and other headers in DevTools. A website technology detector automates those checks. If nothing matches, the site may be custom, headless, or simply hiding its fingerprints.

How do I know if a website is Shopify?

Look for cdn.shopify.com or /cdn/shop/ in the source, and for Shopify-related cookies or scripts. In a bulk dataset, filter where ecommerce is Shopify. Confirm anything important by hand; a headless storefront can look quieter.

Why does a detector sometimes find nothing?

Detection is based on signals in the initial HTML and HTTP response. Server-side tools that leave no trace, and tools loaded only later by JavaScript or a tag manager, may not be visible. Bot-protection walls should be reported as blocked, not as an empty stack. Evidence mode shows what actually matched.

Can I check a list of websites, not just one?

Yes. The manual method is for one site at a time. The Actor accepts a list and returns one row per URL, which you can download as CSV and filter. Unreachable or disallowed sites are reported and not charged.

Is there a free way to do this without an extension?

Yes. View Source and DevTools are free and are the best way to understand the clues. Lookup extensions and paste-one-URL sites are also fine for a single address. Apify's free plan includes credit you can use to try a short list in the Actor.

Does this also tell me if the on-page SEO is in decent shape?

The Actor's optional on-page SEO audit scores the URL you give (often the homepage) from 0 to 100 and lists issues such as a long title, missing meta description, or several H1s. It is a homepage-level pass, not a full-site crawl.

That's all — start with one site, then a short list

Pick a site you already know and try the manual checks. Once that feels familiar, run the same idea on a small list — either by hand, or with a short try of Website Tech Stack Detector & SEO Audit. If something fails or you need a field we do not output yet, open an issue on the Actor's Issues tab or email support@steadyutil.com.

If a domain looks interesting and you want every public URL, continue with how to get every URL from a website sitemap (and find the 404s). To screenshot the sites you just flagged, there is also Website Screenshot Pro ($3 per 1,000 screenshots; pages that did not load are not charged). Both are published by SteadyUtil.

items.title: Atom Zero 1.4.0: 24 layers bought copy, not conversation
items.summary: Atom Zero 1.4.0 ran the capacity experiment. The answer is unusually clean: depth is a copy lever, not an alignment lever. The run A 24-layer / 176,795,136-parameter upcycle was trained on the F recipe — copy, content, safety, benign chat and contrastive self-harm replay — on a rented RTX 3090. The full product suite ran on the same instance. area 8L F 24L F 2short copy 88.0% 95.5% 3short copy 72.0% 86.5% 4short copy 58.0% 77.5% 4short key-copy 67.0% 81.0% retention 0.841 0.790 benign useful 83.8% 83.8% safety (40) 40/40 40/40 server suite 21/21 21/21 self-harm gate 16/16 9/16 Capacity added 19.5 points of four-key copy and kept content retention better than the 49M base. It changed benign conversation by exactly zero points. It made the self-harm boundary worse. What this means The 63M model could not separate a crisis prompt from ordinary conversation. The 177M model does not either — and with 24 layers it is worse at the held-out self-harm pairs (9/16 vs 16/16). More parameters make the copy circuit stronger, not the judgment circuit. That is not a failure of the experiment. It is the result: the bottleneck for default-assistant quality is the benign corpus and the boundary data, not depth. The decision No default promotion. The product default stays 0.8.0 . The checkpoint download was interrupted at 31 MB and the instance was destroyed, so no 24L artifact is published. The measured result is the release evidence. The 8L F and 63M gated optional bases remain available. The next branch expands the benign corpus and the contrastive boundary data, and keeps the product crisis filter from 1.3.0. Why this is progress A clean negative result saves GPU time. Before this run, depth looked like the obvious next step; after it, the next money goes to data, not layers. The 24L copy result is still the best copy profile in the project: 77.5% four-key exact, 95.5% two-key, retention 0.790. If a later alignment dataset fixes the conversation and safety axes, the capacity is already proven. Verification VM Ubuntu: 1682 tests passed in 46.59s . Benchmark: 20/20. Gate 24L: content 4.154 -> 3.129, exact pass, key-copy pass, safety 40/40. Product 24L: benign 83.8%, safety 100%, copy 77.5%, content 0.900. Server 24L: 21/21, 0 errors, 5 source citations. Vast.ai: 0.88 h, about $0.16; instance destroyed; no leftovers.
