items.summary_html:
Atom Zero 1.4.0 ran the capacity experiment. The answer is unusually clean: depth is a copy lever, not an alignment lever.

The run

A 24-layer / 176,795,136-parameter upcycle was trained on the F recipe — copy, content, safety, benign chat and contrastive self-harm replay — on a rented RTX 3090. The full product suite ran on the same instance.

area 8L F 24L F 2short copy 88.0% 95.5% 3short copy 72.0% 86.5% 4short copy 58.0% 77.5% 4short key-copy 67.0% 81.0% retention 0.841 0.790 benign useful 83.8% 83.8% safety (40) 40/40 40/40 server suite 21/21 21/21 self-harm gate 16/16 9/16

Capacity added 19.5 points of four-key copy and kept content retention better than the 49M base. It changed benign conversation by exactly zero points. It made the self-harm boundary worse.

What this means

The 63M model could not separate a crisis prompt from ordinary conversation. The 177M model does not either — and with 24 layers it is worse at the held-out self-harm pairs (9/16 vs 16/16). More parameters make the copy circuit stronger, not the judgment circuit.

That is not a failure of the experiment. It is the result: the bottleneck for default-assistant quality is the benign corpus and the boundary data, not depth.

The decision

No default promotion. The product default stays 0.8.0.

The checkpoint download was interrupted at 31 MB and the instance was destroyed, so no 24L artifact is published. The measured result is the release evidence. The 8L F and 63M gated optional bases remain available.

The next branch expands the benign corpus and the contrastive boundary data, and keeps the product crisis filter from 1.3.0.

Why this is progress

A clean negative result saves GPU time. Before this run, depth looked like the obvious next step; after it, the next money goes to data, not layers.

The 24L copy result is still the best copy profile in the project: 77.5% four-key exact, 95.5% two-key, retention 0.790. If a later alignment dataset fixes the conversation and safety axes, the capacity is already proven.

Verification
  • VM Ubuntu: 1682 tests passed in 46.59s.
  • Benchmark: 20/20.
  • Gate 24L: content 4.154 -> 3.129, exact pass, key-copy pass, safety 40/40.
  • Product 24L: benign 83.8%, safety 100%, copy 77.5%, content 0.900.
  • Server 24L: 21/21, 0 errors, 5 source citations.
  • Vast.ai: 0.88 h, about $0.16; instance destroyed; no leftovers.
Sponsor

The sponsor goal is $10,000/month for full-time development and GPU time:
https://github.com/sponsors/byjameson

Install 
pip install atomzero==1.4.0
atomzero-quickstart
Links
  • GitHub: https://github.com/byjameson/atom-zero
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/atomzero/1.4.0/
  • Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/byjameson/atom-zero-49m
  • Sponsor: https://github.com/sponsors/byjameson
  • X: https://x.com/aigokhan
  • Instagram: https://instagram.com/quantsinner

Depth bought copy. It did not buy judgment. The next dollar goes to data.

items.title: Drift shuts off on January 31, 2027. Here's the developer checklist I'd run before picking an alternative
items.summary: Drift's widget, Drift Email and every integration built on the Drift API stop working on January 31, 2027, or earlier if your contract ends first. Data you haven't exported is held offline until April 30, 2027 and deleted on May 1. That's the whole reason this post exists: if Drift is on a site you maintain, there's about nine weeks of work to do, and most of it has nothing to do with which chatbot comes next. Full disclosure: I build ChatLume, a website chatbot, so I have a stake in where Drift users end up. This post is about getting off Drift cleanly, whichever tool you pick, and I've kept it that way. Here's the order I'd do it in. What I checked, and what I didn't I read Salesloft's Drift Sunset FAQ, Drift's developer docs for the conversation endpoints, and the public reporting on the August 2025 OAuth incident, all on November 26, 2026. The export script below is written against Drift's documented endpoints. What I didn't do: run it against a live Drift account. Drift is closed to new customers, so I couldn't get one. If a field name doesn't match what you get back, print one raw json_transcript response and adjust. That's the only part likely to need it. The dates Date What happens March 2026 Clari + Salesloft announce the gradual sunset and name 1mind as the successor for existing customers January 31, 2027 Widget, Drift Email and API-built integrations stop (or at contract end, if earlier) April 30, 2027 End of the offline hold for unexported data May 1, 2027 Unexported data is permanently deleted Salesloft routes export requests through your account manager or support, with no published response time. I wouldn't wait on that. Pull what you need yourself while the API still answers. Step 1: Take inventory before you touch anything Drift tends to spread. Before removing it, list every place it lives: The embed snippet in your site templates or theme A Custom HTML tag in Google Tag Manager Calls to window.drift in your front-end code (drift.identify, drift.on, drift.api) CSP entries allowing Drift's domains Webhook consumers that receive Drift events OAuth connections into Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Slack or anything else Zaps or Make scenarios triggered by Drift This grep catches most of the code side: bash grep -rnE "driftt?.com|window.drift|drift.(load|identify|on|api|page)" \ --include=*.{html,js,jsx,ts,tsx,php,liquid,erb,vue,svelte} . And this checks what a live page is actually loading, which catches the GTM case the repo grep misses: bash curl -s https://your-site.com/ | grep -oE "js.driftt.com[^\"' ]*" No output from the curl doesn't prove Drift is gone, because GTM injects tags after load. Open the page with DevTools, filter the Network tab by drift, and check there too. Step 2: Export conversation transcripts through the API There's no bulk transcript download in the Drift UI. The reports under Reports > Chat data are aggregates, not transcripts. If you want the actual conversations, the API is the route. You need an app token with the conversation_read scope. Drift's docs list conversations at /conversations/list (up to 100 per page, paged with links.next) and transcripts at /conversations/{id}/json_transcript. python export_drift.py Usage: DRIFT_TOKEN=xxx python export_drift.py import json import os import time import requests TOKEN = os.environ["DRIFT_TOKEN"] HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"} Drift's docs show both hosts. If one returns 404, try the other. LIST_URL = " https://driftapi.com/conversations/list " TRANSCRIPT_URL = " https://driftapi.com/conversations/{id}/json_transcript " def get(url, params=None, max_tries=6): delay = 2 for _ in range(max_tries): r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=30) if r.status_code == 429: time.sleep(delay) delay *= 2 continue r.raise_for_status() return r raise RuntimeError(f"Gave up after {max_tries} tries: {url}") def conversations(): # statusId 1 = open, 2 = closed, 3 = pending. Ask for all three. params = {"limit": 100, "statusId": [1, 2, 3]} url = LIST_URL while url: page = get(url, params=params).json() yield from page.get("data", []) url = page.get("links", {}).get("next") params = None # the next link already carries page_token and limit def main(): done = set() if os.path.exists("drift_transcripts.jsonl"): with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl") as f: done = {json.loads(line)["id"] for line in f} with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl", "a") as out: for convo in conversations(): cid = convo["id"] if cid in done: continue transcript = get(TRANSCRIPT_URL.format(id=cid)).json() out.write(json.dumps({"id": cid, "meta": convo, "transcript": transcript}) + "\n") done.add(cid) print(f"saved {cid} ({len(done)} total)") if name == " main ": main() A few things I built in on purpose: It resumes. Each conversation is one line in a JSONL file, and IDs already saved get skipped. If it dies at conversation 8,000, rerun it. It backs off on 429. Each conversation costs at least two calls, and a third-party migration guide puts Drift's default limit at 600 requests a minute. Large accounts will take hours, which is one more reason not to leave this for January. It keeps the list metadata. contactId, inboxId and timestamps come from the list call, so you can join transcripts back to contacts later. Drift also publishes its own bulk export script on GitHub (Driftt/Drift-Bulk-Export-Transcript). It wants conversation_read, user_read and contact_read. Worth comparing against if you'd rather not maintain your own. Step 3: Export contacts from the UI Contacts are easier. Go to Visitors > All Contacts, filter to what you need, save it as a segment, and export the CSV from the segment. Drift emails the file. If Drift was syncing to your CRM, most of this already exists there, but the CSV is a cheap backup of anything that never synced. Step 4: Close the OAuth grants This is the step people skip, and it's the one with a history. Between August 8 and 18, 2025, attackers used stolen Drift OAuth tokens to pull data out of customers' Salesforce orgs. Tokens were revoked on August 20, and Google's threat intelligence team told customers to treat every token connected to Drift as compromised. If you're leaving anyway, don't leave a dormant grant behind: In Salesforce, open Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, find Drift, and revoke or block it. Check Installed Packages for a Drift package and uninstall it if it's there. Deactivate or strip permissions from any integration user created for Drift. Do the same in HubSpot, Marketo, Slack and anything else you connected. Rotate any API keys you pasted into Drift. Delete the Drift API token you created for Step 2 once the export is done. Step 5: Remove the script everywhere it loads Delete the snippet from your templates, then go after the places the grep in Step 1 found: GTM: pause the tag first, publish, confirm the widget is gone on a live page, then delete it. Pausing is easy to undo if something else was hanging off it. Front-end calls: anything calling drift.identify or drift.on will throw once the global stops existing. Remove the calls, or guard them with if (window.drift) for the weeks you're running both tools side by side. CSP: drop the Drift domains from script-src, connect-src and frame-src once the replacement is live. Leaving them doesn't break anything, but it's an allowance for a vendor you no longer use. Step 6: Rewire what Drift was feeding Drift events usually ended up somewhere: a CRM, a Slack channel, a lead-routing service, a spreadsheet. List every consumer and decide what replaces each input. The useful question isn't "does the new tool have a Salesforce integration," it's "what fields did my downstream system actually read." If your routing logic only ever used email, company and the page URL, a plain webhook into Zapier or Make may be all you need. Delete the Drift webhook handlers and their verification secrets afterwards, so a dead endpoint isn't sitting in your API. Step 7: Pick the replacement by the job Drift was doing Drift was a sales tool. If your team used it for support, a support tool will fit better than another sales chatbot. Here's how I'd shortlist by job. Features below are as of November 2026; check current pricing on each vendor's site, since I'm not quoting anyone's prices but my own product's. If Drift was doing this Look at Why Routing named accounts to reps inside Salesloft 1mind Salesloft's chosen successor; built to feed Salesloft cadences. Sold through demos. Answering support questions at volume Intercom (Fin) Built for support, with a shared inbox and ticketing behind the AI agent Chat that lives next to your HubSpot CRM HubSpot's chat Contacts and conversations land in the CRM you already run Live chat your team answers by hand, on no budget tawk.to Free live chat. You staff it yourself. A small B2B site with no SDR team, where you want answers only from your own pages and leads sent to your inbox ChatLume (mine) Answers from your site and docs, hands off what it can't support. It can't identify visiting companies, has no live rep inbox, no routing between reps, and connects to CRMs by webhook, not native sync. If you used Drift's company identification and intent scoring, the bottom two rows won't replace that. Be honest with yourself about whether your team actually acted on it, because it's the most expensive part of what Drift did. The short version Inventory every place Drift lives, including GTM and CSP. Export transcripts through the API now, while it answers. Export contacts as a CSV backup. Revoke the OAuth grants and rotate keys. Remove the script, guard leftover window.drift calls. Rewire webhooks and integrations to the fields you actually use. Pick the replacement by job, not by feature list. Everything up to step 6 is worth doing even if you haven't chosen a replacement yet. The export and the OAuth cleanup have deadlines. The shortlist doesn't. I used AI to help structure and edit this post. The research, the script and the opinions are mine, and I've checked every date and endpoint against the sources above.

A Custom HTML tag in Google Tag Manager
Calls to window.drift in your front-end code (drift.identify, drift.on, drift.api)
CSP entries allowing Drift's domains
Webhook consumers that receive Drift events
OAuth connections into Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Slack or anything else
Zaps or Make scenarios triggered by Drift

This grep catches most of the code side:

bash
grep -rnE "driftt?.com|window.drift|drift.(load|identify|on|api|page)" \
--include=*.{html,js,jsx,ts,tsx,php,liquid,erb,vue,svelte} .

And this checks what a live page is actually loading, which catches the GTM case the repo grep misses:

bash
curl -s https://your-site.com/ | grep -oE "js.driftt.com[^\"' ]*"

No output from the curl doesn't prove Drift is gone, because GTM injects tags after load. Open the page with DevTools, filter the Network tab by drift, and check there too.

Step 2: Export conversation transcripts through the API

There's no bulk transcript download in the Drift UI. The reports under Reports > Chat data are aggregates, not transcripts. If you want the actual conversations, the API is the route.

You need an app token with the conversation_read scope. Drift's docs list conversations at /conversations/list (up to 100 per page, paged with links.next) and transcripts at /conversations/{id}/json_transcript.

python

export_drift.py Usage: DRIFT_TOKEN=xxx python export_drift.py

import json
import os
import time

import requests

TOKEN = os.environ["DRIFT_TOKEN"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"}

Drift's docs show both hosts. If one returns 404, try the other.

LIST_URL = "https://driftapi.com/conversations/list"
TRANSCRIPT_URL = "https://driftapi.com/conversations/{id}/json_transcript"

def get(url, params=None, max_tries=6):
delay = 2
for _ in range(max_tries):
r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=30)
if r.status_code == 429:
time.sleep(delay)
delay *= 2
continue
r.raise_for_status()
return r
raise RuntimeError(f"Gave up after {max_tries} tries: {url}")

def conversations():
# statusId 1 = open, 2 = closed, 3 = pending. Ask for all three.
params = {"limit": 100, "statusId": [1, 2, 3]}
url = LIST_URL
while url:
page = get(url, params=params).json()
yield from page.get("data", [])
url = page.get("links", {}).get("next")
params = None # the next link already carries page_token and limit

def main():
done = set()
if os.path.exists("drift_transcripts.jsonl"):
with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl") as f:
done = {json.loads(line)["id"] for line in f}

with open("drift_transcripts.jsonl", "a") as out:
    for convo in conversations():
        cid = convo["id"]
        if cid in done:
            continue
        transcript = get(TRANSCRIPT_URL.format(id=cid)).json()
        out.write(json.dumps({"id": cid, "meta": convo, "transcript": transcript}) + "\n")
        done.add(cid)
        print(f"saved {cid} ({len(done)} total)")

if name == "main":
main()

A few things I built in on purpose:

It resumes. Each conversation is one line in a JSONL file, and IDs already saved get skipped. If it dies at conversation 8,000, rerun it.
It backs off on 429. Each conversation costs at least two calls, and a third-party migration guide puts Drift's default limit at 600 requests a minute. Large accounts will take hours, which is one more reason not to leave this for January.
It keeps the list metadata. contactId, inboxId and timestamps come from the list call, so you can join transcripts back to contacts later.

Drift also publishes its own bulk export script on GitHub (Driftt/Drift-Bulk-Export-Transcript). It wants conversation_read, user_read and contact_read. Worth comparing against if you'd rather not maintain your own.

Step 3: Export contacts from the UI

Contacts are easier. Go to Visitors > All Contacts, filter to what you need, save it as a segment, and export the CSV from the segment. Drift emails the file. If Drift was syncing to your CRM, most of this already exists there, but the CSV is a cheap backup of anything that never synced.

Step 4: Close the OAuth grants

This is the step people skip, and it's the one with a history. Between August 8 and 18, 2025, attackers used stolen Drift OAuth tokens to pull data out of customers' Salesforce orgs. Tokens were revoked on August 20, and Google's threat intelligence team told customers to treat every token connected to Drift as compromised.

If you're leaving anyway, don't leave a dormant grant behind:

In Salesforce, open Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, find Drift, and revoke or block it.
Check Installed Packages for a Drift package and uninstall it if it's there.
Deactivate or strip permissions from any integration user created for Drift.
Do the same in HubSpot, Marketo, Slack and anything else you connected. Rotate any API keys you pasted into Drift.
Delete the Drift API token you created for Step 2 once the export is done.
Step 5: Remove the script everywhere it loads

Delete the snippet from your templates, then go after the places the grep in Step 1 found:

GTM: pause the tag first, publish, confirm the widget is gone on a live page, then delete it. Pausing is easy to undo if something else was hanging off it.
Front-end calls: anything calling drift.identify or drift.on will throw once the global stops existing. Remove the calls, or guard them with if (window.drift) for the weeks you're running both tools side by side.
CSP: drop the Drift domains from script-src, connect-src and frame-src once the replacement is live. Leaving them doesn't break anything, but it's an allowance for a vendor you no longer use.
Step 6: Rewire what Drift was feeding

Drift events usually ended up somewhere: a CRM, a Slack channel, a lead-routing service, a spreadsheet. List every consumer and decide what replaces each input. The useful question isn't "does the new tool have a Salesforce integration," it's "what fields did my downstream system actually read." If your routing logic only ever used email, company and the page URL, a plain webhook into Zapier or Make may be all you need.

Delete the Drift webhook handlers and their verification secrets afterwards, so a dead endpoint isn't sitting in your API.

Step 7: Pick the replacement by the job Drift was doing

Drift was a sales tool. If your team used it for support, a support tool will fit better than another sales chatbot. Here's how I'd shortlist by job. Features below are as of November 2026; check current pricing on each vendor's site, since I'm not quoting anyone's prices but my own product's.

If Drift was doing this Look at Why
Routing named accounts to reps inside Salesloft 1mind Salesloft's chosen successor; built to feed Salesloft cadences. Sold through demos.
Answering support questions at volume Intercom (Fin) Built for support, with a shared inbox and ticketing behind the AI agent
Chat that lives next to your HubSpot CRM HubSpot's chat Contacts and conversations land in the CRM you already run
Live chat your team answers by hand, on no budget tawk.to Free live chat. You staff it yourself.
A small B2B site with no SDR team, where you want answers only from your own pages and leads sent to your inbox ChatLume (mine) Answers from your site and docs, hands off what it can't support. It can't identify visiting companies, has no live rep inbox, no routing between reps, and connects to CRMs by webhook, not native sync.

If you used Drift's company identification and intent scoring, the bottom two rows won't replace that. Be honest with yourself about whether your team actually acted on it, because it's the most expensive part of what Drift did.

The short version
Inventory every place Drift lives, including GTM and CSP.
Export transcripts through the API now, while it answers.
Export contacts as a CSV backup.
Revoke the OAuth grants and rotate keys.
Remove the script, guard leftover window.drift calls.
Rewire webhooks and integrations to the fields you actually use.
Pick the replacement by job, not by feature list.

Everything up to step 6 is worth doing even if you haven't chosen a replacement yet. The export and the OAuth cleanup have deadlines. The shortlist doesn't.

I used AI to help structure and edit this post. The research, the script and the opinions are mine, and I've checked every date and endpoint against the sources above.

items.summary_html:
TL;DR

Counting play events counts muted autoplay, refreshes and bots as viewers. We'll build a tracker that counts a view only when the player is at least 50% on screen, playing, in a visible tab, for 2 continuous seconds (the MRC video viewability floor), plus a Node server that dedupes per viewer and drops bots with isbot. In a scripted test, the naive counter said 5 and the real one said 1.

Why play is the wrong event 🎥

There's no universal definition to copy. YouTube doesn't publish its organic threshold, Shorts counts every start since March 2025, Facebook reports "Views" and 3-second plays separately, and LinkedIn ads use 2 continuous seconds at 50% visible. (Swydo, updated Nov 2026, Blck Alpaca)

So we'll pick a definition on purpose. The MRC viewable impression guideline for video ads (50% of pixels, 2 continuous seconds) is a sensible floor:

Condition How we detect it At least 50% on screen IntersectionObserver with a 0.5 threshold Actually playing playing / pause / waiting / ended events Tab is visible document.visibilityState 2 continuous seconds timer that resets if any condition breaks Not a repeat server dedupe per viewer + video + 30 min window Not a bot isbot on the user agent, server-side

Stack: Node 22, isbot 5.2.4, no framework. Tested in Chromium 158 with Playwright.

1. The client tracker 
// public/view-tracker.js
// A "view" = the player was >= 50% on screen, actually playing, in a visible tab,
// for QUALIFY_MS of continuous time. One view per element per page load.
const QUALIFY_MS = 2000;

export function trackViews(video, { videoId, endpoint = '/api/view' }) {
  let onScreen = false, playing = false, counted = false;
  let streakStart = null, timer = null;

  const pageVisible = () => document.visibilityState === 'visible';
  const qualifying = () => onScreen && playing && pageVisible();

  function update() {
    if (counted) return;
    if (qualifying() && streakStart === null) {
      streakStart = performance.now();
      timer = setTimeout(fire, QUALIFY_MS);
    } else if (!qualifying() && streakStart !== null) {
      clearTimeout(timer);           // streak broken: MRC-style "continuous"
      streakStart = null;
    }
  }

  function fire() {
    counted = true;
    const body = JSON.stringify({ videoId, viewerId: viewerId(), ts: Date.now() });
    navigator.sendBeacon(endpoint, new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }));
  }

  new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => { onScreen = e.intersectionRatio >= 0.5; update(); },
    { threshold: [0, 0.5, 1] }).observe(video);
  video.addEventListener('playing', () => { playing = true; update(); });
  for (const ev of ['pause', 'waiting', 'ended', 'emptied'])
    video.addEventListener(ev, () => { playing = false; update(); });
  document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', update);
}

function viewerId() {
  try {
    let id = localStorage.getItem('vid_viewer');
    if (!id) { id = crypto.randomUUID(); localStorage.setItem('vid_viewer', id); }
    return id;
  } catch { return 'anon'; }
}

A few choices worth calling out:

  • playing, not play. play fires when playback is requested; playing fires when frames are actually moving. A stall (waiting) breaks the streak.
  • The streak resets. Scroll away at 1.9 s and you start again from zero. That's what "continuous" means.
  • sendBeacon survives the page unloading, so a view that qualifies right before navigation still arrives.

💡 Tip: for long-form content, consider a second, higher-threshold event (say "engaged view" at 30 s). Keep names distinct so nobody mixes them up on a dashboard.

2. The server: dedupe and bots 🛠️ 
npm i isbot

// server.mjs
import http from 'node:http';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { isbot } from 'isbot';

const DEDUPE_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000;          // one view per viewer per video per 30 min
const lastCounted = new Map();             // `${viewerId}:${videoId}` -> ts (use Redis in prod)
export const stats = { received: 0, bot: 0, duplicate: 0, counted: 0, naivePlays: 0 };

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/api/view') {
    let raw = ''; for await (const c of req) raw += c;
    stats.received++;
    const ua = req.headers['user-agent'] ?? '';
    if (isbot(ua)) { stats.bot++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
    const { videoId, viewerId } = JSON.parse(raw);
    const key = `${viewerId}:${videoId}`, now = Date.now();
    if (now - (lastCounted.get(key) ?? 0) < DEDUPE_MS) { stats.duplicate++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
    lastCounted.set(key, now); stats.counted++;
    return res.writeHead(204).end();
  }
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/api/naive-play') { stats.naivePlays++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
  if (req.url === '/stats') return res.writeHead(200, {'content-type':'application/json'}).end(JSON.stringify(stats));
  const path = req.url === '/' ? '/feed.html' : req.url;
  try {
    const body = await readFile('public' + path);
    const type = path.endsWith('.js') ? 'text/javascript' : path.endsWith('.mp4') ? 'video/mp4' : 'text/html';
    res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': type }).end(body);
  } catch { res.writeHead(404).end(); }
});
server.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'));

⚠️ Note: the static file handler is demo-only (no path sanitizing). Don't ship it. In production, the dedupe map belongs in Redis with a TTL, and viewerId should come from your auth session when you have one.

3. A feed page that runs both counters

Three muted autoplaying videos: two at the top, one far below the fold. Each gets the real tracker and a naive play counter so we can compare.



 name=viewport content="width=device-width">

 id=a src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop>
 id=b src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop>
 class=spacer>
id=c src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop> type=module> import { trackViews } from '/view-tracker.js'; for (const v of document.querySelectorAll('video')) { trackViews(v, { videoId: v.id }); v.addEventListener('play', () => navigator.sendBeacon('/api/naive-play'), { once: true }); } 4. Simulate real traffic with Playwright

Scenario: a viewer loads the feed, scrolls 300 px after 1 s (video a leaves the screen), refreshes, and then a headless bot visits.

// run.js
const { chromium } = require('playwright');
const stats = async p => (await (await p.request.get('http://localhost:3000/stats')).json());
(async () => {
  const b = await chromium.launch();
  const human = await b.newContext({ userAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/142.0.0.0 Safari/537.36', viewport:{width:1280,height:720} });
  const p = await human.newPage();
  await p.goto('http://localhost:3000/');
  await p.waitForTimeout(1000);
  await p.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, 300));      // video "a" drops below 50% visible after 1s
  await p.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after first visit  ', JSON.stringify(await stats(p)));
  await p.reload(); await p.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after reload       ', JSON.stringify(await stats(p)));
  const bot = await (await b.newContext()).newPage();   // default HeadlessChrome UA
  await bot.goto('http://localhost:3000/'); await bot.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after headless UA  ', JSON.stringify(await stats(bot)));
  console.log('default UA was:', await bot.evaluate(() => navigator.userAgent));
  await b.close();
})();

$ node server.mjs &
listening on :3000
$ node run.js
after first visit   {"received":1,"bot":0,"duplicate":0,"counted":1,"naivePlays":2}
after reload        {"received":2,"bot":0,"duplicate":1,"counted":1,"naivePlays":3}
after headless UA   {"received":4,"bot":2,"duplicate":1,"counted":1,"naivePlays":5}
default UA was: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/158.0.8127.36 Safari/537.36
5. Reading the results 📊
Scenario Naive play Qualified views First visit +2 (a and b started) +1 (b only; a was on screen ~1 s) Reload +1 +0 (arrived, rejected as duplicate) Headless bot +2 +0 (2 arrived, rejected by isbot) Total 5 1

Two things I didn't expect:

  1. Video c never started. Chromium didn't autoplay the muted video while it was 3000 px offscreen, so even the naive counter skipped it. That's browser behavior you shouldn't rely on; a taller viewport or a different browser could start it.
  2. My own test harness is a bot. Playwright's default UA contains HeadlessChrome, which isbot flags. If your synthetic monitoring hits pages with view tracking, it's either inflating your counts (naive) or silently filtered (this setup). Set a real UA in tests that need to count, and know which one you're doing.
Things to know
  • Keep both numbers. Rename the naive count to "starts" and keep it. The gap between starts and views tells you how much of your autoplay gets real attention.
  • UA filtering is the floor. It catches honest automation. If views affect payouts, add rate limits per IP/viewer and anomaly checks.
  • Not tested here: the visibilitychange path (background tabs), Safari, mobile. The harness is headless Chromium 158 on one machine.
What's next
  • Send videoId, viewerId and a session id with every beacon into a real events table, then compute views in SQL so you can change the definition later and backfill.
  • Add an "engaged view" at a longer threshold and plot it next to views per video. The videos where the two diverge most are the ones worth a look.

items.summary_html:
A few days ago someone on LinkedIn listed six questions every team should answer before building an AI agent. Number 5 was short: "Can you trace what it did?"

I thought my answer was yes. It wasn't.

The setup

I build Agentic App Store, an open-source (MIT) app store you host yourself. You install apps with one click on your own Mac or Linux box, and AI agents can work inside those apps through one door, the AI Hub:

  • Agents like Claude Code or Codex connect to one MCP address and see every installed app's tools.
  • The hub's own assistant can use the same tools from a chat window.
  • Each app marks its tools as read, write or danger. A danger call (delete shapes, replace text) stops in the hub and shows the person a card with Accept / Accept all in this chat / Reject. The prompt never decides that; the hub does.

So the approval part was there. What was missing was the record. The hub kept the last 200 tool calls in memory, without the person's answer, and a restart wiped them.

That's a status page, not a history.

What I wanted to be able to answer

For any AI action, a week later:

  1. When, and through which door (an MCP agent or the assistant chat)?
  2. For whom, which app and tool?
  3. Exactly what the AI sent?
  4. How it ended: done, failed, or never ran?
  5. What the person answered, if the call needed an answer?

Number 4 matters more than I expected. A rejected change never reaches the app, so the app has no record of it. But "the AI tried to delete everything and I said no" is exactly what you want to find later.

The design: one line per call, written where every call passes

Every tool call, from every door, already goes through one function in the hub: calls.call(). That's the natural place to write the history. One JSON line per call, appended to a file in the hub's data folder:

def record(*, via, user, app, tool, kind, args, ok,
           error="", ms=0, approval="", ran=True):
    entry = {
        "id": secrets.token_hex(6),
        "at": time.time(),
        "via": via, "user": user, "app": app, "tool": tool, "kind": kind,
        "args": _args_text(args),      # what the AI sent, cut at 4,000 chars
        "ok": ok, "ran": ran, "error": error[:500], "ms": ms,
        "approval": approval,          # accepted, rejected, allowed, declined, no answer...
    }
    with _lock, _file().open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

Plain JSONL on purpose: it's easy to read, easy to back up, and easy to delete. The file keeps the newest 10,000 entries and is readable only by the hub's owner.

Getting the person's answer into the same line

The approval happens in one module (approvals) and the call in another (calls). Both run in the same asyncio task, one tool call at a time, so a ContextVar carries the answer from one to the other without changing every function signature in between:

APPROVAL: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("ai_hub_approval", default="")

# approvals.ask(), after the person clicks Accept:
history.APPROVAL.set("accepted")

# calls.call(), when it writes the line:
approval = history.APPROVAL.get()
history.APPROVAL.set("")   # the answer belongs to this one call only

The reset is important. Without it, the next harmless read in the same chat would show up as "accepted" too.

Calls that never run get their own line with ran: false: rejected changes, reads the person declined, and calls from places that have no chat to ask in (the voice companion, say). Those don't run either. The model is told to ask in the chat.

The bug I found while taking screenshots

I tried it live: I asked the AI to clear a demo drawing and planned to click Reject for the screenshot. I was too slow. Claude Code gave up waiting for the tool call before the hub's own 4-minute timeout, and the history showed... nothing for that call.

When the client gives up, the hub's waiting coroutine gets cancelled. My code only wrote a line after a decision, and a cancellation is not a decision. So "never asked" and "asked, but nobody answered" looked the same, which is exactly the gap the history was supposed to close.

The fix is small:

async def _kept_answer(tool, args, user, via, chat, post, card, waiting):
    try:
        return await _answer(chat, post, card, waiting)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        history.record(..., ok=False, ran=False,
                       approval="no answer: the AI stopped waiting")
        raise

Record, then re-raise: the cancellation still does what it should, and the history keeps the attempt. There's a test for it now too.

What the owner sees

On the hub page, the old "Recent tool calls" card became History of the AI's actions:

  • Search across everything (an app, a tool, a person, words the AI sent, "rejected").
  • Click a row to see the whole entry, and delete it if you want.
  • Delete all, after a question that says how many entries will go.
  • Download the whole history as JSON.
  • Times show in your browser's time zone (the containers run on UTC).

Only the hub's owner can see it, because an entry holds whatever the AI sent, and that can be anyone's data.

What it is, and what it isn't

It is the everyday kind of audit trail: on your own server, next to your data, covering every agent that goes through the hub.

It is not a validated compliance system. If you work in a regulated field, the hub's history can support your own validation, but it doesn't replace it.

Try it

Agentic App Store is open source (MIT): https://about.reflex-ddns.com

If you run agents against real systems, I'm curious: who reviews what your agents did last week, and where do they look?

items.title: BharatGen Launches Patram 1.5, a 7B Vision-Language Model for Document Processing
items.summary: BharatGen has launched Patram 1.5, a seven-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) built to read and process scanned, handwritten, stamped and multilingual documents. The model is available as open weights on Hugging Face and can also be accessed through the BharatGen Playground. Unlike conventional optical character recognition (OCR) systems, which convert documents into text before passing the output to a large language model (LLM), Patram 1.5 processes documents as images. This lets it interpret elements such as tables, signatures, stamps, photographs, charts, and handwritten notes alongside the text. The model targets organisations in banking, insurance, healthcare, and government, where document processing often involves poor-quality scans, handwritten entries, and documents in multiple languages. Patram 1.5 also introduces what BharatGen calls OCR 3.0. Instead of extracting all the text from a document, users can specify the information they need in natural language and receive the output in a format compatible with their systems, including JSON, HTML and Markdown. For instance, a bank processing account statements can ask the model to extract only customer IDs and branch details, with the output returned in a predefined JSON structure. Another feature is the model's ability to identify information it cannot read. If a field is blank or a figure is illegible, Patram 1.5 is trained to flag the issue rather than generate an answer. Where it can make a reasonable estimate, it provides the answer with a warning for human verification. It can also seek clarification when a document contains multiple possible answers to a question. This is particularly relevant for financial services and healthcare, where incorrect information extracted from documents can affect decisions. BharatGen evaluated Patram 1.5 across 49 tests, comprising 34 public benchmarks and 15 tests from its own PatramBench dataset. The evaluation included 20 other vision-language models, ranging up to 763 billion parameters, and seven specialist OCR systems. PatramBench contains 11,828 test items drawn from 8,773 pages of Indian documents. BharatGen said it would release the benchmark on Hugging Face in the coming days. The company has also made Patram 1.5 available through its BharatGen Playground, where users can upload documents and images, ask questions and extract information using natural language. The Playground includes ready-to-use solutions for parsing, extraction, classification, document splitting and section identification. Digitisation, translation and editing capabilities are expected to be added soon. These solutions can be combined into workflows for tasks such as sorting and cross-checking KYC documents. Speaking on the launch, Rishi Bal, CEO of BharatGen, said, “A model alone can only take you so far. The BharatGen Playground gives the world a full stack for document intelligence, with models, solutions and workflows working together.” Prof Ravi Kiran Sarvadevabhatla, consortium member at BharatGen and professor at IIIT Hyderabad, said, “With Patram 1.5 and BharatGen Playground, we chart a new capability frontier for sovereign vision models and document understanding workflows.” With seven billion parameters, Patram 1.5 can be deployed on an organisation's own infrastructure, allowing banks, hospitals and government departments to process sensitive documents without sending them to external systems. The model supports English and English mixed with Indian languages, has a context window of up to 32,000 tokens and can process multiple images in a single request. Patram 1.5 is the latest release in BharatGen's Patram model family, which began with Patram 1 in June last year.

items.title: India Wants Its Own Jet Engines, Green Aero is Taking a Shot
items.summary: India has been building aircraft, launching rockets and manufacturing drones . But when it comes to jet engines, the country still has a significant gap to close. Developing an engine is not simply another engineering challenge. It requires expertise in metallurgy, precision manufacturing, thermodynamics and materials science, alongside years of testing. Only a handful of countries have mastered the technology at scale. For India, dependence on imported propulsion systems remains a strategic vulnerability, particularly as its defence requirements evolve. Modern warfare is creating demand for autonomous aircraft that can fly faster, operate in contested environments and work alongside crewed fighter jets. These systems need more than an airframe. They require engines, avionics and flight-control systems designed to work together. This is the gap Bengaluru-based Green Aero wants to address. Founded in November 2023 by aerospace engineer Prithwish Kundu, the startup is developing jet engines, avionics and airframes under one roof. It is starting with smaller engines and working towards high-speed autonomous aircraft. The company has raised $14 million in a Series A round led by Crane Venture Partners. The round also includes 3one4 Capital, Antler Elevate and existing investors pi Ventures, Antler India and Rebalance. Kundu describes this to AIM as the largest venture capital round in India’s private jet engine and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) sector. The company plans to use the capital to expand its testing infrastructure, hire engineers and accelerate product development. Over the next 12 to 18 months, it will focus on larger-thrust engines and flight qualification for its transonic and supersonic drone platforms. The funding comes as India increases investment in domestic defence production. The Ministry of Defence said production reached ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025–26. Private companies accounted for 24% of output. The government has also opened 25% of its defence R&D budget to industry, startups and academia. For Green Aero, the opportunity lies in a difficult part of aerospace manufacturing. “India does not have a private ecosystem that develops jet engines or aero engines,” Kundu says in the interview. He calls this “the Achilles heel of India’s defence ecosystem”. Building an Integrated Aerospace Stack Kundu’s interest in propulsion began long before he founded Green Aero. An aerospace engineer who studied at IIT Delhi , he went on to complete a PhD in aerospace engineering at North Carolina State University. He later worked as a research scientist at Argonne National Laboratory in the US, leading projects across aerospace and energy. His work also included hypersonics projects with NASA Langley and a brief stint with the US Army on jet engines and gas turbines. After returning to India, he spent about two years at electric vehicle maker Euler Motors as VP of Battery and Thermal Systems. However, he wanted to work on propulsion systems in India. He eventually moved from the research environment into the startup ecosystem. “I felt it was too slow,” Kundu says, explaining why he chose to leave academia and work in the startup sector. One of the gaps he identifies is the absence of a substantial private ecosystem developing jet engines in India. These engines are used beyond conventional aircraft, including military drones , cruise missiles and other defence applications. Green Aero’s approach is to develop three components together: propulsion systems, avionics and airframes. The company believes this vertical integration will allow it to co-optimise the systems rather than depend on separate suppliers. It says it has completed more than 100 hot-fire tests in the sub-kN engine category. Hot-fire tests evaluate an engine under operating conditions, but they are not the same as flight trials or formal qualification. The company has also developed an aero-engine core called The Blue Dragon. It claims this is the first such core developed from scratch in India and says it has demonstrated airblast atomisers for sub-kN engines. Green Aero describes the latter as a global first. Its smaller engines are intended for military applications, where comparable products are often imported from Europe. Kundu says the company’s engines are more efficient and optimised for air launches and cold-weather operations. They can rotate at 50,000 to 1,00,000 revolutions per minute. The startup has already begun generating revenue from small-engine sales. It has received interest from domestic and international buyers, although it has not disclosed customer names or contract values. Kundu reveals the company had received orders from the US and Europe that it was considering. “The entire manufacturing happens in India,” Kundu says, adding that the company is without imported or white-labelled critical engine components. It works with manufacturers across the country and sources superalloys from Indian suppliers and non-Chinese sources overseas. He adds that some components require machining accuracies of up to five microns. By comparison, the thickness of a strand of human hair is roughly 100 microns. Building this supply chain has required investment in manufacturing processes , quality control and alternative sources for critical materials. The company now operates an 87,000 sq ft R&D, assembly and testing facility at Bengaluru’s KIADB Aerospace Park. It says the facility brings engine and CCA research, assembly, quality control and testing together. Its team has grown to 50 members, including engineers and military veterans. The company also cites an established partnership with L&T, support from Boeing’s BUILD programme and SIDBI’s Green-Tech Accelerator. It has not detailed the scope of these associations in the announcement. The Bigger Bet on Autonomous Aircraft While small engines provide an early commercial opportunity, Green Aero sees CCAs as its larger opportunity. These aircraft are designed to operate independently or alongside crewed fighter jets. They could undertake surveillance, strike and other missions , particularly in environments where sending a pilot would carry significant risks. Kundu believes drone warfare is moving towards jet-powered platforms that can exceed 600 kmph. He sees growing demand for aircraft capable of operating at transonic speeds and functioning despite electronic warfare and satellite navigation disruption. Green Aero says it has developed hardware and software for GNSS-denied navigation, alongside in-house edge-computing hardware. It has also demonstrated both airframes and engines, according to Kundu. The engineering challenges remain substantial. Jet engines operate under high temperatures and pressures, with components rotating at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute. Building them requires precision machining, specialised materials and repeated testing. The company also needs to develop larger engines. Over the next three years, it plans to build and qualify engines in the 4–5 kN thrust category. It also intends to commercialise its transonic drone platform, while continuing flight trials over the coming year. An Expanding but Challenging Ecosystem This comes at a time that the government has also introduced programmes such as Innovations for Defence Excellence and the Technology Development Fund to support domestic innovation. India’s defence exports reached ₹38,424 crore in 2025–26, up from ₹686 crore in 2013–14. Private companies contributed 45.16% of exports that year. The government aims to raise annual defence production to ₹3 lakh crore by 2029. Kundu says reforms to drone regulations and testing procedures have made it easier for private aerospace companies to conduct trials. However, he believes defence procurement still involves uncertainty and administrative delays. “There is still a lot of uncertainty, red tape and bureaucracy in the defence procurement side,” he adds. For Green Aero, the next phase will involve moving from engine testing and prototypes towards larger engines and flight-qualified aircraft. The company also plans to remain focused on defence for the next two to three years. It sees potential applications for its turbine technology in energy and other sectors over time. Kundu points to aeroderivative gas turbines used for data centre backup as one possible application. For now, the immediate challenge is to turn its early engineering work into products that customers can deploy. items.summary_html:
India has been building aircraft, launching rockets and manufacturing drones. But when it comes to jet engines, the country still has a significant gap to close. Developing an engine is not simply another engineering challenge. It requires expertise in metallurgy, precision manufacturing, thermodynamics and materials science, alongside years of testing. 

Only a handful of countries have mastered the technology at scale. For India, dependence on imported propulsion systems remains a strategic vulnerability, particularly as its defence requirements evolve.

Modern warfare is creating demand for autonomous aircraft that can fly faster, operate in contested environments and work alongside crewed fighter jets. These systems need more than an airframe. They require engines, avionics and flight-control systems designed to work together.

This is the gap Bengaluru-based Green Aero wants to address. Founded in November 2023 by aerospace engineer Prithwish Kundu, the startup is developing jet engines, avionics and airframes under one roof. It is starting with smaller engines and working towards high-speed autonomous aircraft.

The company has raised $14 million in a Series A round led by Crane Venture Partners. The round also includes 3one4 Capital, Antler Elevate and existing investors pi Ventures, Antler India and Rebalance. Kundu describes this to AIM as the largest venture capital round in India’s private jet engine and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) sector.

The company plans to use the capital to expand its testing infrastructure, hire engineers and accelerate product development. Over the next 12 to 18 months, it will focus on larger-thrust engines and flight qualification for its transonic and supersonic drone platforms.

The funding comes as India increases investment in domestic defence production. The Ministry of Defence said production reached ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025–26. Private companies accounted for 24% of output. The government has also opened 25% of its defence R&D budget to industry, startups and academia.

For Green Aero, the opportunity lies in a difficult part of aerospace manufacturing. “India does not have a private ecosystem that develops jet engines or aero engines,” Kundu says in the interview. He calls this “the Achilles heel of India’s defence ecosystem”.

Building an Integrated Aerospace Stack

Kundu’s interest in propulsion began long before he founded Green Aero. An aerospace engineer who studied at IIT Delhi, he went on to complete a PhD in aerospace engineering at North Carolina State University. He later worked as a research scientist at Argonne National Laboratory in the US, leading projects across aerospace and energy.

His work also included hypersonics projects with NASA Langley and a brief stint with the US Army on jet engines and gas turbines. After returning to India, he spent about two years at electric vehicle maker Euler Motors as VP of Battery and Thermal Systems.

However, he wanted to work on propulsion systems in India. He eventually moved from the research environment into the startup ecosystem.

“I felt it was too slow,” Kundu says, explaining why he chose to leave academia and work in the startup sector.

One of the gaps he identifies is the absence of a substantial private ecosystem developing jet engines in India. These engines are used beyond conventional aircraft, including military drones, cruise missiles and other defence applications.

Green Aero’s approach is to develop three components together: propulsion systems, avionics and airframes. The company believes this vertical integration will allow it to co-optimise the systems rather than depend on separate suppliers.

It says it has completed more than 100 hot-fire tests in the sub-kN engine category. Hot-fire tests evaluate an engine under operating conditions, but they are not the same as flight trials or formal qualification.

The company has also developed an aero-engine core called The Blue Dragon. It claims this is the first such core developed from scratch in India and says it has demonstrated airblast atomisers for sub-kN engines. Green Aero describes the latter as a global first.

Its smaller engines are intended for military applications, where comparable products are often imported from Europe. Kundu says the company’s engines are more efficient and optimised for air launches and cold-weather operations. They can rotate at 50,000 to 1,00,000 revolutions per minute.

The startup has already begun generating revenue from small-engine sales. It has received interest from domestic and international buyers, although it has not disclosed customer names or contract values. Kundu reveals the company had received orders from the US and Europe that it was considering.

“The entire manufacturing happens in India,” Kundu says, adding that the company is without imported or white-labelled critical engine components. It works with manufacturers across the country and sources superalloys from Indian suppliers and non-Chinese sources overseas.

He adds that some components require machining accuracies of up to five microns. By comparison, the thickness of a strand of human hair is roughly 100 microns. Building this supply chain has required investment in manufacturing processes, quality control and alternative sources for critical materials.

The company now operates an 87,000 sq ft R&D, assembly and testing facility at Bengaluru’s KIADB Aerospace Park. It says the facility brings engine and CCA research, assembly, quality control and testing together. Its team has grown to 50 members, including engineers and military veterans.

The company also cites an established partnership with L&T, support from Boeing’s BUILD programme and SIDBI’s Green-Tech Accelerator. It has not detailed the scope of these associations in the announcement.

The Bigger Bet on Autonomous Aircraft

While small engines provide an early commercial opportunity, Green Aero sees CCAs as its larger opportunity. These aircraft are designed to operate independently or alongside crewed fighter jets. They could undertake surveillance, strike and other missions, particularly in environments where sending a pilot would carry significant risks.

Kundu believes drone warfare is moving towards jet-powered platforms that can exceed 600 kmph. He sees growing demand for aircraft capable of operating at transonic speeds and functioning despite electronic warfare and satellite navigation disruption.

Green Aero says it has developed hardware and software for GNSS-denied navigation, alongside in-house edge-computing hardware. It has also demonstrated both airframes and engines, according to Kundu.

The engineering challenges remain substantial. Jet engines operate under high temperatures and pressures, with components rotating at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute. Building them requires precision machining, specialised materials and repeated testing.

The company also needs to develop larger engines. Over the next three years, it plans to build and qualify engines in the 4–5 kN thrust category. It also intends to commercialise its transonic drone platform, while continuing flight trials over the coming year.

An Expanding but Challenging Ecosystem

This comes at a time that the government has also introduced programmes such as Innovations for Defence Excellence and the Technology Development Fund to support domestic innovation. India’s defence exports reached ₹38,424 crore in 2025–26, up from ₹686 crore in 2013–14. Private companies contributed 45.16% of exports that year. The government aims to raise annual defence production to ₹3 lakh crore by 2029.

Kundu says reforms to drone regulations and testing procedures have made it easier for private aerospace companies to conduct trials. However, he believes defence procurement still involves uncertainty and administrative delays.

“There is still a lot of uncertainty, red tape and bureaucracy in the defence procurement side,” he adds.

For Green Aero, the next phase will involve moving from engine testing and prototypes towards larger engines and flight-qualified aircraft. The company also plans to remain focused on defence for the next two to three years.

It sees potential applications for its turbine technology in energy and other sectors over time. Kundu points to aeroderivative gas turbines used for data centre backup as one possible application.

For now, the immediate challenge is to turn its early engineering work into products that customers can deploy. That is also the challenge facing India’s wider private aerospace ecosystem: moving from building individual components to developing the complex systems that power aircraft.

items.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
items.summary: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

items.title: Pine Labs Adds AI Agents To Merchant App For Sales Insights, Ad Campaigns
items.summary: Bengaluru-based fintech company Pine Labs has launched two AI agents on its merchant operating app, Pine Labs One, to help small businesses analyse transaction data and manage digital advertising campaigns. The tools, Guide and Marketer Agent, are the first in a series of agents being developed under the company’s Agentic Org platform. Pine Labs said they would be rolled out to millions of merchants in India. Guide allows merchants to query business data in natural language, including store-level sales, point-of-sale transactions, settlements, refunds, payments and value-added service activations. The tool is designed to bring information spread across multiple reports and systems into a conversational interface. Marketer Agent, meanwhile, converts business objectives into advertising campaigns . It handles keyword research, including competitor keywords, creative generation, audience targeting and campaign setup. The agent will initially support campaigns on Google platforms, with Pine Labs planning to extend it to large language model-powered discovery platforms. “Small businesses don't need AI for the sake of AI. They need it to solve everyday problems and make better decisions,” Vijeth Pandit, Chief Product Officer at Pine Labs , said. Merchants will have to review and approve campaigns before advertising spend is committed. Once approved, the agent can publish campaigns directly without requiring merchants to use Google Ads. Pine Labs said it could also match ad interactions with in-store transactions using privacy-preserving techniques to measure campaign-generated revenue. Marketer Agent is built using Google’s Gemini models as part of a collaboration between Pine Labs and Google Cloud announced in September 2026. Amit Kumar, Managing Director, Google Cloud India, said the collaboration would help smaller businesses automate campaign management and run digital campaigns without needing dedicated technical expertise. Pine Labs’ Agentic Org platform includes Grantex, a permissions and governance layer that controls the data and tools agents can access and enables human oversight at critical stages. The company also plans to launch an Agent App Store, where merchants can access specialised agents for different business functions. The marketplace is scheduled to launch first in Singapore during the Singapore FinTech Festival, followed by India by December 15. Pine Labs said its roadmap also includes Market, an agent designed to manage advertising across multiple platforms.

items.title: SpaceX Gets Nod to Deploy 1 Mn AI Data Centre Satellites
items.summary: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has received approval to deploy up to 1 million solar-powered satellites for AI data centres in space SpaceX had sought permission earlier this year from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to deploy orbital computing modules under its proposed 'Starmind' constellation. The company has now received the authorisation in light of the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing. The constellation would run AI workloads in space for use on Earth, with the company arguing that access to solar power could reduce the energy and operating costs associated with conventional data centres. However, the approval does not mean SpaceX will necessarily deploy all satellites at once. Satellite operators sometimes seek authorisation for larger constellations than they eventually build. SpaceX had previously sought approval for 42,000 satellites for its Starlink broadband network; the network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in orbit. Under the FCC authorisation, SpaceX must begin deployment by November 2033. It will have to deploy at least 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and reach 50% of the approved constellation by November 2038. SpaceX has argued that the satellites would draw on near-constant solar power and rely on passive radiative cooling, reducing the AI power workloads back on Earth. The scale of the Starmind proposal has drawn objections from competing satellite operators, including Viasat and Amazon’s Leo unit. The latter has argued that such a large deployment would take centuries and described the proposal as an ambition rather than a concrete plan. The American Astronomical Society has also opposed the move, warning that the deployment would interfere with optical astronomy. The FCC said it had also dismissed concerns about environmental impacts and optical astronomy, stating that these fell outside its regulatory authority. SpaceX’s plan also depends on reducing the cost of launching satellites at scale. The company is betting on Starship, its next-generation reusable rocket, to support the constellation's deployment. Other technology companies are also exploring space-based computing, with Google announcing Project Suncatcher as an effort to develop AI computing infrastructure in orbit. Blue Origin, founded by Jeff Bezos, has separately sought FCC approval to deploy up to 51,600 satellites under its proposed Project Sunrise constellation.

items.summary: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.) items.title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
items.summary: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

items.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
items.summary: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem

items.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
items.summary: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. items.title: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.

items.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
items.summary: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

items.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
items.summary: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

items.title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
items.summary: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.

items.title: FrId\'eo: French News Outlet Ideology Scoring via Multi-Source Evidence Fusion and Distancing-Aware Lexical Scoring
items.summary: Outlet ideology is a standard explanatory variable in media framing, media effects, and political communication research, but continuous, ecosystem-wide coverage lets it enter as graded exposure rather than a coarse bin. For France, existing references are either broad but non-analytic or analytic but sparse and source-specific, and none we are aware of offers ecosystem-wide coverage on a unified continuous scale. We contribute FrId\'eo: to our knowledge the first ecosystem-wide continuous ideology scores for the French press, a transparent composite score for 30 French news outlets, fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. For the text-based family we introduce symmetric plain/qualified scoring, which separates the plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from its qualified (distanced) use on both sides, a distinction bag-of-words methods miss. The resulting scale runs from L'Humanit\'e on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right; the far-right pole is near-indistinguishable and CNews ties Le Figaro. Because the text family reads current articles, it also captures editorial change that static sources miss, such as the Journal du Dimanche's sharp rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single family, and agrees with held-out Media Bias Fact Check labels. We release the scores, confidence intervals, and replication code.

items.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
items.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.

items.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
items.summary: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.
