items.title: HTTP 200 OK, Yet Completely Wrong: How We Built an Observability Engine for AI Agents
items.summary: Traditional monitoring tells you if your agent is alive, not if it’s right. Here is the asynchronous architecture we built to evaluate thousands of production chats overnight. Arnav had just shipped his company’s first production AI assistant. Before launch, he tested it on a carefully curated set of 200 questions. It scored 92%. Everything looked green, response times were fast, and there were zero error logs. Two weeks later, a major client sent an urgent message: “Your AI has been giving us wrong policy answers since last week.” Arnav stared at his monitoring dashboard. Every single API call showed 200 OK. His system was alive, fast, and completely confident—while quietly hallucinating. That afternoon, Arnav realized that traditional server monitoring only tells you if your AI is running, never if it is right. The Trap of the Static Test File At first, Arnav relied on his 200-question test dataset whenever he changed a prompt. That failed almost immediately. Real users didn’t talk like his neat test file — they asked messy follow-up questions, combined two requests into one, and triggered edge cases his static dataset never imagined. [Static 200-Question File] ──► [Manual Eval Script] ──► Score: 92% (Blind to real users) So Arnav abandoned offline-only testing and decided to pull real production conversations directly from cloud storage (S3) on a daily schedule. To avoid adding latency to live user chats, he moved evaluation completely out of the request path into an asynchronous overnight pipeline. A daily scheduler (APScheduler) woke up once a day and sampled a manageable slice of yesterday’s chats from S3. [Live User] ──► [AI Agent] ──► Fast Reply (No eval delay!) │ ▼ [Raw Chat Logs (S3)] │ (Daily Scheduler + Sampler) │ ▼ [Background Grader] The very first night the scheduled job ran, it crashed halfway through. One of the teams had updated their agent and accidentally changed a field name in their chat logs, breaking Arnav’s script. To stop a single malformed log file from taking down an entire night’s batch, Arnav added a strict YAML schema validator right after ingestion. Only conversations matching the standardized format — containing a conversation_id, tenant_id, user turns, assistant replies, and any retrieved RAG documents or tool calls—were copied into a validated evaluation bucket. Rather than throwing all those chats at the grader simultaneously (causing memory spikes and API rate limits), he dropped lightweight job tickets into an Amazon SQS queue so a sequential background worker could pull and grade them safely one by one. [Raw Chat Logs (S3)] │ ▼ [YAML Schema Validator] ──► (Rejects broken logs safely) │ ▼ [Validated Eval Bucket (S3)] ──► [Amazon SQS Queue] ──► [Sequential Worker] Insight 1: Why an LLM Judge Confidently Lies (and Why a 0.98 Faithfulness Score Can Still Mean a Broken Agent) Once the pipeline stopped crashing, Arnav ran into a much subtler problem: he couldn’t trust the scores. Initially, he sent each conversation to an LLM judge with a simple prompt: “Rate this response from 0 to 1.” Running the exact same conversation three times produced 0.78, 0.69, and 0.84. Worse, metric bleed crept in—if the agent used a slightly blunt tone, the judge quietly docked points from its Relevance score, blending unrelated flaws into a single blurry number. Meanwhile, paying an expensive frontier LLM just to verify basic math—like whether the search engine fetched the right document—was burning budget unnecessarily. Arnav replaced his single vague prompt with a three-tier Evaluation Orchestrator : Computational Metrics: Pure, free math (Precision@k and Recall@k) whenever ground-truth retrieval checks were possible. Embedding Metrics: Fast vector-similarity checks for semantic closeness. LLM-as-a-Judge via DeepEval ( GEval): Isolated, step-by-step rubrics using token probabilities where each metric ran independently—so tone never polluted Relevance , and every grade required a written explanation. [Amazon SQS Queue] │ ▼ [Sequential Worker] │ ▼ [Evaluation Orchestrator] ├──► Computational Metrics (Precision@k, Recall@k — Fast & Free) ├──► Embedding Metrics (Semantic similarity) └──► LLM Judge via DeepEval GEval (Isolated rubrics + written reasons) │ ▼ [Results Bucket (S3)] Yet even with isolated metrics, Arnav noticed something bizarre a few weeks later: an agent’s Faithfulness score climbed to 0.98, while users were furiously clicking thumbs-down. When Arnav inspected the turn logs, the realization hit him: a higher Faithfulness score does not mean a better agent. Faithfulness only measures whether the AI stuck to the retrieved documents without inventing facts. When the search engine retrieved an outdated or irrelevant policy document — and the agent faithfully summarized that wrong document — the judge awarded a near-perfect 0.98 for Faithfulness while the user got a useless answer. That taught Arnav never to trust a single metric in isolation — Faithfulness had to be paired with Contextual Precision and Goal Accuracy to tell the true story. Insight 2: Why Evaluating 100% of Conversations Is Worse Than Smart Sampling As daily traffic grew into the tens of thousands of chats, a stakeholder asked: “Shouldn’t we evaluate every single conversation so nothing slips through?” Arnav ran the math and realized exhaustive evaluation wasn’t just expensive — it was actively counterproductive. Grading 100% of traffic with multi-metric LLM judges would burn through their monthly inference budget in four days, forcing the team to downgrade to a weaker, cheaper judge model that missed subtle multi-turn reasoning errors. Furthermore, because 70% of production traffic consisted of repetitive greetings and routine FAQ lookups, grading every chat drowned out rare, complex edge cases in a sea of trivial 1.0 scores. To control both quality and scale, Arnav made the entire pipeline config-driven . Teams registered their agents in a central configuration store (configGroup: schedular-agents) specifying their agent’s name, S3 log location, sample percentage, judge model, and which of the 27 available metrics to track—without touching a single line of pipeline code. Evaluating a curated, representative daily sample using a strong frontier judge model under consistent rubrics gave far sharper signal than running a weak judge over every chat. Insight 3: How a Healthy 0.85 Average Hid a Failing Client After running this orchestrator at scale, Arnav had a new headache: 10,000 raw JSON result files sitting in S3. Looking at thousands of text files — or a single company-wide average score — hid critical failures. When an agent’s overall weekly Goal Accuracy dipped slightly from 0.85 to 0.82, it looked like harmless noise. So Arnav built a background sync service (backed by PostgreSQL) that read the daily S3 results and manifest files and organized them cleanly inside MLflow : Workspaces: Separate workspaces for DEV, QA, and PROD so test runs never mixed with live traffic. Experiments: One dedicated experiment per AI agent. Runs: One run per conversation, tagged with conversation_id, tenant_id, judge_model, metric scores, and the judge’s written reasoning. Artifacts: Interactive Plotly HTML dashboards — weekly trend lines with smoothing sliders, tenant comparisons, token-cost charts, and conversation-by-metric heatmaps — attached directly inside MLflow. Five-Minute Debugging in Production Two months later, when Arnav opened the PROD workspace in MLflow and sliced a minor 0.82 Goal Accuracy dip by client, the company-wide average turned out to be hiding a localized outage: nine enterprise clients were sitting comfortably at 0.88, while Client B had plunged to 0.54. Arnav clicked into Client B’s monthly heatmap. Faithfulness was bright green (0.95), proving the LLM wasn’t hallucinating. Retrieval Precision , however, was solid red. He opened the lowest-scoring conversation run and read the judge’s exact note: “The retrieved context did not contain the client’s updated policy table.” In under five minutes — without grepping raw logs or blaming the LLM — Arnav knew Client B’s search index simply needed a refresh. With the pipeline now running quietly on autopilot every night, Arnav is adding one final piece to the story: automated A/B testing , so whenever his team wants to test a new prompt or switch to a new model, they can run both versions side by side on the exact same real conversations and let the numbers decide which one ships. References 1. LLM-as-a-Judge & Structured Rubrics (GEval) G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment — Liu et al. (2023). The foundational paper introducing chain-of-thought evaluation criteria and token log-probability weighted scoring to reduce LLM judge variance. arXiv: [ https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16634 ] DeepEval Documentation — G-Eval & Custom Metrics — Official guide on building isolated, criteria-driven LLM evaluation metrics and extending custom evaluation classes. Docs: [ https://docs.confident-ai.com/docs/metrics-llm-evals ] 2. RAG Evaluation & Retrieval vs. Generation Metrics RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation — Es et al. (2023). Defines the distinction between retrieval quality ( Context Precision/Recall ) and generation loyalty ( Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy ), explaining why high faithfulness can coexist with poor retrieval. arXiv: [ https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217 ] 3. Experiment Tracking, Observability & Scheduling Infrastructure MLflow Tracking & GenAI Evaluation Documentation — Official documentation on structuring workspaces/experiments, logging per-run parameters/metrics, and attaching custom HTML/Plotly artifacts. Docs: [ https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/tracking.html ] HTTP 200 OK, Yet Completely Wrong: How We Built an Observability Engine for AI Agents was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Traditional monitoring tells you if your agent is alive, not if it’s right. Here is the asynchronous architecture we built to evaluate thousands of production chats overnight.

Arnav had just shipped his company’s first production AI assistant. Before launch, he tested it on a carefully curated set of 200 questions. It scored 92%. Everything looked green, response times were fast, and there were zero error logs.

Two weeks later, a major client sent an urgent message: “Your AI has been giving us wrong policy answers since last week.”

Arnav stared at his monitoring dashboard. Every single API call showed 200 OK. His system was alive, fast, and completely confident—while quietly hallucinating. That afternoon, Arnav realized that traditional server monitoring only tells you if your AI is running, never if it is right.

The Trap of the Static Test File

At first, Arnav relied on his 200-question test dataset whenever he changed a prompt. That failed almost immediately. Real users didn’t talk like his neat test file — they asked messy follow-up questions, combined two requests into one, and triggered edge cases his static dataset never imagined.

[Static 200-Question File] ──► [Manual Eval Script] ──► Score: 92% (Blind to real users)

So Arnav abandoned offline-only testing and decided to pull real production conversations directly from cloud storage (S3) on a daily schedule.

To avoid adding latency to live user chats, he moved evaluation completely out of the request path into an asynchronous overnight pipeline. A daily scheduler (APScheduler) woke up once a day and sampled a manageable slice of yesterday’s chats from S3.

[Live User] ──► [AI Agent] ──► Fast Reply (No eval delay!)
                    │
                    ▼
           [Raw Chat Logs (S3)]
                    │
         (Daily Scheduler + Sampler)
                    │
                    ▼
            [Background Grader]

The very first night the scheduled job ran, it crashed halfway through. One of the teams had updated their agent and accidentally changed a field name in their chat logs, breaking Arnav’s script.

To stop a single malformed log file from taking down an entire night’s batch, Arnav added a strict YAML schema validator right after ingestion. Only conversations matching the standardized format — containing a conversation_id, tenant_id, user turns, assistant replies, and any retrieved RAG documents or tool calls—were copied into a validated evaluation bucket. Rather than throwing all those chats at the grader simultaneously (causing memory spikes and API rate limits), he dropped lightweight job tickets into an Amazon SQS queue so a sequential background worker could pull and grade them safely one by one.

[Raw Chat Logs (S3)]
         │
         ▼
 [YAML Schema Validator] ──► (Rejects broken logs safely)
         │
         ▼
[Validated Eval Bucket (S3)] ──► [Amazon SQS Queue] ──► [Sequential Worker]
Insight 1: Why an LLM Judge Confidently Lies (and Why a 0.98 Faithfulness Score Can Still Mean a Broken Agent)

Once the pipeline stopped crashing, Arnav ran into a much subtler problem: he couldn’t trust the scores.

Initially, he sent each conversation to an LLM judge with a simple prompt: “Rate this response from 0 to 1.” Running the exact same conversation three times produced 0.78, 0.69, and 0.84. Worse, metric bleed crept in—if the agent used a slightly blunt tone, the judge quietly docked points from its Relevance score, blending unrelated flaws into a single blurry number. Meanwhile, paying an expensive frontier LLM just to verify basic math—like whether the search engine fetched the right document—was burning budget unnecessarily.

Arnav replaced his single vague prompt with a three-tier Evaluation Orchestrator:

  1. Computational Metrics: Pure, free math (Precision@k and Recall@k) whenever ground-truth retrieval checks were possible.
  2. Embedding Metrics: Fast vector-similarity checks for semantic closeness.
  3. LLM-as-a-Judge via DeepEval (GEval): Isolated, step-by-step rubrics using token probabilities where each metric ran independently—so tone never polluted Relevance, and every grade required a written explanation.
[Amazon SQS Queue]
         │
         ▼
[Sequential Worker]
         │
         ▼
[Evaluation Orchestrator]
   ├──► Computational Metrics (Precision@k, Recall@k — Fast & Free)
   ├──► Embedding Metrics (Semantic similarity)
   └──► LLM Judge via DeepEval GEval (Isolated rubrics + written reasons)
         │
         ▼
[Results Bucket (S3)]

Yet even with isolated metrics, Arnav noticed something bizarre a few weeks later: an agent’s Faithfulness score climbed to 0.98, while users were furiously clicking thumbs-down.

When Arnav inspected the turn logs, the realization hit him: a higher Faithfulness score does not mean a better agent. Faithfulness only measures whether the AI stuck to the retrieved documents without inventing facts. When the search engine retrieved an outdated or irrelevant policy document — and the agent faithfully summarized that wrong document — the judge awarded a near-perfect 0.98 for Faithfulness while the user got a useless answer.

That taught Arnav never to trust a single metric in isolation — Faithfulness had to be paired with Contextual Precision and Goal Accuracy to tell the true story.

Insight 2: Why Evaluating 100% of Conversations Is Worse Than Smart Sampling

As daily traffic grew into the tens of thousands of chats, a stakeholder asked: “Shouldn’t we evaluate every single conversation so nothing slips through?”

Arnav ran the math and realized exhaustive evaluation wasn’t just expensive — it was actively counterproductive. Grading 100% of traffic with multi-metric LLM judges would burn through their monthly inference budget in four days, forcing the team to downgrade to a weaker, cheaper judge model that missed subtle multi-turn reasoning errors. Furthermore, because 70% of production traffic consisted of repetitive greetings and routine FAQ lookups, grading every chat drowned out rare, complex edge cases in a sea of trivial 1.0 scores.

To control both quality and scale, Arnav made the entire pipeline config-driven. Teams registered their agents in a central configuration store (configGroup: schedular-agents) specifying their agent’s name, S3 log location, sample percentage, judge model, and which of the 27 available metrics to track—without touching a single line of pipeline code. Evaluating a curated, representative daily sample using a strong frontier judge model under consistent rubrics gave far sharper signal than running a weak judge over every chat.

Insight 3: How a Healthy 0.85 Average Hid a Failing Client

After running this orchestrator at scale, Arnav had a new headache: 10,000 raw JSON result files sitting in S3. Looking at thousands of text files — or a single company-wide average score — hid critical failures. When an agent’s overall weekly Goal Accuracy dipped slightly from 0.85 to 0.82, it looked like harmless noise.

So Arnav built a background sync service (backed by PostgreSQL) that read the daily S3 results and manifest files and organized them cleanly inside MLflow:

  • Workspaces: Separate workspaces for DEV, QA, and PROD so test runs never mixed with live traffic.
  • Experiments: One dedicated experiment per AI agent.
  • Runs: One run per conversation, tagged with conversation_id, tenant_id, judge_model, metric scores, and the judge’s written reasoning.
  • Artifacts: Interactive Plotly HTML dashboards — weekly trend lines with smoothing sliders, tenant comparisons, token-cost charts, and conversation-by-metric heatmaps — attached directly inside MLflow.
Five-Minute Debugging in Production

Two months later, when Arnav opened the PROD workspace in MLflow and sliced a minor 0.82 Goal Accuracy dip by client, the company-wide average turned out to be hiding a localized outage: nine enterprise clients were sitting comfortably at 0.88, while Client B had plunged to 0.54.

Arnav clicked into Client B’s monthly heatmap. Faithfulness was bright green (0.95), proving the LLM wasn’t hallucinating. Retrieval Precision, however, was solid red. He opened the lowest-scoring conversation run and read the judge’s exact note:

“The retrieved context did not contain the client’s updated policy table.”

In under five minutes — without grepping raw logs or blaming the LLM — Arnav knew Client B’s search index simply needed a refresh.

With the pipeline now running quietly on autopilot every night, Arnav is adding one final piece to the story: automated A/B testing, so whenever his team wants to test a new prompt or switch to a new model, they can run both versions side by side on the exact same real conversations and let the numbers decide which one ships.

References1. LLM-as-a-Judge & Structured Rubrics (GEval)
  • G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment — Liu et al. (2023). The foundational paper introducing chain-of-thought evaluation criteria and token log-probability weighted scoring to reduce LLM judge variance.
  • arXiv: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16634]
  • DeepEval Documentation — G-Eval & Custom Metrics — Official guide on building isolated, criteria-driven LLM evaluation metrics and extending custom evaluation classes.
  • Docs: [https://docs.confident-ai.com/docs/metrics-llm-evals]
2. RAG Evaluation & Retrieval vs. Generation Metrics
  • RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation — Es et al. (2023). Defines the distinction between retrieval quality (Context Precision/Recall) and generation loyalty (Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy), explaining why high faithfulness can coexist with poor retrieval.
  • arXiv: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217]
3. Experiment Tracking, Observability & Scheduling Infrastructure
  • MLflow Tracking & GenAI Evaluation Documentation — Official documentation on structuring workspaces/experiments, logging per-run parameters/metrics, and attaching custom HTML/Plotly artifacts.
  • Docs: [https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/tracking.html]

items.title: WhatsApp, Claude and Cursor Quietly Ate 60 GB of My Mac. Here’s Where It Hides.
items.summary: My Mac was down to 17 GB. The heaviest things on it weren’t junk. They were conversations. 170.81 GB of System Data, and no ⓘ to look inside. My MacBook got down to 17 GB free this week. Storage settings had the answer, sort of: System Data, 170.81 GB. Every other row has a little ⓘ you can click to see what’s inside. System Data doesn’t. Photos, for comparison: 20 MB. I should admit something first: I build a Mac storage app. So the obvious move would be to tell you to buy it. Instead I went looking for the junk myself, the way I’d tell a friend to. I didn’t find much junk. The three heaviest things on my Mac were a messaging app, an AI app and a code editor, and the biggest of them is the one thing on this machine I’d never want a cleaner to touch. That changed how I think about cleanup. “System Data” isn’t junk. It’s four kinds of files sharing one grey bar. Some your Mac frees by itself, some rebuild on their own, some come back only if you download them again, and one pile never comes back at all. Size tells you nothing about which is which. What is System Data on a Mac? It’s the leftovers bucket. Anything your Mac can’t file under Apps, Documents, Photos and the rest ends up there: temporary files, logs, the search index, app data that doesn’t fit a neat label. So “is System Data safe to delete?” has no single answer. It’s like asking whether it’s safe to clear out the garage. Mostly, yes. Not the box with the passports. What I found when I looked You can see the biggest folders yourself. Open Terminal (it’s in Applications → Utilities), paste this line, and press Return. It only looks; it doesn’t change anything: du -sh ~/Library/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -8 The biggest folders on my Mac. The top one was WhatsApp. Here’s what the top of my list turned out to be. 42 GB: WhatsApp. Years of photos, videos and voice notes from my chats, all stored on the Mac. 7.8 GB: one single file in my code editor. It’s where the app keeps its saved state, and as far as I can tell that includes my AI chat history. One file, bigger than a lot of people’s entire photo library. 12 GB: a whole mini computer inside the Claude app. The app keeps a small virtual machine to run code in. Most of it can probably be downloaded again. But one of its files is called “session data”, and I’m not deleting anything with that name until I know what’s in it. The real junk was smaller and scattered: about 17 GB of leftovers from building apps, temporary files and old downloads, spread across folders most people never open. Size is the wrong question Most storage tools start the same way: sort by size and show you the biggest thing first. On my Mac that puts 42 GB of WhatsApp at the very top. items.summary_html:
My Mac was down to 17 GB. The heaviest things on it weren’t junk. They were conversations.170.81 GB of System Data, and no ⓘ to look inside.

My MacBook got down to 17 GB free this week. Storage settings had the answer, sort of: System Data, 170.81 GB. Every other row has a little ⓘ you can click to see what’s inside. System Data doesn’t. Photos, for comparison: 20 MB.

I should admit something first: I build a Mac storage app. So the obvious move would be to tell you to buy it. Instead I went looking for the junk myself, the way I’d tell a friend to.

I didn’t find much junk. The three heaviest things on my Mac were a messaging app, an AI app and a code editor, and the biggest of them is the one thing on this machine I’d never want a cleaner to touch.

That changed how I think about cleanup. “System Data” isn’t junk. It’s four kinds of files sharing one grey bar. Some your Mac frees by itself, some rebuild on their own, some come back only if you download them again, and one pile never comes back at all. Size tells you nothing about which is which.

What is System Data on a Mac?

It’s the leftovers bucket. Anything your Mac can’t file under Apps, Documents, Photos and the rest ends up there: temporary files, logs, the search index, app data that doesn’t fit a neat label.

So “is System Data safe to delete?” has no single answer. It’s like asking whether it’s safe to clear out the garage. Mostly, yes. Not the box with the passports.

What I found when I looked

You can see the biggest folders yourself. Open Terminal (it’s in Applications → Utilities), paste this line, and press Return. It only looks; it doesn’t change anything:

du -sh ~/Library/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -8
The biggest folders on my Mac. The top one was WhatsApp.

Here’s what the top of my list turned out to be.

42 GB: WhatsApp. Years of photos, videos and voice notes from my chats, all stored on the Mac.

7.8 GB: one single file in my code editor. It’s where the app keeps its saved state, and as far as I can tell that includes my AI chat history. One file, bigger than a lot of people’s entire photo library.

12 GB: a whole mini computer inside the Claude app. The app keeps a small virtual machine to run code in. Most of it can probably be downloaded again. But one of its files is called “session data”, and I’m not deleting anything with that name until I know what’s in it.

The real junk was smaller and scattered: about 17 GB of leftovers from building apps, temporary files and old downloads, spread across folders most people never open.

Size is the wrong question

Most storage tools start the same way: sort by size and show you the biggest thing first.

On my Mac that puts 42 GB of WhatsApp at the very top. It’s the biggest item by far and the least replaceable. All the real junk put together adds up to less than half of it.

So the useful question isn’t “what’s biggest?” It’s “what happens if this disappears?”

The four piles

Every file on your Mac answers that question in one of four ways.

It frees itself. Your Mac quietly hands this space back when it needs room. You rarely have to do anything.

It rebuilds. Temporary files your Mac can recreate from what’s already there. Delete them and the only cost is a slower first launch.

It downloads again. Safe to delete, but it only comes back over the internet. Fine at home, painful on a slow connection.

It never comes back. Chat photos you haven’t backed up. iPhone backups. That one file in Downloads you’ll need next Tuesday. Nothing recreates these.

Nearly every “a cleaner wrecked my Mac” story I’ve read comes down to pile 3 or pile 4 being treated like pile 2.

What to try first (no app needed)

Look first. System Settings → General → Storage. Click the ⓘ next to each category and see what’s actually there.

Check your chat apps. WhatsApp has its own storage screen: Settings → Storage and Data → Manage Storage. It lists your chats by size, so you can clear old videos from one group without touching the rest. Telegram and Messages have similar settings.

Empty the Trash. It sounds obvious, but files in the Trash still take up space until you empty it.

Old iPhone backups. In Finder, click your iPhone, then Manage Backups. Delete only the ones you’re sure you don’t need.

If you write code, that’s where the easy wins are. Xcode’s build folder (~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData) rebuilds itself, and brew cleanup and npm cache verify deal with old downloads. Mine had about 12 GB here I could clear tonight.

So, is a Mac cleaner worth it?

For most people, no. If the steps above get you comfortable again, stop there.

It’s worth it if you keep running into folders with names you don’t recognise and don’t want to Google them at midnight. Or if deleting things with no undo makes your stomach drop a little.

What it’s never worth: a big “12 GB cleaned!” number with no list behind it, things ticked for you in advance, or a subscription for something you’ll open twice a year.

Why I built one anyway

Because I kept being the person staring at folder names I half recognised, wondering which pile they were in.

Most tools tell you how big something is. I wanted one that tells you what it is and what happens if it’s gone. So I built Clean House. It draws your Mac as a little house you walk through room by room, instead of a wall of red warnings. Every item has a “Why?” that says in plain English what it is and whether it comes back. Nothing is deleted for real: it goes to the Trash, and you can undo it.

It’s a one-time $6.99 at launch ($9.99 after), and the first 5 GB are free.

Clean House shows your Mac as a house, room by room.Before anything moves, every item says whether it rebuilds or downloads again.

If the steps above were enough, you don’t need it, and I mean that. If they weren’t, it’s here.

Quick answers

Is it safe to delete System Data on a Mac?
Not as one block. Some of it frees itself or rebuilds. Backups and chat media don’t come back. Ask what happens if each thing disappears, then decide.

Why does System Data keep growing?
Usually temporary files, the search index, and apps that store a lot locally, like chat and AI apps. Check again after big macOS updates.

Do Macs need a cleaner at all?
Not to stay healthy. macOS has built-in malware protection, and most cleanup is a few steps you can do yourself. A tool helps you see what’s there and gives you an undo. That’s it.

How many GB should System Data be?
There’s no normal number. Apple doesn’t publish one, and it depends on the apps you use. Mine was 170 GB and most of it wasn’t junk. Look closer when it’s bigger than your free space, or keeps growing every week.

Why is my System Data 200 GB?
Usually a few big owners, not thousands of junk files. On my Mac it was WhatsApp (42 GB), a virtual machine inside the Claude app (12 GB) and one Cursor file (7.8 GB). The actual junk was about 17 GB.

What’s the heaviest thing on your Mac? I’m curious how many turn out to be conversations too.

I’m Shiva. I make small, pay-once Mac apps, including Clean House.

items.title: LLM vs. LRM: Which AI Should You Pay For?
items.summary: Have you ever asked an AI a hard question and watched it pause for a long moment before replying? Maybe you saw a little “thinking…” message, and you wondered what on earth was going on in there. That pause is the whole story of large reasoning models , or LRMs. They are one of the biggest shifts in AI in recent years, and the idea behind them is surprisingly human: slow down before you answer. In this post, I’ll explain what LRMs are, how they’re trained, why they cost more, and how to decide when the extra thinking is worth it. First, a quick refresher on LLMs You probably know the basics. A large language model, or LLM, predicts the next token in a sequence. A token is a small chunk of text. Given your prompt, it picks the most likely next token, then the next, then the next, and the result reads like human writing. This works wonderfully for many tasks. Ask for a fun social media post or a friendly email, and that fast, reflex-like response is usually perfect. But now imagine asking something harder: “Debug this messy stack trace.” “Trace money through four different shell companies.” A quick reflex isn’t enough. You’d want someone to pause, test ideas, and double-check their work. So what makes a model a “reasoning” model? An LRM still produces text one token at a time. The difference is what happens before the final answer. Reasoning models are language models that reflect on a problem before generating an answer. They sketch a plan, weigh options, check calculations, and sometimes test ideas along the way. Only then do they write the response you see. Think of a student in a classroom. A reasoning model is like a student who takes time to understand the question, splits it into manageable steps, and details the solution process instead of rushing to write the answer. That internal “chain of thought” lets the model try a hypothesis, drop a dead end, and land on a reasoned answer instead of just following a statistically likely pattern. Here’s a quick comparison: LLM (fast reflex) LRM (thinks first) How it answers Predicts the next words straight away Plans, checks, then answers Best at Writing, summaries, simple Q&A Multi-step logic, math, tricky debugging Speed Fast Slower Cost Lower Higher Prompting May need tricks like “think step by step” Usually needs less prompt coaching How do you teach a model to think? This part fascinated me. It happens in stages. Stage 1: Pre-training, learning about the world An LRM usually starts as an existing LLM. In pre-training, it reads billions of web pages, books, and code repositories. That gives it language skills and broad knowledge, like a student who has read a very big library. Stage 2: Reasoning-focused tuning, learning to show its work Next comes specialized training. The model is shown curated problems, such as logic puzzles, multi-step math, and tricky coding tasks, along with full step-by-step solutions. It learns a pattern: take the problem, make a plan, carry out the steps, and reach a solution. It’s learning to show its work. Stage 3: Reinforcement learning, learning from feedback Then the model is let loose on fresh problems of its own, and it learns through reinforcement learning , which is basically trial and error with rewards. The rewards can come from several places: Human feedback, where people rate steps up or down (this is called RLHF). Process reward models, smaller models that judge whether each step of a reasoning chain is good or bad. Checkable outcomes, such as whether a math answer is right or whether code passes tests. That last one is important. The research behind DeepSeek-R1 found something remarkable. DeepSeek-R1 uses large-scale reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, and DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with reinforcement learning directly from a base model, with no supervised warm start. In other words, useful reasoning habits like reflecting and trying alternatives can emerge from rewards alone. As that training progresses, the model generates more tokens, which means more “thinking time,” and behaviors such as reflection and exploring alternative approaches appear. Other methods: distillation There’s another popular technique called distillation. A large “teacher” model solves problems and writes out its reasoning. Then a smaller or newer model is trained on those reasoning traces. If the teacher can think through a puzzle, that path becomes training material for the student. It works well. Distilled models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B maintain strong performance on reasoning benchmarks. One note of caution: researchers have found that small models sometimes copy the look of long reasoning without truly understanding it, which can lead to overthinking. So distillation helps, but it isn’t magic. The result of all this training is a model that can plan, verify, and explain. And that finally makes it possible to untangle those shell-company cash flows. Thinking time: how long should the model think? Training is only half the picture. The other half is inference time , sometimes called test-time compute. That’s what happens each time you ask a question. Different questions can get different amounts of thinking: “Debug my stack trace” might get a large thinking budget. “Write a nice caption” gets a quick pass. During longer thinking, a model may do several things: Run multiple chains of thought and vote on the best one. Backtrack with a search when it hits a dead end. Call outside tools, like a calculator, a database, or a code sandbox, for spot checks. This idea is more important than it first seems. A key insight from OpenAI’s o1 was that performance improved as test-time compute increased, which simply means the more tokens a model generates, the better its response tends to be. It changed how people think about progress. Instead of only making models bigger, you can also let them think longer. The price of thinking I want to be honest about the downside, because it’s real. Every extra pass, self-check, or search branch costs: More compute, which means more GPU time, memory, and energy. Higher bills, since you pay for those extra tokens. More waiting, because replies come slower. So the question becomes: is the boost in accuracy worth the cost? It depends on the problem. For a hard bug that has cost you hours, a minute of thinking is a bargain. For a quick social post, it’s wasted money and time. The pros and cons, side by side What LRMs do well Complex reasoning. They shine on multi-step logic, planning, and abstract problems. Better decisions. Because they can verify and deliberate internally, answers tend to be more nuanced and often more accurate. Less prompt hackery. You don’t need magic phrases like “let’s think step by step,” because the model already does it. Where they struggle Higher cost. More VRAM, more energy, and a bigger cloud invoice. Higher latency. Slower replies while the model works things through. Overkill for simple tasks. A regular LLM or a smaller model can be the better choice. There’s a small joy in all this, too. Reading a model’s thinking steps as it works can be oddly entertaining, a little like watching someone solve a puzzle out loud. Not everyone feels that way, but I do. A simple way to choose If you’re unsure which to use, try this quick guide: Is the task simple or creative? Writing, summarizing, rephrasing, brainstorming: use a regular LLM. Does it need several steps of logic? Math, planning, tricky code, analysis: try an LRM. Is speed more important than depth? Start with a faster model, and escalate only if it fails. Is cost a concern at scale? Use reasoning models only where accuracy really pays off. Can you check the answer easily? If yes, a cheaper model with a retry may be enough. A good habit is to match the effort to the stakes. You wouldn’t call a specialist for a paper cut, and you wouldn’t skip one for something serious. A small caution about “reading the thinking” It’s tempting to treat the visible reasoning as a perfect window into the model’s mind. It’s helpful, but be a little careful. The displayed steps can be a useful guide, yet they aren’t always a flawless explanation of how the model reached its answer. Use them as clues, and still verify important results yourself. AI models used to just spill out words as fast as they could predict them. Now many of them stop to think, and the most capable models on many benchmarks tend to be the reasoning ones. That doesn’t mean thinking is always better. It means we have a new choice: speed or depth, cheap or careful. The best builders and users will be the ones who know when to pick each. So next time you see that pause before an answer, you’ll know what’s happening. Somewhere in there, a model is making a plan, weighing options, and double-checking its work. Isn’t that a little bit wonderful? Have you ever asked an AI a hard question and watched it pause for a long moment before replying? Maybe you saw a little “thinking…” message, and you wondered what on earth was going on in there.

That pause is the whole story of large reasoning models, or LRMs. They are one of the biggest shifts in AI in recent years, and the idea behind them is surprisingly human: slow down before you answer.

In this post, I’ll explain what LRMs are, how they’re trained, why they cost more, and how to decide when the extra thinking is worth it.

First, a quick refresher on LLMs

You probably know the basics. A large language model, or LLM, predicts the next token in a sequence. A token is a small chunk of text. Given your prompt, it picks the most likely next token, then the next, then the next, and the result reads like human writing.

This works wonderfully for many tasks. Ask for a fun social media post or a friendly email, and that fast, reflex-like response is usually perfect.

But now imagine asking something harder:

  • “Debug this messy stack trace.”
  • “Trace money through four different shell companies.”

A quick reflex isn’t enough. You’d want someone to pause, test ideas, and double-check their work.

So what makes a model a “reasoning” model?

An LRM still produces text one token at a time. The difference is what happens before the final answer. Reasoning models are language models that reflect on a problem before generating an answer. They sketch a plan, weigh options, check calculations, and sometimes test ideas along the way. Only then do they write the response you see.

Think of a student in a classroom. A reasoning model is like a student who takes time to understand the question, splits it into manageable steps, and details the solution process instead of rushing to write the answer.

That internal “chain of thought” lets the model try a hypothesis, drop a dead end, and land on a reasoned answer instead of just following a statistically likely pattern.

Here’s a quick comparison:

LLM (fast reflex) LRM (thinks first) How it answers Predicts the next words straight away Plans, checks, then answers Best at Writing, summaries, simple Q&A Multi-step logic, math, tricky debugging Speed Fast Slower Cost Lower Higher Prompting May need tricks like “think step by step” Usually needs less prompt coaching

How do you teach a model to think?

This part fascinated me. It happens in stages.

Stage 1: Pre-training, learning about the world

An LRM usually starts as an existing LLM. In pre-training, it reads billions of web pages, books, and code repositories. That gives it language skills and broad knowledge, like a student who has read a very big library.

Stage 2: Reasoning-focused tuning, learning to show its work

Next comes specialized training. The model is shown curated problems, such as logic puzzles, multi-step math, and tricky coding tasks, along with full step-by-step solutions. It learns a pattern: take the problem, make a plan, carry out the steps, and reach a solution. It’s learning to show its work.

Stage 3: Reinforcement learning, learning from feedback

Then the model is let loose on fresh problems of its own, and it learns through reinforcement learning, which is basically trial and error with rewards. The rewards can come from several places:

  • Human feedback, where people rate steps up or down (this is called RLHF).
  • Process reward models, smaller models that judge whether each step of a reasoning chain is good or bad.
  • Checkable outcomes, such as whether a math answer is right or whether code passes tests.

That last one is important. The research behind DeepSeek-R1 found something remarkable. DeepSeek-R1 uses large-scale reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, and DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with reinforcement learning directly from a base model, with no supervised warm start. In other words, useful reasoning habits like reflecting and trying alternatives can emerge from rewards alone. As that training progresses, the model generates more tokens, which means more “thinking time,” and behaviors such as reflection and exploring alternative approaches appear.

Other methods: distillation

There’s another popular technique called distillation. A large “teacher” model solves problems and writes out its reasoning. Then a smaller or newer model is trained on those reasoning traces. If the teacher can think through a puzzle, that path becomes training material for the student.

It works well. Distilled models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B maintain strong performance on reasoning benchmarks. One note of caution: researchers have found that small models sometimes copy the look of long reasoning without truly understanding it, which can lead to overthinking. So distillation helps, but it isn’t magic.

The result of all this training is a model that can plan, verify, and explain. And that finally makes it possible to untangle those shell-company cash flows.

Thinking time: how long should the model think?

Training is only half the picture. The other half is inference time, sometimes called test-time compute. That’s what happens each time you ask a question.

Different questions can get different amounts of thinking:

  • “Debug my stack trace” might get a large thinking budget.
  • “Write a nice caption” gets a quick pass.

During longer thinking, a model may do several things:

  • Run multiple chains of thought and vote on the best one.
  • Backtrack with a search when it hits a dead end.
  • Call outside tools, like a calculator, a database, or a code sandbox, for spot checks.

This idea is more important than it first seems. A key insight from OpenAI’s o1 was that performance improved as test-time compute increased, which simply means the more tokens a model generates, the better its response tends to be. It changed how people think about progress. Instead of only making models bigger, you can also let them think longer.

The price of thinking

I want to be honest about the downside, because it’s real. Every extra pass, self-check, or search branch costs:

  • More compute, which means more GPU time, memory, and energy.
  • Higher bills, since you pay for those extra tokens.
  • More waiting, because replies come slower.

So the question becomes: is the boost in accuracy worth the cost? It depends on the problem. For a hard bug that has cost you hours, a minute of thinking is a bargain. For a quick social post, it’s wasted money and time.

The pros and cons, side by side

What LRMs do well

  • Complex reasoning. They shine on multi-step logic, planning, and abstract problems.
  • Better decisions. Because they can verify and deliberate internally, answers tend to be more nuanced and often more accurate.
  • Less prompt hackery. You don’t need magic phrases like “let’s think step by step,” because the model already does it.

Where they struggle

  • Higher cost. More VRAM, more energy, and a bigger cloud invoice.
  • Higher latency. Slower replies while the model works things through.
  • Overkill for simple tasks. A regular LLM or a smaller model can be the better choice.

There’s a small joy in all this, too. Reading a model’s thinking steps as it works can be oddly entertaining, a little like watching someone solve a puzzle out loud. Not everyone feels that way, but I do.

A simple way to choose

If you’re unsure which to use, try this quick guide:

  1. Is the task simple or creative? Writing, summarizing, rephrasing, brainstorming: use a regular LLM.
  2. Does it need several steps of logic? Math, planning, tricky code, analysis: try an LRM.
  3. Is speed more important than depth? Start with a faster model, and escalate only if it fails.
  4. Is cost a concern at scale? Use reasoning models only where accuracy really pays off.
  5. Can you check the answer easily? If yes, a cheaper model with a retry may be enough.

A good habit is to match the effort to the stakes. You wouldn’t call a specialist for a paper cut, and you wouldn’t skip one for something serious.

A small caution about “reading the thinking”

It’s tempting to treat the visible reasoning as a perfect window into the model’s mind. It’s helpful, but be a little careful. The displayed steps can be a useful guide, yet they aren’t always a flawless explanation of how the model reached its answer. Use them as clues, and still verify important results yourself.

AI models used to just spill out words as fast as they could predict them. Now many of them stop to think, and the most capable models on many benchmarks tend to be the reasoning ones.

That doesn’t mean thinking is always better. It means we have a new choice: speed or depth, cheap or careful. The best builders and users will be the ones who know when to pick each.

So next time you see that pause before an answer, you’ll know what’s happening. Somewhere in there, a model is making a plan, weighing options, and double-checking its work. Isn’t that a little bit wonderful?

items.title: vistributions 0.2.2
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on Rsquared Academy Blog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

vistributions 0.2.2

vistributions draws the probability and percentile questions you ask of the normal, t, chi-square, F and binomial distributions, with the answer printed on the plot.

Version 0.2.2 is a correctness release. What the plot shades and what its caption prints now agree with the exact probability, and inputs that cannot describe an event stop with a clear message. If you use the binomial functions to size an event, read the first section.

Install from CRAN
Code 
install.packages("vistributions")

The full list of changes is in the release notes.

Shading follows the event

A trial cohort has 40 users, and about 25% of trial users usually upgrade. How likely is it that exactly 10 of them upgrade?

Code 
vdist_binom_prob(n = 40, p = 0.25, s = 10, type = "exact")

The exact value, from base R:

Code 
dbinom(10, size = 40, prob = 0.25)
[1] 0.1443643

The caption and the shaded bar match this value. The change matters most for large n, where bars are grouped. A grouped bar that crossed the cutoff was painted whole: for n = 10000, p = 0.01 and s = 100, the shaded area was 19.26% for an event whose exact probability is 4.01% (release notes). Every event cutoff is now a bar edge, so the shaded bar heights add up to dbinom() or pbinom() for the event.

Inputs that cannot be an event

A count of successes has to lie between 0 and the number of trials. Asking for a negative count used to be accepted, with the caption P(X) <= -1 = 0. It now gives the same clear error as a count above n:

Code 
tryCatch(
  vdist_binom_prob(n = 10, p = 0.3, s = -1, type = "lower"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
[1] "s must be a whole number of successes between 0 and n (n = 10)."

The same release adds checks for the other families, for example whole-number arguments for the binomial and a documented range for percentile probabilities (1e-12 < probs < 1 - 1e-12).

Percentiles under a decimal comma

Delivery times are about 48 hours on average, with a standard deviation of 6 hours. By what time have 95% of orders arrived?

With options(OutDec = ","), which is common in European locales, every percentile and probability export used to fail with NAs introduced by coercion. The decimal mark is now fixed to . wherever numbers are printed and parsed back:

Code 
old <- options(OutDec = ",")
vdist_normal_perc(probs = 0.95, mean = 48, sd = 6, type = "lower")

Code 
options(old)
Code 
qnorm(0.95, mean = 48, sd = 6)
[1] 57.86912
Other improvements
  • Continuous percentile probabilities and the normal scale have documented limits, and every limit stops with its own message.
  • Captions print enough digits for the percentage they show, including probabilities below 0.1%.
  • Binomial captions put the inequality inside P(), for example P(X >= 4), and round once from the exact probability.
  • vdist_t_*(), vdist_chisquare_*() and vdist_f_*() no longer truncate non-integer degrees of freedom.
  • Plot grids have a bounded number of points, however large the scale.

The release notes carry the rest.

Documentation

Documentation and examples for every function are at vistributions.rsquaredacademy.com. Report problems at github.com/rsquaredacademy/vistributions/issues.

items.title: rOpenSci News Digest, November 2026
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on rOpenSci - open tools for open science, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Dear rOpenSci friends, it’s time for our monthly news roundup! You can read this post on our blog. Now let’s dive into the activity at and around rOpenSci!

rOpenSci HQ New release: rOpenSci Champions Program Mentor Guidelines

We’ve released a new version of our guide for mentors in our Champions Program. It includes useful content such how to organize a meeting with one’s mentee, and resources about mentoring skills. Check it out!

Editorial board updates Welcome Francisco!

Francisco Rodriguez-Sanchez joined as a guest editor back in 2023 and has now handled two approved packages. He’s now a full member of the editorial board. Thank you and welcome!

Thanks Jeff and Emi!

Jeff Hollister and Emi Tanaka are stepping off the editorial board. Since 2021 Jeff has handled seven approved packages and served twice as the Editor-in-Chief. Emi joined the editorial board in 2023 and has handled two approved packages. Thank you both and all the best in your next adventures!

Quinceañera

We continue to uncover the stories of the people behind rOpenSci. This month, you can read about:

  • Carolina Pradier, rOpenSci Champion and mentor,
  • Athanasia Mo Mowinckel, rOpenSci mentor (and more),
  • Adam Sparks, editor and package maintainer.

Stay tuned for more rOpenSci stories.

Coworking

Read all about coworking!

  • Tuesday December 8th*, 14:00 Europe Central (13:00 UTC) “Code Linting in R”, with Steffi LaZerte and co-host Etienne Bacher.
    • Read up on Code Linting and apply some linters to your R code
    • Meet co-host, Etienne Bacher, and discuss code linting in general, or flir and Jarl in particular
      * Note that December coworking is a week later than usual
  • Tuesday January 19th, 2027 17:00 (UTC) “Getting to know PREreview”, with Steffi LaZerte and co-hosts Vanessa Fairhurst and Daniela Saderi.
    • Visit PREreview
    • Meet co-hosts, Vanessa Fairhurst and Daniela Saderi, and learn more about PREreview and how you might get involved

And remember, you can always cowork independently on work related to R, work on packages that tend to be neglected, or work on what ever you need to get done!

R Project Sprint 2027, 3 days in week of Apr 12, Boston | Virtual

Join this collaborative event to work on contributions to the code and documentation of base R, or to infrastructure that supports such contributions. Travel funding is available for this event. Limited places are available for novice and experienced contributors to participate in person or online. Applications open now: https://contributor.r-project.org/r-project-sprint-2027 Deadline: Friday 4 December (midnight Anywhere on Earth)

Software

The following two packages recently became a part of our software suite:

  • nert, developed by Sam Rogers together with Adam H. Sparks, Wasin Pipattungsakul, Russell Edson, and Max Moldovan: Provides curated access to raster environmental data published by Australia’s Terrestrial Ecosystem Research Network (TERN; https://www.tern.org.au/), spanning national soil attribute, soil classification, soil biodiversity, soil moisture, actual evapotranspiration, vegetation canopy height and phenology products. The package reads Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF (COG) and virtual raster files directly from the TERN data server via Geospatial Data Abstraction Library (GDAL) vsicurl virtual file system range requests, streaming only the requested spatial and temporal subset for efficient data transfer. The environmental raster data are returned as terra SpatRaster objects. A convenient helper function is also provided that provides a batch-download capability given specific locations and dates, returning the extracted data values in an analysis-ready data.table. Access to the TERN datasets using this package requires a free TERN API key. It has been reviewed by Michael Sumner and Shandiya Balasubramaniam.

  • camtrapReport, developed by Elham Ebrahimi: Provides an extensible workflow for processing camera-trap data in the Camtrap DP format and automatically generating reproducible data-status and ecological reports in HTML or PDF format. The package supports data-quality checks, ecological summaries, visualisations, maps, tables and modular report sections for wildlife-monitoring applications. Optional taxonomic enrichment queries the Global Biodiversity Information Facility Species API https://techdocs.gbif.org/en/openapi/v1/species through taxize. Browser-based map backgrounds use OpenStreetMap https://www.openstreetmap.org, OSM Germany https://openstreetmap.de/germanstyle/ and OpenTopoMap https://opentopomap.org, subject to their usage terms. It has been reviewed by Florian Mayer and Catherine Sun.

Discover more packages, read more about Software Peer Review.

New versions

The following twenty-two packages have had an update since the last newsletter: nlrx (v0.5.0), cffr (v1.4.3), parzer (v0.6.0), nuts (v1.3.0), ghql (v0.1.3), tarchetypes (0.14.2), targets (1.12.1), nert (v2.1.0), coevolve (v1.3.0), srr (v1.1.0), lingtypology (v1.1.27), dittodb (v0.1.12), BaseSet (v1.0.1), dbparser (v2.3.0), dataspice (v1.2.1), naijR (v0.7.1), EpiStrainDynamics (v0.2.0), opencage (v0.3.0), galamm (v0.4.2), frictionless (v2.0.1), DataSpaceR (v1.0.3), and lakefetch (v0.1.14).

Software Peer Review

There are fourteen recently closed and active submissions and 6 submissions on hold. Issues are at different stages:

  • Two at ‘6/approved’:

    • camtrapReport, Camera-Trap Report Generator. Submitted by Elham Ebrahimi.

    • nert, Curated Access to TERN Environmental Raster Data. Submitted by Max Moldovan.

  • One at ‘5/awaiting-reviewer(s)-response’:

    • RAQSAPI, A Simple Interface to the US EPA Air Quality System Data Mart API. Submitted by mccroweyclinton-EPA.

  • One at ‘4/review(s)-in-awaiting-changes’:

    • grumpy, Read NumPy .npy and .npz Files. Submitted by Hugo Gruson.

  • Six at ‘3/reviewer(s)-assigned’:

    • GeneExprLupusMx, Lupus RNA-Seq Data from Mexican Women with Bilingual Lessons. Submitted by Evelia Lorena Coss-Navarrete.

    • emodnet.wcs, Access EMODnet Web Coverage Service data through R. Submitted by Maëlle Salmon.

    • corila, Sparse modelling with grouped and correlated features allowing for privileged information. Submitted by Armin Rauschenberger. (Stats).

    • qualtdict, Generate Variable Dictionaries and Labelled Survey Data for Qualtrics Surveys. Submitted by lyh970817.

    • metasurvey.core, Local Engine for Reproducible Survey Data Processing. Submitted by Mauro Loprete.

    • tezr, Access Thesis Metadata from Turkiye’s National Thesis Center. Submitted by Emrah Er.

  • Two at ‘2/seeking-reviewer(s)’:

    • dyadicMarkov, Pattern Estimation and Identification for Dyadic Sequences Using Transition Matrices in R. Submitted by Mattia Böllenrücher. (Stats).

    • tarpolyglot, Run Python, Julia, Rust, and C++ Inside targets Pipeline Steps. Submitted by Pierre9344.

  • Two at ‘1/editor-checks’:

    • seasight, Tools for Seasonal Adjustment Diagnostics and Reporting. Submitted by Philipp Wegmueller. (Stats).

    • OptSurvCutR, Optimal Survival Cut-Point Discovery for Time-to-Event Analysis with OptSurvCutR. Submitted by Payton Yau. (Stats).

Find out more about Software Peer Review and how to get involved.

On the blog

  • Kindness, Curiosity, and Kitties: A rOpenSci 15th Anniversary Interview with Mo by Yanina Bellini Saibene. As part of rOpenSci’s 15th anniversary, Community Manager Yani talks with Mo about her journey from a first software review to years of contributions across the rOpenSci community. Mo shares what keeps her involved and offers advice for newcomers.

  • From Brisbane to the rOpenSci Community: Ten Years of Open Research Software by Adam Sparks. A look back at ten years of involvement with rOpenSci, from attending a Unconf to package development, peer review, editorial work, and building open science communities. Through stories of collaboration, learning, and lasting friendships, the post highlights how welcoming communities can shape careers and make open research software stronger. .

  • Splitting Large Queries to Brazil’s Official Statistics API with ibger by André Leite, Marcos Wasiliew, Hugo Vasconcelos, Carlos Amorim, and Diogo Bezerra. How ibger estimates result sizes and splits large IBGE API queries automatically.

  • Carolina Pradier, rOpenSci champion and mentor by Yanina Bellini Saibene and Alejandra Bellini. This story is that of Carolina Pradier, main maintainer of the eph package. We review her participation in the Champions program and the impact of her work in different organizations and communities.

  • Making the incidental an invitation in building community by Mara Averick, Hadley Wickham, Mark Padgham, Yanina Bellini Saibene, Julia Stewart Lowndes, Stefanie Butland, and Andy Teucher. Blog post summarizing Openscapes Community Call Open Communities in the age of AI.

  • Hacking Two Hours of Contributions to R by Yanina Bellini Saibene. What we did during HackeaR, a LatinR event where we got together to make contributions to our favorite programming language. Other languages: Hackeando dos horas de contribuciones a R (es).

Calls for contributions

Refer to our help wanted page – before opening a PR, we recommend asking in the issue whether help is still needed.

Package development corner

Some useful information for R package developers.

Coverage on GitHub Actions without codecov

How to get coverage information displayed without codecov? A roundup of current efforts:

  • Earlier this year, Adam Sparks wrote up his strategy for generating a README badge displaying test coverage, without using a third party such as codecov.io.
  • The covr2gh package by Dragoș Moldovan-Grünfeld provides an automated way to summarise the impact of a pull request (PR) on test coverage directly within GitHub.
  • The development version of covr gained a to_badge() function to create an svg badge of coverage.
  • Elio Campitelli added a GitHub Actions workflow and script to create a coverage report for a package.
AI as Forklift: Andrew Heiss’ R + AI 2026 keynote

Andrew Heiss published a write up of his talk Friction Worth Keeping: What Keeps Us Human When AI Makes Everything Easy, including a useful extension of the AI/forklift analogy. You can also watch the recording.

LLMs as last resort

Bastián Olea Herrera shared a post by Ben Harrap: “Limited Learning Mode: Why LLMs are my last resort”. One of the reasons is “People like to help”!

Last words

Thanks for reading! If you want to get involved with rOpenSci, check out our Contributing Guide. This guide will help direct you to the right place, whether you want to make code contributions, non-code contributions, or contribute in other ways such as through sharing use cases. You can also support our work through donations.

If you haven’t subscribed to our newsletter yet, you can do so through our signup form. Until it’s time for our next newsletter, you can keep in touch with us through our website, Mastodon, or LinkedIn. See you soon!
